author: AfricanFeminism
title: Naming the Violence: FGM Survivors Take Their Fight for Justice Online
content:
I was just 17 years old, in a WhatsApp group with peers discussing sexual and gender-based violence when I first heard that Female Genital Mutilation (FGM) was violence. I remember being agitated by the turn the discussion took. Though much of that conversation is murky now, I remember repeating the same lines: ‘

FGM is culture; if we can advocate for abortion, then surely we could allow others to practise their culture in peace

’. A colleague then insinuated that such statements were why more girls and women were being harmed – that I was, in fact, supporting violence against women and girls.


Teenage me had just started her activism journey, but carried the authority of someone who thought she knew it all. For her, FGM was a normal part of existence. My mother, aunties, cousins and almost every woman I knew had gone through it. I had heard stories of older women travelling for days to be cut. Being cut was an honour. Families paid the woman who performed the cutting. There was no way, teenage me would think, that love and violence could coexist. So being called a perpetrator on that platform did not sit well with her.


I left pressed to prove someone wrong. I decided to learn more about FGM, hoping to win the next argument. I dove into its history, beyond what I had absorbed socially.


Why were women cut? How had it become part of our history? As I travelled from one district to another, I heard stories about female chiefs, hints from the Sunnah, and other explanations. Whatever argument I would make next had to be concise. It had to convince others – and, by this point, myself – that FGM was not violence. 


But the more I learned and met the women in different locations, the more my need to prove a point faded. The research kept returning me to the same message: FGM is violence. Teenage me found stories of women discovering they had been cut as children. Older sisters fighting to protect younger sisters. Communities and countries organising against the practice. Women whose genitalia had been sewn together until marriage. Girls being forced into marriages, with FGM part of a much larger system of control over their bodies and futures.


And somewhere in that search, she had to confront a question she had never thought to ask: what if something could be culture and still be violent? The more she learnt, the more she was shattered by the harm done to her own body, and to the bodies of millions of girls before her. 


A woman during a march against FGM in Sierra Leone. Photo by

Massah Brockarie.


 


Facing the fear of naming as a survivor


FGM was the first issue I was ever truly scared to write about. There have always been stories of women being kidnapped, physically assaulted, and even killed for advocating against FGM. And the women who sold dresses, the men who sponsored the cutting, these were people I had loved and admired all my life. Talking negatively about a practice they held dear felt like a betrayal of their trust. And, to be honest, I also thought ”I am okay for now. So, what I experienced was not great harm, right?”


Then one day, on a trip travelling back from Waterloo, eastern…Sierra Leone, I saw girls as young as six walking along the streets. Something shifted in me. Suddenly, this was no longer a debate about culture, history or what I had been taught to believe. These were children. Girls who, like me, had yet to understand the lifelong implications of what could be done to their bodies. If I remained silent, this violence would continue to be meted out upon young girls and women across the country. 


I went straight to Facebook and wrote, “

I’m a cut woman; I once believed that this was an African thing. It never was”, and there I named

t the

harm that FGM is.

 I was surprised by how many people agreed with me. Of course, some people told me to stop. Was it the first time to publicly say that? And really, to look at this as a personal experience that connected to millions of other girls and women, and it needed to be named. Not faceless statistics. 


Since then, I have kept writing. I kept sharing my

 story

 and other advocacy work across social media platforms. The first post opened a conversation with my cousin, who had also been cut. We talked about the harm and absurdity of it and promised that our daughters, if we had them, would not be subjected to the same harm.


The bravery to speak about FGM online, and the conversations it sparked, has stayed with me, and it has …

author: Mzi Velapi
title: Memorial service held for victims of the Strand mass shooting
content:
In the early hours of Sunday morning, 27 September, gunmen opened fire on patrons at a shisanyama in Lwandle, near Cape Town, killing ten people. “Five individuals died on the scene while five others succumbed to injuries sustained after being transported to medical facilities. Eleven others are receiving medical treatment for injuries sustained. Lwandle police have opened murder and attempted murder cases,” said the police. The community believes the mass shooting is related to the extortion racket that is ravaging Cape Town townships.


One of the victims, Khululekani Ndlovu, will be laid to rest this weekend. The nine other people killed will be buried next weekend in the Eastern Cape. The Nomzamo Community Hall in Strand, south east of Cape Town, was packed with mourners and members of political parties for the memorial service.


Speaking to

Elitsha

, the chairperson of the police board in South Africa, Francina Lukas, said that extortion and business rivalry and lack of opportunities for young people are some of the factors contributing to high crime rates in the townships of Cape Town. She said that the lack of trust the community has in the police contributes to high crime rate.


“The police need to do much more than what they are doing in terms of compliance to make sure that businesses in the township comply with their licenses and bylaws. But the issue of trust is still a burning issue in our communities. So we need to overcome that issue to see that trust in the police is restored,” she said.


Families of the Strand 10


Speaking on behalf of the Sikweza family who lost their daughter, Avuyile, her uncle, Luyanda Macokeni, said she had plans to return to school next year. The 20-year-old passed her matric in 2024. She applied to continue her education next year and had just received responses from two universities offering her a place to study. She was expected to make a choice between the two. “Avuyile is supposed to the one burying us as elders but we are the ones burying her. It’s not God’s will that we are here today, it is because of someone’s will,” he said.


Siyathemba Jilaji was one of the victims who died on his way to the hospital, according to his friend. “He said he was going to change in the car so when the shooting began, I thought he was still in the car. A bullet grazed me under my arm. After the shooting, I went to the car to check for him. But, I didn’t know that he was amongst the bodies that were lying next to the entrance that I ran past,” she said.


Sivenathi Manxiwa’s father, Lubabalo Ndamane, said that he is not going to forgive the person who murdered his son. “I also don’t want to know who they are. Even if they can be arrested, I would not go to court. I leave everything to God and God will deal with him. I want to know what drove him to shoot at the young people who were out enjoying themselves,” he said.


The 10 people who died during the mass shooting in Strand last weekend

.

Photo from Facebook

.


The police said that the investigation into the mass murder is still ongoing.

author: ROAPE
title: What is the Real Marxist Tradition in Africa?
content:
John Molyneux’s classic statement of Marxist theory and practice

What is the Real Marxist Tradition

? was first published in 1984. The short book provided an incredibly sophisticated description of Marx’s method, and his relentless and insistent focus on the core agency of the working class.


Only the working class – however it is interpreted, described or labelled in social theory – can deliver a revolutionary anti-capitalist project. There cannot be, Molyneux argued, any substitute – no enlightened project of state development, or ‘socialist’ military leadership who deliver socialism on behalf of working people. Molyneux – in restating Marx’s central tenet – emphasised the role of the working class in their self-emancipation. Marx was the original prophet of the self-emancipation by working people. Without this class, and this project, there is simply no Marxism, no socialism, and no possibility of international revolution.


For an African audience the book speaks to multiple failed projects of socialism delivered by military coups, ‘enlightened’ governments and guerrilla movements. Each of these movements at different times dressed themselves in the language of Marxism, class and anti-imperialism but systematically broke genuine efforts at working class power.


What is the Real Marxist Tradition

? speaks directly to those on the continent trying to find a way to a genuine and emancipatory theory and practice of liberation.


Molyneux’ brilliant short book has now been reissued by the UK based publisher Bookmarks, and the Ugandan publisher Editor House Facility (EHF) who focus on readers across the African continent.


The new issue of the book comes with a major new introduction by the Ghanian socialist Gyekye Tanoh. Tanoh writes about the development and transformation of the working class on the continent since Molyneux wrote the book, and the continued capacity of this class to bring about socialist and revolutionary transformation across Africa.  


Join us for the launch of the African edition of

What is the Real Marxist Tradition?

 on 22 October at 18.30 (BST) with Gyekye Tanoh, Tafadzwa Choto

, 

Martin Empson and Mark Thomas. Reserve your place 

here

.


For readers based in Africa, John Molyneux’s 

What is the Real Marxist Tradition?

 can be purchased through Editor House Facility


here

. 


Endorsements of the book:


‘John Molyneux cuts through a century of distortion to recover Marxism’s authentic, revolutionary essence. This classic work distinguishes between living theory and dead orthodoxy, showing that Marxism is not a relic of the past but a vital method for understanding and transforming the world. It is essential reading for anyone seeking to understand capitalism and how to change it. For young activists and students alike, it is a must-read as it offers a powerful weapon for today’s struggles.’ 


Tafadzwa Choto

, International Socialist Organisation, Zimbabwe


‘In this book, John Molyneux undertakes a principled exercise by applying Marxism as a “method of analysis” to Marxism itself. He thereby provides not just a description of what Marxism is, but a method for detecting what isn’t. His application of this exercise—in the form of an autopsy of the interests and classes represented by three self-proclaimed Marxist tendencies—provides a valuable model for defining Marxist politics and organizations in our own contexts while enabling us to avoid the “hybrid ideologies of the petty bourgeoisie.” This is crucial, for us in the Global South, where reality differs greatly from that of Europe, thereby demanding a Marxism of contextualized design, not rigid imitation. The method offered is therefore a vital tool in enabling Marxist projects capable of fulfilling its role in “guiding revolutions to victory.” Such is true whether in the Global South or in global contexts marked by increasing economic complications and the co-option of Marxism by bourgeois ideologies fighting for survival amid the clear failure of neoliberal models … One need not agree with all of Molyneux’s conclusions to find his method a timely and indispensable resource.’


Muzan Alneel

,Marxist researcher and writer from Sudan

What is the Real Marxist Tradition in Africa?

author: Caleb Okereke
title: Matthew Blaise wants to be your friend and neighbor
content:
Matthew Blaise and I must have been in our mid teens when we first met. I don’t remember the exact year, but I remember that it was on Facebook. It did not take long for that online connection to become a real friendship, and it is one that has persisted despite life carrying us in different directions.   


When we sit down for this conversation in September, I am in Philadelphia and Matthew is in Brazil. He is preparing for

Friends and Neighbors

, a new art and literary festival in Lagos built around a deceptively simple question: What responsibility do we have to the people we call our friends and our neighbors?


It is a question that makes our own friendship an interesting place from which to begin. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 


Caleb:

 Something I find provocative about the title “Friends and Neighbors” is that you also seem to be making a statement about the ways queerness shows up in the ordinary. I’m thinking about this song, “Your driver could be LGBT, your friend could be LGBT, your neighbour could be LGBT.” Was that part of the conceptual framing?


Matthew:

 Actually, that’s another way to see it. When I thought of this concept, I thought of proximity within our community. A trip from Lagos to Europe is cheaper than a trip from Lagos to Abidjan, which is a neighboring country. For me, that’s a metaphor for what a lot of friendship within the African continent, especially around queerness, has been due to bad policy, homophobia and criminalization.


Queer people within Africa are not so familiar with themselves. And in that sense, we really haven’t constructed what queer Africanness is because we are still not so close to ourselves. But I find it interesting that you also see it from the point of everyday life, where people you come in contact with could be of this community or could possess these identities without you knowing.


Caleb:

 That’s what immediately came to my attention. Even when you say, “Hello, friends. Hello, neighbors,” you’re talking to all of us, right? It’s not “queer friends and neighbors.” The implicit read is that even if you’re straight, queer people are all around you. They’re your friends. They’re your neighbors. They might not tell you that they’re queer, but they’re there.


Matthew:

 From the perspective of bell hooks, societies should be built on love and friendship. This very important foundation of love has been taken away from queer people, or we’ve not been given that due to our queerness. Governmental policies and criminalization also make us live our lives in isolation. What it means to be friends right now is also very transactional, especially for queer people.


Caleb:

 One thing that has defined our friendship, at least for me, is honesty. There are things I can tell you that I can’t tell anybody else, obviously, so a sort of radical honesty. And as you were talking about transactional relationships, it made me think, what is the place of honesty in friendship, especially in a context where being honest about yourself can carry consequences?


Matthew:

 I think you don’t owe everyone that truth about yourself. For those who I truly trust, I owe them that responsibility of truth. And I do believe, for every friendship, there has to be that investment in honesty.


Caleb:

 But friendship in and of itself is a risk. I don’t think we realize that, but every friendship is a risk.


Matthew:

 Yeah, friendship sometimes, I mean, it’s not a constant state of feeling a certain way. It’s a roller coaster of emotions. It’s a journey. It’s an adventure. So you encounter a lot of things on the way.


You stretch your hand to someone and they actually bite your hand, then you know they are not really having that good intention towards you. So you can decide to stretch your hand again or push them away. But for me, I think it’s important that we’re able to stretch our hands and bring people together and do the work of educating them until we just know they’re irredeemable.


Caleb:

 Yeah…


Matthew:

 What responsibility do you think you owe me as your friend?


Caleb:

 You are now the one asking me questions. But no, I mean, I think you owe your friend loyalty. That’s one of the things that I’m non-negotiable on. I mean, there are many other things you owe your friend.


Matthew:

 You owe them honesty also?


Caleb:

 You owe them honesty. You also owe your friends grace. I give grace a lot. Maybe it’s not even grace. I’m also like, oh …

author: WoMin
title: Women on the frontlines: Organise, Educate, Liberate, Celebrate!
content:
Across social justice movements, both in the Present and in the Past, education has been a central piece binding theory and praxis. It is from this understanding that, from the 17

th

 to the 18

th

 of September, the

Afro-International Feminist Organising School (AFRO-IFOS),

 a movement building space that uses popular education to strengthen our collective knowledge, share our experiences, and grow our international movement, hosted a School of Facilitators in Nairobi, Kenya, to support the deepening of a Decolonial Feminist Popular Education praxis across the more than 30 countries and territories represented, from Africa and the Americas.


There is power in naming the inequalities and wounds we carry as peoples who have been dispossessed of land, livelihoods, cultures and Knowledge. However, our greatest challenge is creating spaces that encourage us to dream of a world beyond the limits of colonial imagination.


Popular education has been a powerful practice for creating such spaces. Rooted in the knowledge and lived experiences of the people, it invites us to learn not only from books and institutions, but from one another.


Education is a political commitment


In the 1971 BBC film “

Behind the lines

”, Maria, a Mozambican guerrilla fighter explains that education was at the heart of why she decided to join the liberation struggle. In her experience

“If a girl reached a certain class [The colonialists] said that is enough for us, Africans.”


(Literacy Campaign, Guerrilla warfare in Angola, 1968. Photo: Augusta Conchiglia)


Our feminist

herstories

 across Africa and beyond have been deeply shaped by anti-colonial struggles. It was within the liberation movements that many women and men encountered education as a practice of freedom, in learning to question colonial power, reclaiming their histories and wisdom, fighting to protect their sovereignty and imagining forms of collective life beyond the impositions of heteropatriarchal, capitalist, colonial systems.


As feminist ancestor Nawal El Saadawi reminds us

“good education means creating dissatisfaction and disobedience.”

 Her wordsspeak to the transformative power of education to nurture the critical consciousness needed to both understand the conditions that constrain us and to connect them to our personal experiences, which is fundamental to organise collectively towards liberation.


But liberation cannot be achieved by a few, full liberation requires all of us. Our political project must be sustained by an intentional educational project that deepens our proposals and equips us to build the worlds we envision.


The educator is a pollinator


Through processes of learning, unlearning, relearning and imagining together, we become both teachers and students in our movements. This is one of the many ways in which decolonial feminist popular education inspires us to cultivate relational ways of working together that are grounded in mutual learning, listening, solidarity and care.


Instead of positioning the educator as the one who holds all the answers, popular educators create spaces where all can collectively formulate the questions that emerge from our struggles and where all can develop the knowledge needed to respond.


“Vou aprender a ler

 /

Para ensinar minhas camaradas

 /

I will learn how to read

 /

To teach my comrades”


Brazilian struggle song


The same way bees are essential for healthy environments, popular educators are an important part of feminist movements infrastructure. Popular educators nurture the power that already exists within movements.


Like the flower, each individual carries something that can nourish the collective. Learning is never only for ourselves. What we learn becomes a good we carry around our movements, to share, to exchange, to teach and to transform. Knowledge moves between us, allowing new ideas, possibilities and material actions to be activated. It is through this circulation of knowledge that we can produce the sweet taste of hope needed to build different futures.


Organising and liberating as we educate


“The beast is too big, and we need a political project that inspires us to build something every day and not just to fight and destroy the world as we know it.” –


Sandra, Guatemala


A decolonial feminist popular education praxis can build bridges across our different struggles, experiences, beliefs and movements, creating the conditions to move beyond simply resisting what exists …

author: William Shoki
title: Brazil’s racket society
content:
Brazil’s presidential election is headed for a runoff. In the first round on October 4, far-right Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, edged out President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva 47 percent to 45 percent. The right also consolidated its hold on Congress, with Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party now the largest bloc in the Senate. The result came despite Flávio’s thin record, his documented ties to Rio de Janeiro’s militias, and his father’s 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election.

As Latin America’s largest economy and its most populous democracy, Brazil has long served as a bellwether for the region, and increasingly for the world. Analysts of neoliberalism have used “Brazilianization” to describe a future of informal work, fortified elites, and hollowed-out states that they see arriving in the global North. The outcome of the runoff will help decide whether Brazil holds out against a regional turn toward Trump-aligned strongmen, a wave that has already swept Argentina, Ecuador, and, most recently, Colombia.

The stakes are high. Lula’s third term delivered growth, rising wages, and record-low unemployment, but it was hemmed in by a hostile Congress, and household debt and the cost of living kept climbing. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has intervened with unusual openness. It has imposed punitive tariffs and sanctioned a Supreme Court justice, and it has designated Brazil’s two largest criminal factions as terrorist organizations. As Benjamin Fogel

wrote in


Jacobin

 before the vote, “something deeper and more paradigmatic is going on” than ordinary frustration with an incumbent.

In this conversation, editor William Shoki speaks with Fogel, a historian of Brazil and contributing editor at

Jacobin

 and an alumnus of

Africa Is a Country

, to unpack the first-round results, the coalition of interests behind Flávio, and the political economy that makes it cohere. They discuss why Brazilian capital has made its peace with predation, why anti-corruption politics so often breeds cynicism, how “security slop” became the right’s signature policy, and what Brazil and South Africa reveal about everyone else’s future.

William Shoki

For readers who haven’t followed Brazil since Lula came to power for his third term in 2022, what happened on October 4?

Benjamin Fogel

To give a little background: Lula won the election in 2022, but at the same time, what people were calling the most right-wing Congress ever was elected. So if Bolsonaro was defeated at the polls, Bolsonarismo — and we can get into what that is later — was still very much alive.

That election was contested. Apart from all sorts of maneuvers before the vote — trying to discredit it through disinformation channels, trying to buy votes, voter intimidation, and obstruction by the Federal Highway Police on the day — there was an attempted coup, which led into the events of January 8, 2023. That bore some resemblance to January 6, in that you had a bunch of fanatical Bolsonaro supporters storm Congress and trash the place. But Brazil, unlike the United States, has a history of military coups, and it was touch and go whether the military would back it. There were other aspects to this, such as a plot to assassinate Lula, his vice president, and the Supreme Court justice who was overseeing the elections.

So it was defeated, and some people had thought this would discredit the right. It certainly weakened them for a while. But having a right-wing Congress made it really difficult for the Lula government to govern. In terms of the macroeconomic agenda, there were some successes. We’re not talking about anything dramatic, but the economy was growing at three or four percent, and the minimum wage increased. Overall, people were slightly better off than when Lula started, but there wasn’t a massive shift in wealth, and there were other factors we should get into later.

Bolsonarismo persisted. Then last year, Bolsonaro was successfully prosecuted for the failed coup, along with a bunch of his allies — the first time anybody has ever been successfully prosecuted for one. He was in prison and then placed under house arrest for health reasons — as people like to say, he’s permanently ill. What that meant is that the throne of the Brazilian right was up for grabs, and there were a number of pretenders. These included the governor of São Paulo, Tarcísio de Freitas, who’s just been reelected by a huge …

author: Jon Abbink
title: Ethiopia’s volatile politics: the June 2026 parliamentary elections, the National Dialogue, and violent conflict
content:
In a surprise to absolutely no one, Ethiopia’s ruling Prosperity Party (PP) led by PM Abiy Ahmed won the 1 June 2026 parliamentary elections in a

landslide

. The outcome has evoked

few commentaries

 in the global media or even in Ethiopia itself. There was a c.

90% win

 of parliamentary seats for the PP. This is, like in

previous

 elections (

2021

, or

2015

), a kind of Communist country result. It indeed was a well-organised operation, a classic case of what in Ethiopia since the

Derg

-regime (1974-1991) is called an “organisational operation” (Amharic:

dirigitawi sera

). That may be regretted or lauded but reflects political reality. Ethiopia still has no deep-rooted democratic

political culture

, certainly not on the national level: there was always violent competition for power and lack of freedoms, and people mostly went to the polls because of a mixture of duty, pride, and fear.


At around the same time, in August, some results of the ‘

National

 Dialogue’ process were announced – a nation-wide ambitious consultation initiated in 2022 and closed off after a conference (15 July-22 August), and they may prove to be more important than the elections as such. The yet unpublished full recommendations of this unique although

not perfect

Dialogue were

offered

 to the federal government on 3 October and will have to be addressed by the newly elected parliament. Interesting in the discussions and the recommendations was a growing ambivalence about ‘ethnic politics’.


First about the June elections. What did they show? Technically efficient, they were a repeat of the process of elite consolidation: the incumbent can continue as usual. The security situation also prevented voting in at least

143

 polling stations in

46

 constituencies. Since early September we also saw an escalation of violent strife, especially in Tigray, Amhara, and Oromia Regions, and the national political arena seems to further fragment: clearly, the elections did not have a stabilising effect.


What few people talk about is the

electoral system

 that facilitates the return of the incumbent party, time and again. Ethiopia does not have proportional representation but a district system, with a ‘first past the post’ mechanism (created by the previous, EPRDF regime). It means that the more parties participate (there were 48 registered parties..), the more the chances are that the most powerful and influential party – of course the one in power, i.e., the PP – will reach the threshold first, even if it has, say, only 15% of the votes in the voting district. In addition, there is a, to many

analysts

, unhealthy preponderance of

ethnic-based

 parties:  a divisive element in any election system, leading to uncritical, loyalty block-voting rather than a focus on

issue

politics and coalitions or on evaluating the concrete

results

 and human impact of policies. My argument is that this ‘district system’ and the ethno-federal formula mean that the incumbent cannot lose. This hinders effective democratic representation. In an alternative system, however, ‘ethnic’ parties should be discouraged, because that would, under current conditions of elite politics’,

de facto

 continue the ethnic block voting. Realistically, however, this will not happen soon, and thus, political quagmire and conflicts will continue.


With PP hegemony in parliament confirmed and only a marginal role for opposition parties or civil-society forces, the question is if pressing national concerns will be tackled in a new way. These include the (effects of) ongoing armed conflicts, the large number of IDPs, regionally unbalanced developmental policies, the weak justice system, and the perpetual economic problems. This is not to deny the achievements: the completion of the Blue Nile dam for hydro-electric power generation, the new initiatives in infrastructure expansion, digitalisation of the economy and services, agrarian expansion and agro-industry plans, tourism facility investments, etc. Political elites and the people connected to them are doing well; most of the population not yet. Many citizens

are

 proud of the achievements. But the sorry state of human rights, everyday corruption, the high poverty rate, hundreds of victims of armed violence, and lack of equal access to justice in the courts (for instance, for political detainees and the urban or rural displaced) produce gloom and despondency among the public.


In general, elections are …

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Supreme Court delivers landmark decision on Indigenous offenders and victims
content:
A Supreme Court of Canada decision on Friday has clarified the factors that judges should account for when a defendant and victim are both Indigenous.


The landmark case,

R. v. Cope

, concerns Harry Arthur Cope, a Mi’kmaw man from Nova Scotia who pleaded guilty to assaulting his partner, a Mi’kmaw woman, in 2021.


The Supreme Court weighed in on a trial judge’s decision to sentence Cope to five years in prison and the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal’s decision to reduce that sentence to three years.


On Friday, the Supreme Court upheld the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal’s ruling, which accounted for Cope’s mental illness and substance use.


“The sentencing judge should have linked the mental health factor to the offender’s moral blameworthiness on the aggravated assault offence, but failed to do so,” wrote Justice Michelle O’Bonsawin, writing for the majority of the judges. “The court of appeal was therefore correct to intervene and it arrived at a just and appropriate sentence.”


Four of nine judges sided with the Nova Scotia provincial court’s original ruling, which dismissed recommendations from community members who proposed no further jail time and opted for a treatment program instead.


Anne Crawford, an Iqaluit lawyer who handles family and domestic violence cases, said the Supreme Court judgement uplifts the role that Indigenous victims, their families and their community should play in criminal sentencing.


“It provides emphasis on the value of women, mothers and partners,” said Crawford, who has previously worked as a defence lawyer. “I think it’s part of a broader shift in Canadian society towards accountability for offenders.”


That shift includes changes to the Criminal Code that came into effect in June, she said. The law now defines murders “that occur within a pattern of coercive” behaviour toward an intimate partner as first-degree murders, and it asks courts to consider life imprisonment when somenone commits manslaughter within such a pattern.


“I don’t think our courts come anywhere near addressing what victims need,” Crawford added about the landmark judgement. “(But) I do think it comes closer to holding offenders to account.”


Twenty intervenors, including provincial and community prosecutorial services, legal aid centres, and organizations representing lawyers and Indigenous women, all participated in the hearings, held Dec. 11 and 12 at the Supreme Court in Ottawa.


Philippe Boucher, a doctoral candidate in legal studies at Carleton University, serves as a Gladue report writer, which provides judges with a portrait of an Indigenous offender before they decide the length and severity of a sentence.


He said the court’s message is that condemning violence doesn’t always require longer prison sentences.


The Supreme Court judgement also provides guidance on how judges should balance their responsibility to avoid imprisonment when offenders are Indigenous with protecting Indigenous women and girls, Boucher said.


O’Bonsawin proposed a three-step test. Judges must first assess the gravity of the offence and responsibility of the offender in light of the Indigeneity of both the offender and the victim.


Second, they must identify what the sentence is meant to achieve while considering denunciation and deterrence, a key addition to the Criminal Code after the National Inquiry into Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls.


Third, they must chose a proportionate sentence with everything in context.


“What the Supreme Court said this morning is that denunciation and deterrence doesn’t automatically mean a custodial sentence, it doesn’t mean prison, and it can also be another alternative to detention,” he said.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Trump Administration, Accused of Crimes Against Humanity, Sanctions Entire ICC
content:
Officials announced the sanctions just hours after the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to a former ICC judge.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

Trump administration officials, facing numerous allegations of war crimes in its actions ranging from Iran to Cuba, issued punishing sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Friday that threaten the future of the entire body and its work to hold war criminals and genocidaires to account.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, fresh off of his ultra-nationalist speech at the Acropolis this week, said in a video announcing the sanctions that the U.S. is banning “transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate against us.”

The sanctions are slated to cut the court off from using U.S.-based financial services, companies, and even the U.S. dollar after six months — a move that is ruinous for the court’s officials, as the global financial system is highly dependent on the U.S. dollar.

The administration announced the sanctions just hours after Navi Pillay, who was formerly the UN’s human rights chief and an ICC judge, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. Last year, Pillay led the independent UN commission that declared genocide in Gaza. The prize announcement incensed President Donald Trump, who reposted a message saying that the Nobel Committee “shamed itself beyond repair” on Truth Social.

The ICC warned that the sanctions are unprecedented, and called on its 125 member states to fight back against the U.S.’s actions.

“It is an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the Court from doing what it was created to do. It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law,” the ICC said in a statement. “Future generations, and above all the victims of mass atrocities, will ask how we responded when an institution created to protect them came under attack.”

The U.S. has already sanctioned 13 other ICC judges and prosecutors in recent months, including numerous officials who have worked on the ICC’s prosecution of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The Trump administration has also previously demanded that the ICC formally end its investigation into U.S. soldier wrongdoing in the U.S.’s invasion of Afghanistan that was already previously put on pause.

Rubio said that the move is about supposedly protecting U.S. sovereignty and shielding American officials and allies from being targeted by the ICC. “Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC,” Rubio said.

Similar claims have previously been debunked by legal experts as an attempt by Rubio to use rhetorical scare tactics to paper over Trump officials’ real desire in dismantling the ICC: impunity for themselves and violent allies like Israel. Trump administration officials have faced numerous accusations of war crimes and violations of international humanitarian law, for their massacres of civilians across numerous fronts; ICE raids and mass deportation campaign; and transfers of weapons to countries committing or implicated in war crimes.

Rather than threaten U.S. sovereignty, the sanctions on the ICC actually threaten the sovereignty of many states and peoples who have been victimized by powerful war criminals with no other method of recourse, critics said.

“By sanctioning the entire International Criminal Court, the Trump administration has taken a sledgehammer to the most important development in international justice in half a century,” said Omar Shakir, executive director for Democracy for the Arab World Now (DAWN). “U.S. sanctions threaten to shut the last viable road to justice for millions of victims of serious crimes, from Gaza and Sudan to Afghanistan and Ukraine.”

DAWN is one of several organizations that have filed lawsuits against previous U.S. sanctions against the ICC. The group called on the European Union to use its Blocking Statute, as it has for previous U.S. sanctions, to prohibit the EU from complying with the sanctions. The group also called on the ICC to prosecute Trump, Rubio, and other U.S. officials for the sanctions, which DAWN Advocacy Associate Isabelle Hayslip said are a crime under the ICC’s founding statute.

author: Maya Schenwar
title: We Must Move Beyond the Era of State-Sponsored, State-Celebrated Murder
content:
This story was co-published with


Truthout

.


  Christa Pike woke up on October 6 in a Tennessee hospital with a blood clot and pneumonia, handcuffed and shackled to her bed, having become the first known person to survive an execution via lethal injection. On September 30, the state of Tennessee tried to murder Pike. Instead, it put her through an hour and a half of difficulty breathing as she intermittently gasped for air and was eventually sent into critical condition, in a notoriously “botched execution” — in other words,

torture

. As Sandra Babcock, one of Pike’s attorneys,

put it

 on

Democracy Now

: “Christa Pike … has just experienced the most agonizing attempt at lethal injection in the country’s history.”


  Conversations in the wake of this torture have, understandably, focused on the exceptional circumstances of the attempted killing. However, this is also an important moment to recognize the depths of brutality in which this country wallows, such that the killing of a person by their own government only tends to make front page news when it is “botched.” It is also a key time to push ourselves to imagine beyond that violence, and to ask: What kind of world can we build, in which an execution is unthinkable?


  First, we must contend with the extent of our status-quo brutality. This vicious, not-so-new normal is illustrated by the fact that in the end, Pike’s attorneys, who fought persistently for her sentence to be commuted, were forced to argue for her to be

hanged

, as Pike rightly predicted that her small veins would make lethal injection a long and terrifyingly painful process. Let that sink in: We live in a country where mercy is a

hanging.


  Death penalty proponents have responded to Pike’s survival by advocating even harsher methods. U.S. Senator and Tennessee gubernatorial candidate Marsha Blackburn responded, “The answer is simple: Bring back the electric chair and deliver justice for these victims swiftly.” (Multiple state supreme courts have ruled the electric chair to be cruel and unusual punishment, citing examples like

six-inch flames

 erupting from the head of an electrocution victim.)


Tennessee State House Speaker Cameron Sexton

said

, “I don’t think there’s any method that’s off the table at this point.” And in a cameo that should shock no one, Former Deputy Assistant Attorney John Yoo, infamous for authoring the

Torture Memos,


said

 on

Fox News

, “Tennessee is trying to use what is considered the most humane method of capital punishment, which is lethal injection. The court has allowed, and Tennessee could use, far more … hurtful, you know, methods like firing squad.”


  These pro-cruelty statements mark a chilling counter-trend regarding the death penalty. Throughout the early 21

st

 century, thanks to the efforts of an enduring anti-death penalty movement, executions significantly declined, pharmaceutical companies fled the execution-drug market, and medical professionals overwhelmingly refused to participate in executions.


  These shifts, of course, never went far enough, and states’ insistence that the alternative must be a lifelong prison sentence — death by incarceration, as dedicated organizers have termed it — has ingrained the use of endless punishment, marking another uphill battle.


This week, Trump approved the first U.S. military execution in more than 60 years, and the Pentagon plans to livestream it.


  Yet even these changes are on thin ice. The last two years have witnessed a pronounced resurgence of executions. In the U.S., more people were killed by the state in 2025 than in any year since 2009. And by July of this year, Trump had already

begun

 more capital prosecutions than he’d launched in his whole first term in office. This week, Trump approved the

first U.S. military execution

 in more than 60 years, and the Pentagon plans to

livestream it

.

executive order

, which claimed that “only capital punishment can bring justice and restore order” in relation to “the vilest crimes.” In a memo in April of this year, Trump’s Department of Justice (DOJ) called on Congress to

broaden and accelerate

 use of the federal death penalty. And in a

author: Giovanna DeStefanis
title: JAWS Reception Celebrates Legacy of Women in Journalism
content:
The Journalism and Women Symposium (JAWS) celebrated the legacy of women journalists at a reception on October 2 hosted at the Ms. office. The gathering brought together journalists, longtime JAWS members, and feminist advocates to recognize the women who helped shape media and discuss the importance of preserving their work for future generations.

The reception highlighted the connections between JAWS, Ms. and the Feminist Majority Foundation (FMF), publisher of Ms. magazine. Kathy Bonk, a longtime feminist advocate and leader, recalled how Ms. founder Gloria Steinem reached out to ask FMF to keep the magazine alive. With the support of Ellie Smeal, Katherine Spillar, Peg Yorkin, and others, FMF committed to sustaining Ms. feminist journalism.

Bonk also reflected on the role of feminist journalism in advancing the women’s movement, arguing that the journalists who documented the movement helped make its progress possible. Bonk shared, “It’s no longer just news coverage. It’s looking for an impact. It’s looking at how we change people’s lives.”

A central focus of the reception was JAWS’ Legacy Fund and its efforts to preserve the history of women in journalism. Pam Morland, a former JAWS president and longtime journalist, described donating decades of professional and personal materials to archive her materials going back to 1985.

Morland encouraged fellow journalists to preserve their own work rather than discard it, explaining that materials that may seem unremarkable today can become valuable historical records. The archives offer researchers an opportunity to explore the experiences and contributions of women journalists and document the development of organizations such as JAWS.

The reception highlighted the importance of preserving women’s experiences in journalism, particularly as the profession continues to confront challenges. JAWS is helping ensure the future generations can study their work and understand the history of feminist media.

As Ms. approaches its 55th anniversary in December, marking 25 years with the Feminist Majority Foundation as publisher, the gathering celebrated the relationships, reporting and feminist organizing that have sustained the magazine and the broader movement. Speakers closed by celebrating Ms., Gloria Steinem, and the community of women journalists whose work continues to shape feminist media.

author: Gary Chartier
title: Con il Mercato, Contro il “Capitalismo”
content:
Di

Gary Chartier

. Originale pubblicato il 25 gennaio 2013 con il titolo

Embracing Markets, Opposing “Capitalism”

. Tradotto da Enrico Sanna.


Articolo scritto da 

Gary Chartier

 e pubblicato su 

Bleeding Heart Libertarians

 il 22 marzo 2011.


Essere libertari significa opporsi all’uso della forza che impedisce uno scambio spontaneo e pacifico. Ma non significa approvare il capitalismo.


Il senso di una tale affermazione dipende da cosa si intende per “capitalismo”. Per qualcuno è semplicemente il libero scambio. In tal caso è corretto affermare che non esiste un vero e proprio contrasto tra capitalismo e libertarismo.


Ma a volte si intende qualcos’altro. L’informazione stampata e digitale, ad esempio, per “capitalismo” intende “l’attuale sistema economico”. Ma è anche relativamente diffusa l’accezione di “capitalismo” come “il potere che i capitalisti, detentori di una grossa fetta di beni capitali, hanno sul posto di lavoro e sulla società”. Secondo i principi libertari di cui parlo il capitalismo non è né l’una né l’altra cosa.


Il sistema economico attuale è,

in misura molto significativa

, un sistema che esclude lo scambio pacifico e spontaneo. Un intreccio di privilegi legali e normativi favoriscono chi è ricco e ben posizionato a spese di tutti gli altri (pensiamo ai brevetti e i copyright, ai dazi, alla limitazione dell’attività creditizia, alle licenze professionali, alle norme edilizie, eccetera). Il complesso militar-industriale assorbe quantità incredibili di denaro, è il caso di dire sotto minaccia, dalle tasche della gente per versarle nei conti bancari di società d’appalto e clientele. Sussidi di ogni genere alimentano un insieme di attività privilegiate e no profit. Inoltre lo stato riconosce la proprietà di terre prese con la violenza o con mezzi legali arbitrari e poi distribuite a singoli e gruppi di favore. Le economie di Stati Uniti, Canada, Europa occidentale e Giappone non sono a pianificazione centralizzata, lo stato non sancisce (gran parte de)i mezzi di produzione, ma dato il suo coinvolgimento a più livelli nel garantire e promuovere i privilegi economici è difficile dire che il nostro sistema economico è libero. Se questo è “capitalismo”, chi vuole la libertà ha buone ragioni per essere scettico.


I privilegi che caratterizzano l’attuale ordine economico, comunque lo si chiami, attirano soprattutto chi ha più potere di condizionamento politico e ricchezza. È una rete che finisce per rafforzare i privilegi dei capitalisti sul posto di lavoro. I privilegi limitano il lavoro autonomo (innalzando i requisiti di capitale o i costi d’ingresso e riducendo le risorse disponibili per avviare e mantenere un’attività). Restringendo le alternative al lavoro salariato e imponendo limiti all’attività sindacale, e riducendo così il potere contrattuale collettivo, lo stato finisce per rafforzare il potere dei datori di lavoro. In breve: non si comprende il potere attuale dei “capitalisti” se non si conoscono le mascalzonate dello stato. Ancora una volta: se questo è “capitalismo”, chi vuole la libertà ha buone ragioni per essere scettico.


Qualcuno potrebbe dire che, se la parola “capitalismo” indica spesso un fenomeno sociale detestabile, altrettanto spesso indica un sistema economico che pone al centro la libertà. Non so in che proporzione e con quale peso. So però che il “capitalismo” è visto negativamente da tempi immemori (“capitalista” è inteso in senso spregiativo da sostenitori entusiasti del libero mercato come

Thomas Hodgskin

 nella prima metà dell’Ottocento) e oggi è ancora così. Mi capita molto spesso, quando sento parlarne positivamente, di pensare che è una sorta di parola portmanteau (come

sottolinea opportunamente

 Roderick Long) che significa “libero scambio”, “situazione attuale”, “potere dei capitalisti” o un insieme di tutto ciò. È una parola corrotta. Quando nei paesi in via di sviluppo la gente scende in piazza e urla contro il “capitalismo”, intendendo non la vera libertà ma il dominio imperiale del governo statunitense e i suoi alleati, credo che sia importante che i libertari sappiano distinguere questo regime statale oppressivo da quello invocato da chi vuole la libertà.


Gli editorialisti del

Wall Street Journal

 o di

Faux News

 e i vari portavoce delle élite economiche e politiche possono continuare a chiamare “capitalismo” tutto quello che gli fa comodo. Non sono libertari, i quali non hanno nessuna ragione di emularli. Volere un mercato libero (o …

author: Brittany Boschman, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: A century after it was taken, ancestral tipi cover returns to Kawacatoose First Nation
content:
Using wooden pins and great care, Kawacatoose First Nation members fasten an Ancestor’s painted tipi cover on Aug. 28, after it was finally returned to their Saskatchewan community from ‘Washington, D.C.’

Photo by Brittany Boschman


“We’re gonna take you home now.”


Those were okimâw (Chief) Cory Dustyhorn’s words when he first touched the tipi cover connected to his great-great-great-grandfather, sîpiskwêsîkan.


After a century away from

Kawacatoose First Nation

, the ancestral item has returned to the Cree community.


Community and family members gathered around the tipi cover after it was brought back from the

Smithsonian Institution’s National Museum of the American Indian

 in “Washington, D.C.” 


They prayed over it and welcomed it home.


“When I first touched it, I just felt so emotional,” Dustyhorn said. 


“I was thinking of all those that are gone on before me.”


He thought about his parents, grandparents and ancestors — who preserved the history of the item through generations.


He prayed for them to be present as the community finally brought home a piece of their history. 


“I told all of them, ‘Come with us, come and attend with us,” Dustyhorn recalled. 


“I know they were in between all of us — and they were here, too.”


Members of the Dustyhorn family and supporters celebrate the return of their Ancestor sîpiskwêsîkan’s painted tipi cover. From left: Oral Dustyhorn, Joyce Pratt, Philip Dustyhorn, okimâw (Chief) Cory Dustyhorn, Vanessa Dustyhorn, and researcher Andrew Miller.

Photo by Brittany Boschman


Colonizers’ ‘vanishing Indian’ narrative


The tipi cover remained in the community for four nights before being temporarily housed at the

Royal Saskatchewan Museum

 in

oskana kâ-asastêki

 (Regina). 


Until the First Nation can build a permanent museum or cultural centre to house it safely, they plan to bring it home each year.


The return followed a reparation process that lasted almost three years. 


Andrew Miller, an associate professor at the First Nations University of Canada, helped the Dustyhorn family locate the item and communicate with the Smithsonian.


Miller described the tipi cover’s return as a meaningful example of reconciliation in action. 


“One of my friends from the Royal Saskatchewan Museum said, ‘Congratulations, you’ve just realized reconciliation,’” Miller said. “That’s what this is.”


But for Miller, reconciliation means more than merely acknowledging past injustices. It also requires returning ancestral belongings and supporting communities as they restore cultural teachings.


READ MORE:


Indigenous leaders celebrate belongings returned from the Vatican: ‘We welcome them home’


Dustyhorn said the return also highlights the need for stronger support from governments and museums — for all Indigenous communities hoping to recover what was taken away from them. 


“They talk about truth and reconciliation,” he said. “They splash that all over the news for a few years. 


“But where’s their help? How can we get the stuff back that was taken from us, too?”


Miller and Dustyhorn said the tipi cover was taken during an era when museums and governments declared that Indigenous cultures were disappearing and needed to be archived. That view justified an urgent push to collect ceremonial belongings and other ancestral items from Indigenous communities worldwide.


“They were wanting to capture the disappearing Indian,” Dustyhorn said.


Miller said museums particularly sought items connected to regalia, ceremonies, and other cultural practices as part of that colonial narrative.


“They were targets,” Miller said, describing sacred belongings as part of the “vanishing Indian culture” narrative.


But, Dustyhorn emphasized, “We’re still here.”


Kawacatoose First Nation members look at and touch the sacred tipi cover painted in the early 1920s by sîpiskwêsîkan — before a collector from the Smithsonian Institution took it to ‘Washington, D.C.’ — promising payment that never came.

Photo by Brittany Boschman


‘Let’s get it back’


Miller first learned about the tipi cover from a former student, Andrea Dustyhorn. Years later, while researching

ethno-ornithology

 — the relationships between people and birds — he found the tipi cover in the Smithsonian’s catalogue.


So he reached out to Dustyhorn.


“You should see this,” he told the chief. “What do you want to do?”


“And he said, ‘Well, let’s get it back.’”

author: Alison Avigayil Ramer
title: After October 7, I learned that movements need grief spaces
content:
This article

After October 7, I learned that movements need grief spaces

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


Since the massacres on Oct. 7, now three years ago, the news has brought a steady stream of horror and broken promises. The ceasefire in Gaza has been broken thousands of times; the ceasefire with Iran only holds until the next strike. Many of us have responded by going numb or turning away. Over these three years, I’ve come to believe that collective mourning can help movements build sturdier organizing infrastructure, move through paralysis and numbness, and get back to the long-term work of creating systemic change.


I’ve spent nearly two decades living and working as a human rights defender, mostly in Palestine and Israel. For years, I responded to atrocities the way much of the dominant organizing culture did at the time: strategically. I prepared statements, launched campaigns and mobilized our base. I worked through several wars and the ongoing ethnic cleansing and genocide. Even though my colleagues and I were often physically together, we rarely had the opportunity to collectively mourn. In fact, mourning was often seen as something only the privileged could afford. As organizers and solidarity activists, we were the ones who needed to push past the pain and keep mobilizing.


And then, after each war, large swaths of colleagues and organizers would burn out, and our movement would suffer a setback. Movement researchers Paul Gorski and Cher Chen, studying U.S. human rights and social justice activists, found that an estimated 50 to 60 percent of organizers eventually walk away from movement work and never return, burned out by a culture that treats overwork and self-sacrifice as necessary. That culture also leaves no room to mourn and process the secondary trauma that accumulates, hastening burnout. These kinds of cycles make it especially hard for movements seeking systemic change to sustain themselves.


Sign Up for our Newsletter


We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


When Hamas attacked Israel in October 2023 and I was waiting in anticipation of the retaliation against Gaza, I knew I couldn’t respond with the same kind of organizing strategy that we usually use: preparation of advocacy statements, social media campaigns and fundraising appeals. I knew that while some people should and would continue that work, there also needed to be spaces for organizers and our base to mourn. And so, on Oct. 8, I opened a space for collective mourning online, sharing it in the many community, political and religious groups I was a part of, for anyone who needed somewhere to process what they were witnessing and feeling. Dozens of people joined: primarily my Jewish community at first, and then people from many faiths and chapters of my life, from Palestine to Palo Alto. 


As the assault on Gaza and the genocide continued, the room stayed open. More colleagues, including community organizers, artists, chaplains and psychologists, joined me in facilitating, and we held space for hundreds of people from across our communities to mourn together. We formed a collective called the

Social Change Sanctuary

 and developed a format that included facilitation and participation from attendees. Over time, we were invited to hold spaces for other communities in mourning. We’ve held spaces to grieve the ongoing genocide; climate catastrophes like the fires in Los Angeles; ICE raids, arrests and murders; and the war on Iran.


The Social Change Sanctuary hosts an Interdependence Day circle in 2025. (Alison Avigayil Ramer)


Participants repeatedly shared the difference it made in their lives to know they had a consistent space to mourn.


“In daily life, when something hurts, I turn away, I distract myself,” one participant told us. “But the collective mourning practice helped me move through the frozenness that constant news induced — helped me stop doomscrolling — and I’m able to return to my work.”


That participant went on to organize her community and raised $20,000 for refugees in Gaza. 


Another participant returned to their role as a chaplain, and extended her work to include “movement chaplaincy” holding one-on-one spaces for people doing solidarity work. 


Many participants also shared how witnessing the news with others enabled them to feel the emotions provoked by the headlines, leaving them feeling less isolated and more connected. That is co-regulation happening at …

author: Admin101
title: ATX Solidarity Network is Fighting Wage Theft, La Migra, and Apathy
content:
AK, a founding member of ATX Solidarity Network, discusses their experience organizing immigrant workers to confront wage theft and other issues in right-to-work Texas.


Increased ICE enforcement has raised fears about fighting back, turning many to seek services in a field dominated by


nonprofits. In this interview we explore the tensions organizing for direct action amid these conditions.


Black Rose/Rosa Negra (BRRN): We understand that you all in Austin, Texas have begun to build a solidarity network. What is that? How is it structured?


AK:

 A solidarity network is basically made up of workers and tenants from all over the city (or, in some cases, parts of a city) who have or may have issues with their bosses and landlords. Instead of organizing with our immediate coworkers or neighbors, we are individuals from different workplaces and living in different areas of town who fight for each other where we are at. Solidarity networks are meant to fill the void where workplace unions and tenant unions don’t exist. Since Texas is a “right to work” state, capital strategically undermines workers from building fighting organizations like unions. Solidarity networks are flexible enough to meet one or a few workers at one workplace or tenants at a complex, and temporarily bypass the immediate need for longstanding organizations.  


When you meet someone with a workplace or tenant issue, the whole solidarity network takes on the demands of the case, with those with the grievance–the issue(s) they want to fight around that directly affects them–being core organizers of their own campaign. We use direct action tactics, which means we don’t go through the courts or ask the cops or nonprofits to take care of the situation for us; we rely on just us to get the demand met by putting pressure on the boss or landlord until it becomes so unbearable they have no choice but to give in.


Like most solidarity networks there is a small group of core organizers who respond to the day- to-day needs of the organization. The people with the demands must be a part of this group. Then, there is a larger membership which is involved in many of the functions of the organization, but not all of its functions. They may pass out flyers with us, make phone calls, or research campaign targets, for example. Then there is a much larger network of people who will come out to actions when called on.


BRRN: Walk us through how you started it. Why this kind of organization, and what kinds of fights do you take on?


AK:

 Our specific solidarity network wanted to take on wage theft campaigns as our main, but not exclusive, area of struggle. We began working with another organization here that works in immigrant communities around stopping deportations. They were getting a lot of calls about wage theft, and helped us start the solidarity network to meet this need. Most of our initial calls came directly from them, and our first campaign came out of one of these calls. We also understand that the immigrant community, especially here in Texas, is very vulnerable to wage theft, and they often feel they do not have a lot of options for getting back stolen wages. We want to change that! Eventually, we want to create a citywide network of people who can respond to wage theft grievances, and other workplace and housing issues. We want to make bosses and landlords scared to even think about messing with us! 


In ATX, we have a small and unorganized left with a larger activist scene. A solidarity network is one form of organization that can work well under these conditions because you really only need a handful of core organizers and access to lots of people to show up to actions. We also see this form of organization being one in which committed leftists can develop relationships with other members of the working class. We see a lot of the left in ATX being very insular and removed from other everyday people. We feel it is important to be organizing in working-class communities since it is us as a class that are capable of transforming society. 


We also want to help normalize direct action tactics to push our collective ability to struggle even further. Ultimately, we would like to see more working-class organizations in our neighborhoods, workplaces, schools, and more. The solidarity network isn’t meant to be

the form

 of organization for widespread worker rebellion, but it is one form of organization that can respond to specific conditions that …

title: French Youth Take the Streets against a Bleak Future : A Report
content:
This past week, thousands of teenagers have taken the streets of France, clashing with police as they demonstrate against the deplorable conditions in their high schools and a rapidly collapsing future. This is a promising sign, shifting attention from the seemingly unstoppable rise of the extreme right to the question of what people can do on a grassroots basis to defend themselves. Our correspondents in Paris explore the situation in detail.


Another unprecedented summer of record

heatwaves

,

droughts

, and

wildfires

 throughout Europe underlines the desperate situation we are all facing today, while politicians of all stripes and their techno-industrial sponsors continue to turn a blind eye, forcing us down the path to catastrophe in the name of progress.


Hoping to turn the page on these environmental disasters, the French government has hurriedly shifted focus to other priorities. The coming months represent a crucial transition for Emmanuel Macron and his government, as they will bring Macron’s second term to a close, opening a new political era in France. Candidates are already battling to succeed Macron in power at the beginning of May 2027.


In the midst of this political spectacle, during an increasingly

menacing surge

 in the popularity of the National Rally (formerly, the National Front), the extreme-right party, it is especially meaningful that teenagers have started to organize at a grassroots level to defend themselves. This organizing gained momentum last week, when blockades of high schools, demonstrations, and riots erupted across France, taking everyone by surprise.


Students clash with police forces in Montpellier on October 2, 2026.


Licensed to Kill?


Since Macron was elected President for the first time in May 2017, the political discourse in France has been even more dominated by an emphasis on authoritarian and far-right ideologies in terms of security, immigration, and economic and social issues.


This political shift towards an even more aggressive form of governance has led to increasing state violence targeting the social movements and uprisings that have emerged since. From the eviction of the

ZAD

 at Notre-Dame-des-Landes in 2017 to the

riots

 following the murder of Nahel in 2023, not forgetting the

Yellow Vest

 sequence and the COVID-19 pandemic lockdown experimental

doctrines

, we have experienced a headlong plunge into a world of surveillance, repression, and loss of individual freedoms. This has become today’s new normal.


It was in this already suffocating context that last July, the French government decided to vote on a new bill giving police officers more latitude to use their firearms without consequences—a demand that the far right has promoted for years. If voted through, this legislation could set a

dangerous precedent

, as it would establish “a presumption of ‘legitimate use of arms’ by police and gendarmes ‘in the exercise of their duty’.”


Police arrest a student in Lyons on October 1, 2026.


In other words, not only will police officers be able to freely use their weapons if in any situation they claim to fear for their lives or the lives of others, but authorities will no longer have to prove that the officers acted within the framework of the law, as they are required to do today. It will be up to the victims and their families to provide evidence that the use of firearms was not justified. We can already see how this new law represents a legislative tool enabling law enforcement agents, and therefore, the state, to cover up future murders.


Unwilling to let such a law pass without resistance, political opponents and radicals, who had rightly rebranded this law the “license to kill,” decided to organize massive demonstrations and events throughout France on the weekend of September 18 to 20.

Thousands

 of people took part in these protests in different major cities alongside traditional leftist politicians, rights groups such as Amnesty International and the League of Human Rights, and various lawyers and magistrates’ unions.


In the meantime, another call for action reusing all the codes of the Yellow Vest movement spread online. The origins of this call remain obscure, as some national

newspapers

 have raised the possibility that AI-generated accounts had flooded social media platforms with this rumor on purpose. Nevertheless, media and politicians began commenting on this potential resurgence of the Yellow Vest movement due to the …

author: Valerie Anne
title: Horror Comedy ‘The Blood Countess’ Imagines Elizabeth Báthory as a Lesbian Vampire
content:
If I had a nickel for every piece of queer media about 17th century Hungarian countess Elizabeth Báthory released this year, I’d have two nickels. Which isn’t a lot, but it’s weird that it happened twice. After her strange appearance in Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story, she also appears in the vampire horror comedy The Blood Countess directed and co-written by lesbian filmmaker Ulrike Ottinger. In the film, Báthory (played by Isabelle Huppert) wakes from a long slumber and finds herself in modern-day Vienna, searching for a book that could cure her vampirism.

I find two things interesting about the fact that the countess has appeared in two queer adaptations this year. The first is that Lizzie Borden actually never really portrayed her as a lesbian, even though she was set up parallel to Lizzie and lesbian serial killer Aileen Wuornos and was played by the same actress who played Lizzie’s lover. Before the much-later rumors that Elizabeth Báthory bathed in the blood of virgin girls, the crimes she was accused of were more along the lines of torture and cannibalism. So it’s interesting that was then interpreted as lesbianism. Then again, she was luring young women to her castle with three of her closest gal pals, so, who knows I guess. It is just fascinating to me that despite the fact that she has been in folklore for centuries, no new media has come out about her in years, and now these two instances pop up in the same year. Three, if you count the experimental film Báthory by Carlos Atanes. Something seems to be in the (bloody) water.

Unfortunately, it seems like perhaps The Blood Countess isn’t quite as gay as it could be. Then again, apparently Ottinger wrote the screenplay in 1998, almost 30 years ago, so that could potentially account for that. But still, I won’t say no to a lesbian vampire film so I’ll probably still check it out when it makes its North American theatrical release in spring 2027.

author: anred
title: «De acá me sacan muerto»: intentaron desalojar a una comunidad mapuche tehuelche en favor de una empresa
content:
El operativo se realizó el jueves 8 de octubre en el paraje La Japonesa, sobre la costa del río Colorado. La Policía de Río Negro y personal judicial llegaron al territorio de la comunidad Lof Peñi Núñez-Álvarez para ejecutar una orden de desalojo impulsada por la firma Exelia S.A. Tras la resistencia y la tensión generada, los efectivos se retiraron y el procedimiento quedó suspendido. El conflicto tiene antecedentes judiciales y de violencia contra integrantes de la comunidad. Por ANRed


La comunidad mapuche Lof Peñi Núñez-Álvarez enfrentó el jueves un nuevo intento de desalojo en el paraje La Japonesa, departamento de Avellaneda, provincia de Río Negro. Efectivos policiales y personal del Poder Judicial se presentaron en el territorio para ejecutar una orden de desahucio en el marco de una causa promovida por la empresa Exelia S.A. El operativo estuvo encabezado por el oficial de Justicia Marcelo Orofilo.


Desde el territorio, integrantes de la comunidad denunciaron la presencia de niños y niñas y anunciaron que permanecerían en el lugar para defender sus viviendas y sus animales. Ante la gravedad de la situación, reclamaron el acompañamiento de organizaciones sociales, comunidades originarias y organismos de derechos humanos.


Finalmente, la Policía se retiró y el desalojo quedó suspendido. Sin embargo, la amenaza judicial continúa vigente y mantiene a las familias en estado de alerta.


Una disputa territorial con antecedentes


El conflicto judicial se remonta a una sentencia de abril de 2023, cuando el Juzgado Civil de Choele Choel hizo lugar a la demanda de Exelia S.A. y ordenó el desalojo de tres fracciones del Lote X. La decisión alcanzó terrenos ubicados en La Japonesa, donde las familias mapuches tehuelches desarrollan actividades de subsistencia y crían animales.


En junio de 2026, el Superior Tribunal de Justicia de Río Negro rechazó un recurso presentado por la defensa de la comunidad, dejando firme la orden de desalojo. La resolución fue cuestionada por quienes defienden el territorio, que reivindican la ocupación ancestral y los derechos reconocidos a los pueblos originarios.


En agosto, los representantes legales de la comunidad promovieron un planteo de nulidad. Sostuvieron que las parcelas mencionadas en la orden judicial no coincidirían con los terrenos que efectivamente ocupan las familias. Según la presentación, un informe de agrimensura permitió identificar diferencias entre las fracciones incluidas en el mandamiento y las tierras donde viven y desarrollan su economía de subsistencia.


El expediente también expone una discusión sobre la documentación que acredita la propiedad. Según reconstrucciones periodísticas, Exelia S.A. se constituyó en 1974 y en 1978 recibió las fracciones en disputa mediante un aporte de capital de su entonces titular, Umberto Francisco Conforti. La reconstrucción de la cadena de titularidad anterior y el arraigo histórico de las familias forman parte de los cuestionamientos al reclamo empresarial.


Exelia S.A. y las tierras en disputa


La firma Exelia S.A. es la demandante que obtuvo la sentencia favorable para recuperar las fracciones en litigio. La comunidad y referentes del Parlamento Mapuche Tehuelche cuestionan el origen de los títulos y denuncian que la disputa reproduce una historia de desplazamientos de familias indígenas en la zona.


Según los testimonios recogidos por medios regionales, las familias Álvarez y Núñez tienen vínculos con ese territorio que anteceden a la constitución de la sociedad anónima. Sus integrantes sostienen que sus abuelos y padres vivieron allí durante generaciones y que la crianza de ovejas, chivas, vacas y caballos constituye parte de su forma de vida.


Referentes mapuches también describieron un proceso histórico en el que empresas llegadas desde Buenos Aires se presentaron con documentación sobre los campos y, en algunos casos, dejaron a las familias originarias en condición de puesteras. Tras el abandono de esos territorios por parte de algunas firmas, varias familias regresaron a reivindicar los lugares donde habían vivido sus antepasados.


El conflicto de La Japonesa vuelve a poner en discusión la distancia entre los títulos registrales invocados en los tribunales y los derechos territoriales de comunidades indígenas cuya presencia histórica es anterior a la formación de las sociedades que reclaman esos predios.

El acto central estuvo a cargo del triunvirato que conduce la central. El cosecretario general también apuntó contra el Congreso y la dirigencia política en general: “La política toda, que se dejen de hacer los distraídos. El Congreso, basta de joder. En ese marco, reivindicó un “Estado presente, transparente”, y advirtió: “No creemos en un Estado subsidiario, pero tampoco creemos en un Estado que se desentienda de los problemas estructurales que tiene la gente”.


EL PUEBLO TRABAJADOR SALIÓ A DEFENDER EL FUTURO DE LA ARGENTINA


Frente a un modelo que privilegia la especulación, profundiza la recesión y condena a miles de familias a la incertidumbre, el movimiento obrero organizado reafirmó su compromiso con la producción nacional, el empleo y la justicia social.


Necesitamos un país que produzca, genere oportunidades y garantice derechos.


— CGT (@cgtoficialra)

October 9, 2026


La marcha fue convocada bajo el lema “Las Malvinas son argentinas, la industria nacional también” y contó con la participación de dirigentes del transporte, servicios y comercio exterior, entre ellos Juan Carlos Schmid (CATT), Daniel Mallotti (Aduana), Mariano Vilar (Conductores Navales), Juan Pablo Brey (Aeronavegantes), Graciela Aleñá (Viales Nacionales), Roberto Coria (Guincheros) y Mario Preiss (Caucho), entre otros representantes gremiales.

La jornada culminó con el anuncio de que la CGT se sumará el jueves próximo a la quinta Marcha Federal Universitaria el 15 de octubre, donde confluirán con las dos CTA y organizaciones estudiantiles, políticas y sociales.
