author: Maira Escardovelli
title: Terror das feministas: radicais, deputadas conservadoras disputam poder na extrema direita
content:
Investigamos o que importa para os brasileiros além do que passa na campanha eleitoral. Leia mais reportagens como essa clicando

aqui

.


O terror das feministas. É como se autointitulam Ana Caroline Campagnolo e Eduarda Campopiano, as deputadas estaduais mais votadas em Santa Catarina e São Paulo. Ambas do Partido Liberal (PL), elas se apresentam como amigas em posts nas redes sociais e se dizem admiradoras  de Olavo de Carvalho. Juntas, as duas somaram mais de 2,3 milhões de votos na eleição de 2026. Ao lado delas, ocupando o posto de deputada estadual mais votada do Estado, está Índia Armelau, também do PL, que conquistou 248.504 votos para a Assembleia Legislativa do Rio de Janeiro. 


São

mulheres que se unem ao clã de Michelle Bolsonaro (PL-DF), Damares Alves (Republicanos-DF), Bia Kicis (PL-DF) e Celina Leão (PP-DF) pela pauta anti-identitária e antiaborto

, mas que, segundo especialistas ouvidas pela

Agência Pública

, não pertencem ao mesmo grupo de suas antecessoras, inclusive considerando a construção de narrativas para o eleitorado. 


Na visão de Lívia Reis, coordenadora de Religião e Política no Instituto de Estudos da Religião (ISER), a extrema-direita conquistou uma pluralidade de candidaturas femininas nesta eleição, o que pode criar uma disputa pelo poder de influência entre as próprias eleitas. 


“O Valdemar [Costa Neto, presidente do PL] não está preocupado com o alinhamento ideológico de uma influenciadora, ele quer que ela seja eleita e vote com ele”, argumenta a antropóloga em referência a eleição de Eduarda Campopiano, atualmente com mais de 2,5 milhões de seguidores do Instagram.

 “Vejo que talvez isso seja também um dos atritos que a própria Michelle vai ter com ele, porque ela quer centralizar o PL Mulheres

 e as candidaturas femininas, mas o próprio PL vai apostar em quem quiser”, explica Reis. 


Vereadora de Praia Grande, no litoral paulista, Eduarda Campopiano foi eleita para a Assembleia Legislativa de São Paulo como uma espécie de discípula de Nikolas Ferreira (PL-MG), deputado federal mais votado da história do país, com mais de 22 milhões de seguidores no Instagram. Outro aliado é o vereador paulistano Lucas Pavanato (PL), que detém mais de 5 milhões de seguidores na rede social da Meta e foi eleito para deputado federal com mais de 3 milhões de votos. 


“O PL sabe o poder das redes sociais. Todas as candidaturas se forjam ali, eles estão elegendo influenciadores há muito tempo e agora chegaram ao ápice dos candidatos mais votados serem os influenciadores. Por isso, eu diria que a Eduarda chega [ao partido] com tanto poder quanto a Michelle. E vai disputar isso”, explica Reis. 


A esposa do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro, preso por tentativa de golpe de Estado, protagonizou em junho deste ano o seu primeiro embate público com o Partido. Após a rejeição da sigla ao nome indicado por ela ao Senado pelo Ceará, o da deputada Priscila Costa (PL-CE), Michelle publicou um vídeo contando que Flávio Bolsonaro a havia desrespeitado durante a formação dos arranjos partidários nos estados. “Ele disse que seria melhor eu ficar fora das decisões do partido. Disse que eu havia chegado ontem e não entendia nada de política”, afirmou a ex-primeira dama.


No vídeo, ela exaltou sua atuação à frente do PL Mulher, ala de mulheres conservadoras do partido: “[em 2024] elegemos 45,8% mais mulheres que em 2020. Foram 1.005 mulheres eleitas”, disse. Com a instauração da crise, que abalou a campanha à presidência de Flávio Bolsonaro, e após se reunir com Costa Neto, Michelle anunciou sua saída da presidência do PL Mulher. 


Na visão de parlamentares próximos ao PL, Campopiano representa um discurso mais radical da extrema-direita, capitaneado por Olavo de Carvalho

, conhecido como o “guru” do bolsonarismo. “Eu acho que ela [Eduarda] vem muito daquela linha do Olavo de Carvalho, que é essa juventude conservadora formada. Mas creio que com a maturidade ela vai entender que a pauta feminina não é uma pauta feminista. A gente vai ter ainda um tempo para fazer esse convencimento”, disse à

Pública

 a senadora Damares Alves, que também afirmou que irá dialogar nesse sentido com a deputada Índia Armelau.   


A pesquisadora do Centro Brasileiro de Análise e Planejamento (CEBRAP) Jacqueline Teixeira aponta que o discurso de Campopiano pode ser entendido a partir dos efeitos produzidos por políticas que começaram, entre 2014 a 2016, a proibir gênero nos parâmetros curriculares. author: Nahuel Lag
title: Masabia: alimentos agroecológicos de una comuna santafesina con reconocimiento internacional
content:
Por Patricio Suárez Area


Ubicada sobre la ruta 33, a mitad de camino entre Rosario y Pujato, la localidad de Zavalla puede autodenominarse con orgullo una comuna en transición agroecológica desde hace 15 años, a partir de la

ordenanza que limitó las fumigaciones con agrotóxicos

 y la posterior creación de un tributo anual que respaldó a los productores para iniciar

el cambio de modelo productivo

. Los tiempos políticos cambiaron y el tributo se descontinuó, pero el cambio ya había iniciado. Sobre ese mapa periurbano sin fumigaciones,

un grupo de productores creó la Cooperativa de Trabajo Zavalla para levantar un viejo molino familiar

 e iniciar un camino que, en la actualidad, es de

producción de maíz, girasol y trigo agroecológico

. La estrella son los productos elaborados a partir del trigo bajo la

marca Masabia

 (harinas integrales, fideos frescos, fideos secos y pre pizzas sin agroquímicos), que fue reconocida por la FAO entre las nueve experiencias agroecológicas más destacadas del mundo.  


Una política pública que impulsó la agroecología


En 2011, la Comuna de Zavalla

promulgó la ordenanza (45/11)

 que prohíbe la radicación de depósitos de plaguicidas en el área urbana y suburbana, además de proscribir la circulación de vehículos cargados de agroquímicos. La norma crea

una zona de exclusión de aplicación aérea de 3.000 metros y de 800 metros terrestres en relación a la zona urbana

. Ese antecedente mereció el reconocimiento de la Red Nacional de Municipios y Comunidades que fomentan la Agroecología (Renama), que se acercó a la localidad y comenzó a colaborar con una decena de productores. En 2019, el Municipio de Zavalla se integró definitivamente a la Red.


A mediados de 2021, el gobierno comunal fue más allá y

 creó la tasa ambiental (en ese momento, de 600 pesos anuales) para financiar la transición agroecológica

. Los

fondos generados por la tasa ambiental permitían subsidiar a los productores

 —entonces, con 2.400.000 pesos al año, equivalente al costo de un arrendamiento—

para la compra de insumos, el pago del alquiler del campo donde se producía o para maquinaria específica para la producción agroecológica

.


La gestión del nuevo presidente comunal —Matías Suarez, del oficialismo santafesino; quien impidió la reelección de Guillermo Rajmil— derogó esa tasa. Sin embargo, y a pesar de todas las dificultades que van desde el plano local al nacional, los frutos de aquella política pública siguen vigentes.


Foto: Cooperativa agroecológica Zavalla


El ejido urbano de Zavalla ocupa alrededor de un cinco por ciento del territorio de la jurisdicción, el 95 por ciento restantes son tierras rurales aptas para la actividad agropecuaria primaria. De ellas,

200 hectáreas quedaron habilitadas para el desarollo agroecológico dentro de la zona de exclusión

. Nacida en 2021, al calor de la tasa ambiental, la Cooperativa de Trabajo Zavalla fue gestada por el productor Julián Graziosi, quien convocó a un grupo de pares para aprovechar el impulso comunal, el respaldo de la Renama y la contribución de la Facultad de Ciencias Agrarias de la Universidad Nacional de Rosario (FCA-UNR), sumada a la vinculación con el grupo ecologista Génesis.


“Había una política pública integral en respuesta al conflicto periurbano, basada en la construcción de una gobernanza responsable para producir alimentos a la vez que proteger el ambiente. Sobre todo, la salud de los residentes cuyas viviendas colindaban con lotes productivos”, explica Griselda Muñoz, directora de Género y Derechos Humanos de la FCA-UNR y presidenta de la Sociedad Argentina de Agroecología (SAAE).


Recuperar, producir, asociarse


En aquel 2021, Graziosi vio la oportunidad de poner en marcha un viejo molino familiar, que había quedado en desuso. El objetivo:

producir alimentos sanos, agregar valor en origen y generar fuentes laborales

 en la localidad. El paso siguiente fue alquilar 60 hectáreas dentro de las 200 que quedaron en la zona de exclusión. “Fueron años de mucho trabajo. Primero hubo que reacondicionar el molino y después empezar a producir, aprender, vender y seguir creciendo.

Hoy tenemos nuestra marca, hacemos harina integral y fuimos incorporando otros productos y comprando maquinarias para seguir agregando valor

”, cuenta Graziosi, presidente de la cooperativa.


Desde que pusieron el molino en marcha, en 2023, la cooperativa se fue posicionando en el mercado de productos orgánicos y agroecológicos y llegó a las góndolas …

author: La Zarzamora
title: Comunicado público ppm Caso Grollmus
content:
Frente a las exuberantes condenas y tras un viciado proceso declaramos:

Mari mari pu machi, pu lonko, pu werken, kom pu che. El día de hoy nos dirigimos a la sociedad en general, a todos y todas quienes nos han brindado su apoyo y respaldo en este proceso denominado “Caso Grollmus”.

Actualmente a nosotros como comuneros mapuche se nos ha condenado a penas que marcarán un precedente como obscenamente políticas, se nos condena por decisión política, por ser mapuche que vivimos y recuperamos nuestro territorio.

Tras el gigantesco despliegue comunicacional, y tras el espectáculo montado por el Ministerio Público y la PDI, la familia Grollmus demanda al estado en busca de indemnizaciones y reparaciones.

La fiscalía con el aval del tribunal logró su objetivo: condenar a una pena que ponderada resulta en 1055 años de prisión contra nosotros. La prensa vociferó la sentencia y el poder político respaldo, claridad absoluta.

Les decimos, su ocupación contra nuestro pueblo y su territorio apenas tiene 143 años. Nuestro pueblo resistió al imperio español casi 300 años.

Hoy Chile soberbio y republicano nos condena a más de 1000 años. Por el único motivo de luchar por nuestra soberanía, por nuestro buen vivir y dignidad. Lo anterior tendrá la más necesaria respuesta: continuar con el legado de nuestro pueblo, luchar por nuestra dignidad y libertad.

Los Grupos de Tarea y la BIPE de la PDI recorren los penales de forma morbosa buscando testigos a quienes poner corbata de protegido y sin rostro. Sólo por cuatro relatos de estos “testigos” se dictó sentencia y veredicto. Nuestro territorio se militariza y vuelven a saquear nuestros recursos naturales, vuelven las concesiones mineras, CMPC y Mininco cual mecenas entregan dinero y donaciones a Postas y Escuelas.

Queremos manifestar nuestro agradecimiento por todo el respaldo de nuestros hermanos y hermanas en otros territorios y ciudades. No renunciaremos jamás a la lucha por un debido y objetivo proceso.

Nos movilizaremos por nuestra libertad y juicio justo.

Finalmente los invitamos a sumarse a la próxima movilización articulada en distintos territorios para este 12 de octubre, Día de la resistencia de nuestros pueblos.

¡NULIDAD Y LIBERTAD! ¡NO MÁS TESTIGOS PROTEGIDOS! ¡UNIDAD EN EL WEYCHAN! ¡LIBERTAD A TODOS LOS PRESOS POLÍTICOS MAPUCHE!

Presos Políticos Mapuche del Caso Grollmus de la Franja Lavkenche, CP Biobio, CERECO Coronel, Cárcel Llancahue de Valdivia.

author: Comunizar
title: Revista Crítica Anticapitalista 6 – La Comuna, la clase y la lucha de clases
content:
PRESENTACION


¿Qué relación existe entre la Comuna como forma política de la emancipación social y la clase, entendida ésta no como categoría positivizada y sociológica, sino en su carácter dual y contradictorio? ¿Es la Comuna una manera de entender la clase y la lucha de clases en clave no identitaria, no positivizada? ¿La oposición entre Comuna y clase es algo derivado de una concepción anti-dialéctica de la lucha de clases? En ese campo ¿a qué dialéctica nos referimos? ¿A la dialéctica hegeliana orientada a la síntesis estatal como forma política de la identidad? ¿A la dialéctica negativa que la cuestiona? ¿La lucha de clases, entendida en clave dialéctica no-identitaria, permite entender la Comuna como proceso contradictorio de disolución de la clase? ¿Implica esto un desafío a nuestro concepto de proletariado y a la idea de revolución calcada en el canon leninista?

author: Kodao Productions
title: A supporter asks: ‘Why Is Leni Welcoming Israel?’
content:
By

 Pia Montalban


I have a question about Leni Robredo’s recent meeting with Israeli Ambassador Dana Kursh.


It is not a question I raise lightly. And it is not a question I raise because I have suddenly become an opponent of Leni Robredo.


I voted for her in 2022. I even campaigned for her in Tarlac, in the middle of that sea of pink, alongside Aeta communities. But I was never a full-fledged Kakampink. I still am not.


I supported her because, given the choices before us in 2022, there was a political calculation to make. I do not want a Marcos to return to Malacanang.


I decided to gamble. I gambled that a Robredo presidency could create more political space for the demands of workers, peasants, indigenous peoples, human rights defenders and other communities I worked with. I gambled that there would be more room to organize, to criticize, to make demands, to defend people, and to push our calls into government.


But a gamble is not surrender. People gamble on a candidate. I belong to those who did not gamble away their principles. That distinction matters to me. Because I had already questioned Leni long before I campaigned for her.


I had questions before I wore pink


In 2021, when

 Leni expressed support for the National Task Force to End Local Communist Armed Conflict

, I was deeply troubled.


For me, this was never an abstract policy question.


I had already experienced what the machinery of red-tagging and counterinsurgency could do to people like me and to the communities and organizations I worked with. The language of “security” was not neutral. It could turn organizers into suspects, defenders into enemies, and communities demanding their rights into targets.


So when I questioned Leni’s position on NTF-ELCAC, I was not asking from the safety of an academic debate about government policy. I was asking as someone who knew what it meant to be on the receiving end of that machinery.


I remember writing then that NTF-ELCAC had accomplished something terrible: it had sown deceit and fear where truth and courage should have been allowed to grow.


I asked whether Leni wanted that machinery too.


My objection was never simply about individual red-taggers or the personalities who occupied the institution. My concern was the machinery itself, and what it meant for communities already experiencing militarization, surveillance, threats and political repression.


People do not organize simply because someone gives them an ideology. People rise because their material and social conditions demand it. Farmers organize because they cannot survive on what they produce. Workers organize because wages do not meet the cost of living. Fisherfolk organize because their fishing grounds are threatened. Indigenous peoples defend their territories because someone wants to take them. Communities resist militarization because militarization changes the conditions of their everyday lives.


If the state responds to these conditions primarily through repression, it does not address the roots of social unrest. It only tries to silence its expression. And silenced anger does not disappear. It accumulates.


That was my objection to NTF-ELCAC then. It remains my objection to state repression now.


Which brings me to Israel?


This is why Leni’s meeting with Israeli Ambassador Dana Kursh should trouble us.


Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo and Tel Aviv envoy Dana Kursh. (Naga LGU Tourism Office photo)


I am not arguing that every meeting with a diplomat automatically constitutes an endorsement of everything that diplomat’s government does.


Diplomacy is complicated.


States maintain relationships with governments whose policies they disagree with. A meeting, by itself, is not proof of complete political alignment. But political acts have context. There are moments when the symbolism matters. There are moments when choosing to meet someone matters. There are moments when choosing to publicly release photographs of that meeting matters.


And Palestine is one of those moments.


Palestinians have endured occupation, dispossession, displacement and violence for decades. The catastrophe did not begin on October 7, 2023. Its history reaches much further back, through the Nakba of 1948 and the decades that followed.


Since October 7, the devastation in Gaza has reached a scale that cannot simply be treated as another diplomatic disagreement between states.


People are being killed. Families are being destroyed …

author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: VP Sara impeachment: ‘It is now about how evidence will be used’
content:
A protester raises a placard with the message “Impeach Sara” during a protest in commemoration of Bonifacio Day on November 30, 2024. Photo by Carlo Manalansan/Bulatlat

It has been more than 35 days since the commencement of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, and the prosecution panel continues to present evidence on the allegations faced by the second-highest official of the land.

For human rights lawyer and former Bayan Muna Rep. Carlos Zarate, however, the trial is no longer about confirming if there is clear evidence to convict Sara. The real fight, he stressed, is how the evidence could survive reconciliation, cross-examination, and constitutional scrutiny.

“That is where accountability can still disappear into the maze of all of this evidence,” he said during a roundtable discussion on Sara’s impeachment on Thursday, October 8. “There are now so many that either side can select the pieces most convenient to each narrative and story.”

Read: Filipinos urged to focus on morality of VP Sara’s threats

The trial is currently focused on Article II of the articles of impeachment. The said article accuses the Vice President of having unexplained wealth and false statements of assets, liabilities and net worth (SALNs).

A witness from the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) was supposed to be scheduled to testify on Thursday morning, but the prosecution proposed to present another witness instead, saying that counsel Erwin Matib was unable to attend due to health reasons. The defense panel expressed opposition, which was granted by the impeachment court.

The prosecution had already presented evidence on Article IV (alleged assassination threats) and Article I (misuse of confidential funds), while the panel decided not to pursue Article III (alleged bribery) because it said the evidence of alleged wrongdoing had already been presented.

Zarate stressed that the ultimate stakeholder in this accountability mechanism is the Filipino people, as they did not elect public officials to have unexplained wealth, questionable expenditure of funds, or to issue threats.

“Has she [Vice President Sara] lived up to her oath of office?” lawyer Christian Monsod, one of the framers of the 1987 Philippine Constitution, asked during the same discussion, saying that Sara’s threats “violated her oath to do justice to every man.”

Read: VP Sara’s assassination threats notable, difficult to refute

Renato Reyes Jr., president of Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan) said the Senate that serves as the impeachment court is not insulated from the Marcos-Duterte conflict, as well as to the widespread allegation of corruption, citing people’s sentiment that corruption cases may become a factor in how senator-judges rendered their votes in the impeachment trial.

He said this reflects the situation of a broken system. “Why corruption scandals needed to be exposed for the impeachment to move forward.”

Reyes urged Filipinos to witness the impeachment proceeding and call out those senator-judges who tend to become legally strict when it comes to the Rules of Court. The people, he said, should push accountability as the objective in the trial.

“Our voices would be the most important decisive factor in securing a Duterte conviction,” Reyes stressed. (RVO)

author: groundxero
title: Rise of Gen Z: Its Effect on West Bengal’s Politics
content:
A massive youth rally in Kolkata on 24 July, held in solidarity with protests against exam-paper leaks at Jantar Mantar in Delhi, has raised questions about the future of traditional student politics in West Bengal. With most participants being unaffiliated to political organisations, the rally appeared to signal a new form of youth and student mobilisation.

Subho Maitro

 examines what this generational shift may mean for the Left, campus democracy and the state’s wider political landscape. 


 


“Did you take permission from your parents?” a young boy of seventeen or eighteen asked the girl sitting beside him on the local train. The girl replied conspiratorially, “No, I said I’m going to a friend’s birthday party.” And they laughed,” said Kalatan Dasgupta, a young left-wing leader, describing his experience of the student and youth protest rally in Kolkata on 24 July. A massive youth rally, from Sealdah station to Esplanade, took place in solidarity with the ongoing Gen Z protest against the exam paper leak in Delhi and across the country. The rally stunned Kolkata, a city once known for its student movements and politics. Will this rally shake away the slumber and rejuvenate the present moribund student politics of West Bengal? To answer this, one must look at the prevailing atmosphere of student movements and politics in the state.


 


The massive turnout at the rally on 24 July made everyone realise that something new is happening, and Bengal cannot look away. Student protest and movement is not a new thing in West Bengal, once a bastion of left politics. From Naxalbari to the Singur and Nandigram movements, students and young in Bengal were always engaged with larger political issues. Along with that, a fiercely competitive campus politics was always present dominated by the student organizations affiliated to political parties. But it was always more about ideology than campus. Students voiced support for Vietnam and protested against the US imperialism with equal vigor as against the rise of college fees.


 


Yet from the beginning of the 21st century, with the exception of the Nandigram movement, which saw substantial student and youth participation, the politics narrowed down into campus issues only. After the end of Left Front rule, TMC came to power and the student politics changed, which also changed the nature of the politics.


 


During the last fifteen years of TMC rule, the state saw a steep decline in government jobs, especially in the education sector. The scam of the School Service Commission stalled the employment process, and even in higher education permanent employment dried up. Students fresh out of colleges and universities struggled to secure other government jobs. While in the colleges the student unions were captured by the student wing of the ruling party named Trinamul Chhatra Parishad. Their grip was firm in most places, with only one or two exceptions, such as Presidency University and Jadavpur University in Kolkata and the student union elections were withheld indefinitely. Thus, there was anger and frustration on the one hand, and little scope for campus politics on the other. SFI, the student wing of CPIM and other left-wing student organisations fought this onslaught within their limited capability. But the student politics remained more or less on campus issues and of scams around SSC which couldn’t connect to a greater mass.


 


The rape and murder of a junior doctor on duty at RG Kar Hospital changed the situation, as large numbers of students and young joined the protests, particularly women. That was one of the game changers which created a huge anger against the incumbent government. There was spontaneous participation from people across the state, especially women. But though the primary protestors were junior doctors, the movement known as ‘Abhaya Andalan’ remained apolitical overtly and left student or youth organizations though gained some ground neither could control nor lead it. In the May assembly election, the BJP seized power in the state. The right-wing BJP used this discontent to gain in the election (though the mass deletions of voters through SIR will never let us know how much gain the BJP actually made).


 


The sheer number of Gen Z protesters and the enthusiasm they brought is now raising one question – will West Bengal see a new kind of youth movement and politics in West Bengal? Traditionally here the student politics revolves around campuses …

author: Aizel Tugalon
title: Progressives renew solidarity with Palestinian resistance
content:
MANILA – Progressive formations led by Philippines-Palestine Friendship Association (PPFA), Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan), and International League of Peoples’ Struggle (ILPS) Philippines marched toward the US embassy on the third year since the Al-Aqsa flood. They condemned U.S., Israel and its allies for the continued genocide of Palestine and military aggression on West Asia.

The Al Aqsa Flood refers to the October 7, 2023 attacks led by Hamas that followed Palestine’s long history of resistance against Israel colonial rule and occupation.

For progressives, the Al-Aqsa Flood is not what the west would label as “terrorist attacks” but rather an act of resistance similar to the Philippines, rooted in decades of oppression and colonialism by imperialist nations like the U.S. and Israel. For PPFA, it is the “beacon to our own resistance… It inspires all people struggling for national and social liberation, and therefore, we must support their resistance as if it were our own.”

By the end of the program, progressives burned the flags of U.S. and Israel, calling to stop the genocide, and reaffirming to fight for genuine freedom and the downfall of Imperialism.

title: The cost of US imperialism that we are fighting against
content:
with added reports from Jessica Obciana and Kline Vergara

“Homes are destroyed, livelihoods are lost, nations are lost by interests that are made far beyond our own borders. Even now, initiatives like Pax Silica, supply chains for critical minerals and semiconductors are being reordered around the needs of the US war machine, and countries like us [the Philippines] are being asked to serve as suppliers and now become their targets, rather than being allowed to decide our own development,” said Dr. Giovanni Tapang, convener of the Stop the US-Israel War on Iran Network.

Various anti-imperialist groups gathered for the webinar Updates from the Resistance: The Current Situation in Iran, Palestine, Venezuela, and Cuba, co-organized by BAYAN, the International League of Peoples’ Struggle (ILPS) Philippines, the Philippines-Palestine Friendship Association (PPFA), and the Stop the US-Israel War on Iran Campaign Network, to express people’s solidarity in lambasting US imperialism following its sanctions, blockades, military aggression, and other forms of intervention and coercion against the people.

“This is the war machine that we are fighting against. And as we listen to those who are on the front lines, we learn of their resistance, deepen our understanding, and together strengthen solidarity to defeat this war machine,” Tapang added.

“We have seen the case of Venezuela: how this warfare has been attacking the Global South, attacking the country, and in many, many aspects, not only the political one, military, economic, and cultural, and in social consciousness. Venezuela is under siege now,” said Richard Lobo, Venezuela’s Chargé d’Affaires.

Venezuela possesses the world’s largest proven crude oil reserves, estimated at around 303 billion barrels as of 2023, according to the US Energy Information Administration.

Lobo noted that US intervention in Venezuela extends beyond economic sanctions to political, military, economic, and cultural intervention.

In January 2026, the US launched Operation Absolute Resolve as a large-scale military operation in Venezuela framed around drug trafficking and national security that led to the capture of President Nicolás Maduro and First Lady Cilia Flores and their transfer to the United States. Such an operation also targeted Venezuelan military infrastructure across Caracas and other locations.

Months after Maduro’s capture, the US laid out an agreement to gain access and control over an estimated 65 billion barrels of oil reserves, mineral wealth, and other resources.

Meanwhile, Lobo emphasized that the situation has only amplified the resistance among Venezuelans in defending their sovereignty and their right to determine the country’s political and economic direction.

“Even though we have been under attack […] the people there in Venezuela have been resisting and have been struggling. And one thing that I can say right now is that even with the kidnapping of our president, they believe the government is still in power,” Lobo stated.

More than 5,000 civilians have been killed in the US-Israel aggression against Iran, including 168 girls who were killed when a school was struck in March this year.

“Iran is experiencing aggression by the United States and Israel since the 1979 revolution against a very corrupt government, the Shah’s government. The United States has been trying to overthrow the revolutionary government in Iran, engaging in economic warfare for 46 years,” said Dr. Foad Izadi, associate professor at the University of Tehran.

The 1979 Iranian Revolution overthrew Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, whose government had maintained close relations with the US. The revolution fundamentally changed Iran’s relationship with the US, posing decades of diplomatic confrontation, economic sanctions, and political pressure.

“(The US) has also asked Iran to reduce its support for the Palestinian cause. As you know, Iran has been a strong supporter of Palestine. Not only with words, not only with speeches, but with military aid. Iran is the only country that is helping Palestinians with military aid,” said Dr. Izadi, noting that other governments should also learn from them by providing help to those countries fighting against aggression and genocide.

“Iran has learned that if you allow Israelis, genocidal people, the apartheid regime to get away with their crimes in Palestine, they they would want to take over the Middle East and go beyond,” he added.

author: ALR Editors
title: Announcing Asian Labour School Oct-Nov 2026 Semester
content:
Dear friends,


We are back with an amazing list of new and returning courses for the Asian Labour School. If you are interested in

acquiring democratic facilitation skills, navigating conflicts and taking collective care, working cooperatively, strengthening a union core or leading your own radical walking tours

, please check out the course information below and study with Asian Labour School.


Building Movement Democracy through Democratic Facilitation (Course Starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Facilitator: Chie Matsumoto


We all have attended meetings where decisions were made by only a few members, most outspoken ones or someone at the top. We may have once thought, “Why am I even here?” and left without saying a word. Democracy starts in the smallest conversations, dialogues and meetings by raking in most diverse opinions and ideas, piecing them together to create something new and meaningful to all participants.


Building Movement Democracy through Democratic Facilitation (Course Starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Worker Cooperatives: Can Cooperating Transform How We Work Together? (Course Starts on Oct 10, 2026)


Facilitators: Emi Do and Matt Noyes


Worker cooperatives are enterprises that are owned and governed by workers. When all of our working experiences have been in profit-maximizing enterprises, or in workplaces that are structured hierarchically, it is no wonder that we can encounter challenges when attempting to work together cooperatively. In this course we will explore the challenges and tensions when there are no bosses to hate!


Worker Cooperatives: Can Cooperating Transform How We Work Together? (Course Starts on Oct 10, 2026)


Careful, We’re Organizing aka How to Fight without Falling Apart (Course Starts on Oct 21, 2026)


Facilitator: Nash Tysmans


Movements are built through relationships. Yet the pressures of organizing (urgency, conflict, exhaustion, political disagreement, and unequal power) can strain those relationships and undermine our collective capacity. How can we build movements that are both effective in challenging injustice and caring in how we work together?


Careful, We’re Organizing aka How to Fight without Falling Apart (Course Starts on Oct 21, 2026)


Building Strong Union Committee at Workplace (Course starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Facilitator: Sithar Chhim


In order to win any campaign at workplace, unions need to be strong enough to pressure the company. Building a strong and representative committee is the only way to win over the bosses who have well organized structure at workplace compare to workers.


Building Strong Union Committee at Workplace (Course starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Designing Radical Walking Tours (Course Starts on Oct 12, 2026)


Facilitator: Kevin Lin


Have you ever thought about leading your own radical walking tour to share with friends the significance of places and histories in your city? Leading and participating in a radical walking tour is not only educational but fun and always memorable. A walking tour provides a concrete sense of places, people, and histories. This course will walk you through the conceptualisation, research and logistics of a radical walking tour, and hear ideas and experiences from other participants across Asia.


Designing Radical Walking Tours (Course Starts on Oct 12, 2026)

author: rti_admin
title: Why do we Protest? A Moral and Philosophical Basis
content:
The protests that have sparked in most South Asian countries in the last few years have sparked hope for socio-political, economic, and cultural change. Bangladesh’s protest over the job crisis in 2024, Nepal’s Gen Z protest (2025), and Sri Lanka’s protest of 2022 shocked the nations and their corrupt political systems. The Gen Z protest forced ruling BJP minister Dharmendra Pradhan in India to resign and raised demands for educational reform and accountability in 2026. The growing unrest of youths and their protests demand an objective analysis. This article asks some fundamental questions on the moral, philosophical, existential, and political basis of protest. More than answering the question of why we protest, this article is about why we should protest. While the outward manifestation and result of protest are obvious, the inward changes that protest brings are pertinent in shaping the morale of individuals in particular and society in general.

Let us ask, therefore, why shall we protest? Do we protest because we are bad? Bad as citizens, bad as human beings, bad daughters, and sons? Why do our youth protest? Why does this act of protest arouse so much fear? Fear from society and the state. Aristotle writes that “young men (and women) have strong passions and tend to gratify them indiscriminately” (Aristotle 2012). The younger generation possesses tremendous energy, creative force, and potential. More importantly, they are full of life, and life, to thrive, needs proper conditions that the current regime has failed to provide. However, it is the nature of life to expand itself. Hence, the protest of the youths. The old society, religion, and state use force to serve their purpose, and they try to control the boundless possibilities of youths. When any social and political structure downplays human nature and the necessities of life, we can no longer contain ourselves and remain silent. There is a limit to the control of the inner nature of humanity. Family, society, religion, and political power have always been terrified of human nature. They are forever trying to control, subjugate, and overpower the true potential of humanity.

Gods came, religion came, and then came the state! But is it possible to contain our boundless humanity that runs in our veins? History has proven again and again that it has never been, and never will be, able to suppress the beauty of humanity. The way religion, society, and the state forever wish to control individuals, individuals, in return, have forever rebelled and protested in every way possible. No god, no religion, no society, or no state can contain our boundless humanity. Is it possible to contain a forever-flowing river? We might try to control and put a brake on its flow for a temporary period of time, or it may dry out in a particular season. But for how many days? For how many seasons and years? It will return in the next season; it will return next time; eventually, with more vigorous force, it will make its own course. Nothing can stop it from reaching its destination.

In the same way, human beings possess immense potentiality. Hence, their free actions, thinking, and will cannot be stopped. Protest and rebellion can manifest in different ways. It may not always be political in nature. Sometimes it is chaotic, enigmatic, mysterious, decadent, and even in the form of telling the truth. When politics reduces to a level of tyranny, we rebel not only in the political domain but also in art, literature, science, and even in philosophy. Rebellion is a part of human life and its very existence. Reducing everyone who reads, thinks, and creates to the level of ‘Dimagi Naxal’ by none other than Narendra Modi, PM of India, is absurd and brands basic human nature and constitutional rights as criminality. His comments came in the wake of the Gen Z protest that was led by highly educated minds of India. Hence, delegitimising them while branding them with various tags is an act unbecoming of a leader of the nation. It must have been an act of rebellion that attracted people in power. All of these are various forms of negotiation with the existing socio-political structure. When we refuse the dictates of family, society, religion, or the state, that act of refusal becomes a site of protest. The protest must be understood as an act of negation. Camus rightly asked, “What is a rebel? A man who says no” (Camus 2013). While saying ‘no’ to negative politics, organisations, and beliefs …

author: Tom Sullivan
title: Housing protests lead to general strike in Spain
content:
“I haven’t managed to defend my house, but I have tried so that others can learn how to defend theirs.” These were the words of an 87-year-old Madrid woman, Maricarmen, who posted a video from her hospital bed after Spanish authorities evicted her from the apartment she had lived in for the past 71 years. In the video, she promoted an upcoming protest at Madrid’s Plaza del Sol “so that we can eliminate this problem once and for all”.

Her eviction sparked a fire across the Spanish state. Within days, protesters had set up an encampment in the Plaza del Sol, famously the site of mass anti-austerity protests in 2011. They quickly spread to dozens of other cities, along with mass protests. A few days later came the first victory of the movement, when the vulture fund that had bought Maricarmen’s apartment building agreed to allow her to return with a new, eight-year contract and her rent capped at 30 percent of her pension.

But this victory only fuelled the protests. On Saturday 3 October, nationally coordinated rallies saw around half a million people protest across the country. Three days later, the country’s two major union confederations called a general strike.

Few recent examples illustrate the power of protest as clearly as the last two weeks in the Spanish state. When the authorities forced their way into Maricarmen’s apartment, she was meant to be just another of the nearly 70 people who are evicted from their homes every day across the country. But the footage of her being removed on a stretcher into an ambulance tapped into a rage that millions of people feel living at the whim of the housing market.

In Spain, it is particularly sharp. Over the last decade, rental prices have risen by more than 80 percent, according to the National Institute of Statistics. And the market is becoming increasingly concentrated in the hands of a small minority. From 2008 to 2025, the share of single property owners fell by 4 percent, while the share of people with at least ten properties rose by 35 percent, according to a recent government report.

These statistics prove the main point of the Tenants’ Union, the group leading the protests: the main problem is that under capitalism, housing is a commodity for investors to make a profit from and not a basic good provided to all people. They’ve combined this general perspective with a series of concrete demands, including automatic renewal of rental contracts, a 50 percent rent reduction, and the expropriation of empty properties.

Importantly, the union’s approach has been to spread the protests, while also raising new, more radical slogans as the movement developed. In the first few days, the movement played out under the generally defensive slogan “Not one more Maricarmen”. But as the movement exploded, the slogan shifted to “towards a general strike,” directly calling on the two major union confederations to call one.

Since Maricarmen’s eviction, the government of Pedro Sanchez’s Socialist Party (PSOE) and its junior partner Sumar, heavily influenced by the Communist Party, has scrambled to respond. It put forward two bills in parliament, including measures such as a pause on evictions until 2030 and indefinite rental contract extensions, with twelve months’ compensation for tenants if landlords break the agreement. However, the government is a minority in parliament and, among other parties, it relies on the centre-right Catalan independence party, Junts, to pass any laws. Junts joined the right to defeat the two bills.

Even though the government put forward the bills knowing they would be defeated, the fact that they included reforms like a pause on evictions until 2030 illustrates the power of the movement. Similarly, the movement’s rejection of the bills as inadequate testifies to mass popular support for genuine solutions to the housing crisis and a radical approach to achieving them. A recent poll published in elDiario.es showed 73 percent support for a general strike, 58 percent support for the main encampment in Madrid, and that 40 percent of people would be prepared to engage in a rent strike.

With the bills defeated, however, Sanchez is dissolving parliament and calling snap elections for 29 November. It’s a shrewd political move. His message will be simple: the right-wing parties used their majority to block housing reform, so a majority Socialist Party government is necessary to get real action.

But Sanchez’s record shows how fickle this message is. He is a …

author: @ndy
title: Yeah Nah Pasaran #300 w Emma Hagberg on ‘Comrades, Not Friends’ & The Revolutionary Front : October 8, 2026
content:
This week on Yeah Nah Pasaran! we talk to Emma Hagberg. Emma is the author of Comrades, Not Friends: The Revolutionary Front, Antifascism, and Class Struggle (PM Press/Working Class History, 2026), translated by Gabriel Kuhn and with a preface by Tomas Rothaus (both of whom have been previous guests of the show).

According to Hagberg, RF had ‘a strong collective identity, the view of fascists as class traitors, and the critique of an autonomous left that often had no place for working-class people’; Comrades was originally published in Swedish as 18.6 – Kamrater, Inte Vänner (B.E.L Publishing, 2024) and is also available in a German translation.

The Revolutionary Front (RF), 2001–2015, was the most militant organization on the left in recent Swedish history. Staunchly working class, the first generation of RF members engaged in numerous street battles with Swedish fascists. When the fascists retreated from the streets, RF attacked them in their homes. The police cracked down on the organization in 2013, raiding the apartments of several alleged members at the crack of dawn. The courts handed out prison sentences of up to six and a half years. Two years later, the organization folded.

See also : Presentation on the book about Revolutionära Fronten (Revolutionary Front) (April 13, 2025).

author: AWSM
title: Why I Won’t Vote ~ A SYMPOSIUM #1
content:
Anarchy 37, March 1964, Why I Won’t Vote

Voting : “The instrument and symbol of a freeman’s power to make a fool of himself and a wreck of his country”

The saying that ” only a fool would put a loaded gun into the hands of an idiot ” is an especially apt analogy of government. An idiot (usually well-meaning) considers himself clever enough to run the affairs of a large number of people by taking a seat in parliament. A large number of people, acting like fools, vote for his party’s policy then spend the next few years grumbling about the results. The error in approach is that the voter thinks that he will get what he voted for. If he could vote for those who in fact control the country, say the Governors of the Bank of England, the directors of the industrial corporations and those behind the ministries, the illusion of democracy would be more understandable.

The real centres of power lie far beyond the people’s influence at elections. These remain constant whatever Party is ” in power “. In the terms of centralised ” democracy ” the only possible argument to justify voting is that marginal benefits may be gained. The state only incidentally attends to the well-being of its subjects. Its main concern is its power relation to other states, of which the most perfect expression is in war.

I am on the side of people anywhere who are prepared neither to live nor die for something that in the long run can only militate against survival and the conditions that make life worth living. Our immediate action must, by its nature, be to oppose that pathetic gesture, voting. It must be direct and direction. We can learn to live as free men and women only by organising against the condition we are in.

The Tenants Association, Consumers Association, and Direct Action in industry all provide opportunities for people to experience directing their own lives in positive ways towards positive ends.

Only by direct involvement in society can the individual hope to transform himself and his world. Freedom cannot be given, it must be taken; and the free society can only grow from experiments in the problems (ethical and organisational) of community.

Voting does not, and cannot, mean government by consent. By voting, one acts on the assumptions that certain men are fit to govern, and that a majority is necessarily right. Also should the state, acting in the name of a (frequently fictitious) majority, declare war, the individual loses the right to live, if he ever had it.

To me, voting is complicity with the State and a negative action, therefore I do not vote.

author: Lance Selfa
title: What’s up with Jacobin’s “Working-Class Win-o-Meter”?
content:
Every few months, 

Jacobin 

magazine announces what it purports to be a secret to win working-class voters based on a finding from its associated Center for Working Class Politics (CWCP). Its 14 September editorial “

Report: The Working Class Vote is Not Lost

” was the latest in this series.

CWCP’s latest innovation is the “Working-Class Win-o-Meter”, which Jacobin describes as “a data-driven road map for winning back working-class voters”. It purports to demonstrate the optimal combination of social and political appeals to move working-class voters to vote for a hypothetical Democratic candidate.

Two points should be made at the outset. When

 Jacobin

 and CWCP talk about “winning working class voters,” they don’t mean winning the working class to socialism. They mean “winning” the working class to vote for Democrats. And they define the “working class” as non-college-educated people with family incomes of between $30,000 and $150,000.

This supposedly groundbreaking survey and analysis is an exercise in political message-testing for Democratic candidates. It uses the definition of “working-class” that is the standard in lazy polling and media commentary, and thus adds no new insights. Attaching the labels of “socialist” and “working-class” doesn’t change the fact that what

 Jacobin

 and CWCP are engaged in is a completely conventional activity that regularly earns millions for Democratic Party consultants.

Without digressing into a long discussion of the inadequacies of the study’s understanding of class, it’s worth pondering why, under its definition, a non-college educated small business owner is “working class” but a college-educated nurse or K-12 teacher who is a union activist is not considered working-class. It’s the same sort of logic that 

had Democratic Socialists of America (DSA)-adjacent consultants and 

Jacobin

 fawning over

 working-class avatar “oyster farmer” Graham Platner as a US Senate candidate in Maine before Platner’s campaign imploded.

The study’s key findings include “lead with working-class economics” and “adopt culture and climate positions that resonate with working-class voters”. These takeaways are supposed to increase the hypothetical Democratic candidate’s support over what it calls a “Kamala Harris-2024 style Democrat.”

For working-class economics or economic populist policies, the winning positions come from a list of ordinary policies from tuition-free community college to protecting Social Security from cuts to capping prescription-drug prices. There is nothing wrong with these proposals. But they are hardly bold. In fact, many of them are the same poll-tested offerings that Democratic Party politicians have included in their campaigns for years.

The fact that they are repackaged here as keys to victory should emphasise how little the Democrats have done to implement these when they have held power in the past. And it’s noteworthy that “Medicare for All,” the signature proposal that social democrats like 

Jacobin

 and DSA have championed for more than a decade, didn’t make the list.

But what really gives the game away are the “culture and climate” positions the analysis considers

losing

 messages for Democratic politicians. For anyone who is familiar with 

Jacobin’s

 antipathy to 

“subcultural leftism”

, the losing positions won’t surprise: reducing funding for police, “abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE),” and letting “trans girls play in girls’ sports.” Other so-called “social issues,” such as defence of abortion rights, don’t significantly move the needle toward the Democrats, CWCP finds.

Mainstream Democratic Party campaigns in the midterm electoral cycle are following this script without even dialling up the “Win-o-Meter”. It’s an article of faith that serious Democratic candidates run on “kitchen-table issues” like the price of groceries and gasoline, and “don’t take the bait” by engaging with Republicans over “silly culture war” issues. Or they try to get ahead of the Republican attacks by pre-emptively jumping to the conservative side. For example, Texas U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico said he too 

opposes trans girls in girls’ sports

. As the liberal journalist 

Perry Bacon

 explained:

“‘Economic issues not cultural wars’ produces a party that both loses elections and abandons moral causes and vulnerable people. That’s not a theoretical argument—it’s the story of the Democratic Party of my entire adulthood. The …

author: John Mullen
title: France: Workers mobilise to support inspiring school student revolt
content:
There were vibrant mass demonstrations in dozens of French towns, on October 6, as five of the nation's six main trade union confederations mobilised in support of the escalating school student movement.

Entering its third week, the historic uprising against years of cuts in school budgets continues to gain momentum in the face of brutal police violence and state panic.

The movement has involved far more high schools than the last comparable movement eight years back. More than 1000 high schools (for 15 to 18-year-olds) and more than 100 middle schools (for 11 to 15-year-olds) have been blockaded.

Thirty universities have joined the movement in the past few days.

Daily student mass meetings in every establishment decide on the day’s actions. On the demonstrations you can see thousands of home-made placards with imaginative slogans. They range from quoting the 1793 Declaration of the Rights of Man (on the duty of insurrection) to quoting popular rap artists; from “Generation X, Generation Z, one struggle!” to “The 6-7 generation is aiming at 68” (referring to the uprising of May-June 1968).

Desperate to extinguish the flames of revolt, authorities resorted to mass lockouts, preemptively closing hundreds of schools and several university campuses this week.

Macron’s minority government, eager to pass its austerity budget before the end of the year, has reacted in three ways:

First, with violence and intimidation. In the hope of scaring away as many young protesters as possible, they ensured that the police repression was extreme. A couple of hundred teenagers have been injured by cops, and some of the examples are heartbreaking.

In the Paris region, an officer fired a tear gas canister point-blank into the face of a 14-year-old boy, shattering his jaw in two places and knocking out all his teeth; his family is now suing for attempted murder. In Tours, a 16-year-old lost an eye to a rubber bullet fired directly at him — on video, police can be heard boasting about blinding protesters.

Elsewhere, multiple students suffered severe eye injuries. A viral video captured an officer pinning a young girl in a violent chokehold, while in Lens, a bystander schoolchild lost a hand to an exploding crowd-dispersal grenade (he did not “pick it up” as the media have claimed).

In a further attempt to intimidate, more than 5000 young people have been arrested — only 1800 were subsequently charged with an offence. Even now, the government refuses to rein in the police thugs. Interior minister Laurent Nuñez spoke on October 6 of “supposed excesses” in police action, while former minister Bruno Retailleau demanded loudly that the age of criminal responsibility be lowered.

Secondly, the government has offered tiny concessions, which are only cosmetic. Proposals to hike some higher education tuition fees were abruptly shelved, and school student union leaders have been invited to talks with the education minister. The regime has also launched a token online portal for grievances and they have scheduled managed "consultation sessions" in all schools for the end of the week.

Finally, a propaganda offensive is trying to paint the young people as manipulated by the radical left organisation la France Insoumise (France in Revolt, FI). The old lie of “outside agitators” is being mobilised, because the FI is playing an excellent role in the movement.

Even previously sceptical far-left commentators have written that the young protestors consider the FI to be their party. Its leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon insisted that FI Members of Parliament and local elected councillors position themselves between the police and students to help protect them. All of them were present and vocal in denouncing police violence.

In parliament, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said one could not speak of “police violence” and complained that the FI “were implying that the police forces of the Republic … were racist”!

School student leaders are not fooled by the cosmetic concessions, and are showing their confidence by announcing a new day of action, only two days after the previous one. Trade union leaders could learn from the youngsters, but are dragging their feet, suggesting a strike in November.

The establishment media are working hard at slandering the movement and twisting the truth.

Media watchdog, Acrimed, measured the time spent discussing the events on the prime-time national public news channel, France 2, this week. It found that 75% of the time …

author: Yuanyi Tham
title: Mega Anthropic data centre to blight Queensland
content:
Queensland is set to become home to Australia’s largest AI data centre. Last month, Liberal National Party Premier David Crisafulli announced a landmark deal with Anthropic to develop the Western Downs Digital Park, near the town of Dalby, about 250 kilometres northwest of Brisbane. Led by Singaporean developer Zerra DC, the site will be constructed in four phases, with the first building expected to be operational next year.

The data centre will occupy 725.5 hectares, an area twice the size of New York’s Central Park. Its estimated value is $32 billion, nearly five times the 2032 Brisbane Olympics infrastructure budget.

Data centres suck up huge amounts of power, driving up energy prices and accelerating climate change. When fully constructed, electro-mechanical engineer Dr Andreas Helwig told the ABC it would use the equivalent of 25 to 30 percent of Queensland’s total energy consumption.

The data centre will run primarily on electricity generated by coal and gas, drawn from the state’s electricity grid. Greenpeace estimates that the data centre would raise the grid’s emissions by 6.6 million tonnes, the equivalent of two million extra cars on the road.

Last month, Crisafulli wrestled with the federal government and eventually won a state exemption from the requirement that data centres run on renewable energy. The exemption, Crisafulli argued, was simply “common sense”; according to him (and now the Labor cabinet), environmental protections shouldn’t get in the way of AI investment opportunities.

While workers worry about AI’s impact on their jobs, power bills and the environment, Crisafulli has never been happier. He celebrated the data centre deal as the fruits of his five-day trip to the US in early September, where he met with the CEOs of OpenAI and Anthropic. On the same trip, he met with US Vice President J.D. Vance and discussed Queensland’s potential to become the next link in the American critical minerals supply chain.

Crisafulli’s MAGA meetings highlight that this data centre is a story of more than just environmental degradation and corporate greed. Attracting investment in areas like AI and critical minerals is a part of a broader mission to strengthen Australia’s alliance with the US. The data centre boom is driven in part by the AI arms race between the US and China. In this context, striking a deal with the US’s largest AI corporation is not just a step towards turning Queensland as an AI investment hub. It also further integrates the Australian and US economies, so both countries are better placed to outpace competitors in the global tech arena.

Anthropic’s new project adds to the 225 other data centres currently in development in Australia and supported by both major parties. Politicians and tech billionaires have no compunction about the impact of their actions on people or the environment, so long as they are making money and moving up the imperialist pecking order. We need a political alternative that will fight for an immediate moratorium on data centres and a socialist society where we can all have a say in the future of our lives and the planet.

author: Jonathan Strauss
title: Qld NTEU members rally against wage cuts
content:
More than 500 university workers, members of the National Tertiary Education Union (NTEU), struck from 11am on October 8 before rallying at Queens Gardens in the city.

They came from Magan-djin/Brisbane’s three universities: Griffith; Queensland University of Technology (QUT); and the University of Queensland (UQ). The rally was joined by students and other unionists.

Members of the NTEU branches at all three universities are bargaining on pay and conditions with their universities’ managements. The latter have made either below-inflation pay offers or none at all. Both QUT and UQ managements are trying to have the Fair Work Commission intervene on their behalf, while Griffith’s bosses are saying they will not negotiate until next year.

NTEU members repeatedly said the workers were the ones creating the valuable things universities provide, but are being continually squeezed for money and time by management.

They contrasted this with the recent surpluses declared by UQ and QUT managements, and the spending on buildings by Griffith, including $67 million to purchase a building, opposite the rally site, that did not have the offices needed for university activities.

NTEU members said a fair pay rise would at least maintain the value of their pay against cost-of-living rises.

They are also looking to win equity in superannuation payments for casualised staff and an end to the job cuts and spiralling workloads, including among administrative, other professional and technical staff whose work underpins academics’ teaching and research.

The range of speakers from the union’s three branches — local office bearers, casually-employed activists and others — reflected the on-the-ground activism the bargaining campaigns are achieving.

This rally was larger than a similar one during bargaining four years ago, as the development of workplace organising by the union has started to take hold.

National NTEU president Alison Barnes was the lead speaker, alongside NSW Greens Senator Mehreen Faruqi and two student union representatives. Barnes noted that the cross-campus action is inspiring.

author: Mary Ellen Murphy
title: Hospital doctors strike for wages, safe hours and public health
content:
In July, Victorian public hospital doctors voted 97 percent in favour of taking industrial action for the first time in 20 years. The reason is simple: the healthcare system is unsafe for patients and staff.

The Victorian healthcare system is in crisis. Systemic failures at every level compound one another. Limited access to primary care and community services leaves people more unwell and reliant on emergency departments for care. This results in long wait times, overcrowding and unsafe workloads.

Bed shortages, often caused by delays in discharging patients due to the lack of support services, are also an issue. For example, recent data from the Victorian Health Department shows that nineteen of 21 mental health units fail to admit acutely unwell patients from the emergency department within eight hours. This results in staff attempting to care for patients in under-resourced and unsuitable environments in which they are at greater risk of violence. The lack of suitable facilities for mental health patients and adequate staffing also contributes to the ongoing failures to meet goals for the reduction in use of restrictive interventions such as seclusion and restraint.

It is no wonder then that burnout is endemic among public hospital doctors like me working in this broken system. We are expected to be machines and cope with unsafe workloads, under-resourcing and excessive hours without complaint. The system relies on unpaid overtime, guilt and obligation to keep going.

Our industrial claims highlight the punishing hours and minimal protections Victorian doctors currently face. They include a pay rise in line with what the nurses won in 2024, better guarantees of overtime for all non-rostered hours worked, permanent employment as a default model (instead of many thousands of “junior” hospital doctors, many with over a decade of experience, being given only yearly contracts), maximum shift lengths of 12.5 hours (rather than the 14 hours commonly worked at the moment), at least four rostered days off per fortnight including two consecutive days, a maximum of four consecutive night shifts, minimum doctor-to-patient ratios for safe care and mandatory 30-minute paid rest breaks every five hours.

During the fourteen months of unsuccessful bargaining discussions, the Victorian Hospitals Industrial Association (the association of employers in the public health industry) backpedalled on its previous agreement to simplify overtime payments, arguing it would cost too much to pay doctors the hours they actually work.

It is not only at work that public hospital employees are coming under attack. Over the last few months, we have seen our regulator, AHPRA, conflate antisemitism with anti-Zionism to silence healthcare workers speaking up about Palestine, including outside of work and on social media. This violates democratic rights and sets a terrible precedent for other professions. Many healthcare workers feel particularly obliged to advocate for Palestinians based on our roles as health workers. We suffer moral injury when we are prevented from speaking out about the atrocities committed against our colleagues in Gaza and against the Palestinian people as a whole.

When confronted about the lack of a public response to this attack on our freedom of speech, the Victorian branch of the Australian Medical Association admitted it was scared to address it publicly for fear of backlash, and that the federal organisation was engaged in back-room discussions with AHPRA. This approach aligns more with a lobby organisation than a trade union.

A union’s strength comes from its members’ involvement and activity. This also protects unions when they want to speak out about political issues important to their members. There is a reason that the Australian Salaried Medical Officers Federation (the part of the Australian Medical Association that is engaged in bargaining) in New South Wales—the branch involved most recently in prolonged industrial action with an active rank and file—was the only branch of our union that put out a statement condemning the AHPRA adoption of the pro-Israel International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance definition of antisemitism.

Turning to the current campaign for a better agreement in Victoria, we have so far had multiple four-hour stop-works across different sites and services on different days. At these rallies, workers were asked to vote on whether they supported a statewide strike on 14 September. The …

author: Rachel Evans, Mark Gillespie
title: Inquest into Jesse Deacon’s shooting by NSW Police ends
content:
Jesse Deacon’s coronial inquest, which ended on October 2, heard details about the actions of NSW Police in July 2023 which led to his death.

A coronial inquest aims to establish what happened in the lead up to the death of a person, and the people involved in the incident.

Police forcibly entered the 43-year old’s home, ostensibly for a welfare check, on July 20 of that year. Jesse was kettled by three police, with one tasering him and another fatally shooting him in the back.

Judy Deacon, Jesse’s mother, represented herself and questioned the witnesses. She was supported by Leesa Topic, the mother of 22-year-old Courtney Topic, who was shot dead by police in 2015.

Deacon has led a successful campaign for health providers to supply mental health responders to replace police in mental health emergencies.

Jesse was a well-read, talented artist and musician, who struggled with “treatment resistant” schizophrenia. He had spent time in inpatient mental health facilities. A shy person, he also had an illicit drug and alcohol addiction.

In 2023, a neighbour called 000 for an ambulance after Jesse asked them for a cigarette. He had a knife and was using it to cut himself.

Three police officers, Constable Riley Avery, Sergeant Hugo James and Officer A*, arrived before the ambulance. The inquest heard that they saw blood near Jesse’s apartment, but did not discuss an approach plan. Their only attempt to communicate with Jesse was Avery asking Jesse to open the door before he kicked it in.

None of the three officers had undertaken training in how to undertake mental health call-outs.

Jesse was still holding the knife when the police intruded. Still, none of the officers attempted to deescalate the situation. Jesse became trapped between two officers.

Barrister Donna Ward, senior legal counsel assisting the coroner summarised the situation as: “Riley Avery shot a taser into Jesse’s front torso. Simultaneously, Officer A* fired into Jesse’s back, which killed him.”

It took less than eight seconds from Avery kicking Jesse’s door down, to Officer A* shooting Jesse in the back. None of the three officers took up a medical first aid kit to the unit.

Deputy state coroner David O’Neil conducted the inquest over a week in July, hearing from NDIS care workers, hospital workers and police officers, and a further week over September-October.

In the second week, the inquest heard expert medical witnesses, a General Practitioner, a boarding house manager and methadone clinic witnesses.

The Deacon family, including Jesse’s father Michael Deacon and Jesse’s sister, Lucinda Deacon, also gave testimony. An accomplished soprano singer, Lucinda had compiled photos and videos of Jesse’s life and the campaign for justice with a soundtrack “Creep” by Radiohead, covered by Avie Sheck and his mother who sang in Hindi. Lucinda finished her video statement by singing “Traum”.

Deacon and the Ward put forward their recommendations for changes to policing practices, housing and mental health to the coroner, and requested that Jesse’s case be heard in court.

If the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions and the Attorney-General agree, the case could go to trial. This has only happened twice in recent history, both times under NSW Coroner Teresa O’Sullivan.

Deacon said she wants “real changes to stop these things happening again”. She has been leading a three-year fight to replace NSW Police with trained mental health responders in cases of mental health emergencies. Some $270 million over 10 years was announced for a Virtual Mental Health Hub within NSW Ambulance and eight Mental Health Acute Assessment Teams on July 30. One hundred mental health responders will replace police in parts of NSW.

“The mental health responders program is Jesse’s legacy and will save lives,” Deacon told Green Left. “There is no justice when someone dies, but at least we have this legacy. It is only a first step and needs refining and a funding boost. We also need supported accommodation.

“Jesse’s death could have been prevented if there had been enough supported accommodation for people with schizophrenia.”

Crown counsel assisting Ward admitted to the inquiry that there was “little behind the media release” of the mental health responder program. “To date, there’s no further details of the roll-out of the new initiative to have mental health trained responders attend call outs through NSW Ambulance.”

The coroner’s report is due in the next few months …

author: Vashti Fox
title: Three years of Palestine solidarity
content:
In mid-October 2023, after the first major march against Israel’s attacks on Gaza, the director of the Palestine Solidarity Campaign UK, Ben Jamal, said to his staff: “We are probably going to need to be responding to this through marches until potentially Christmas”. He was wrong. The protests did not abate. As Israel’s offensive in Gaza continued, the number of actions across the world multiplied rapidly, eventually blossoming into one of the largest and most sustained antiwar movements in generations. From the world’s largest cities to the smallest hamlets, millions of voices rose in the same chant, with the same cadence: “Free, free Palestine!” 

The numbers tell part of the story. The Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED), an international monitor, estimated that, in the three weeks after 7 October, some 3,700 demonstrations calling for a ceasefire and showing solidarity with Palestine took place in almost 100 countries and territories. In the first months of the genocide, most were in the Middle East and North Africa and were especially frequent in Yemen, Iran, Turkey and Morocco. In several of these countries, major government or religious institutions backed the demonstrations. 

In the West, however, governments were overwhelmingly hostile. In France, for instance, pro-Israel demonstrations were legal and encouraged. But the Macron government banned all Palestine solidarity demonstrations on 12 October, Interior Minister Gérald Darmanin determining that they were “likely to generate public disorder”. Nevertheless, on 22 October, 15,000 people took to the streets chanting “Gaza, Paris is with you!”

Two years after 7 October, ACLED provided data to SBS Australia showing 50,122 Gaza-related protests, the overwhelming majority in support of Palestinians—more than 40,000 Palestine solidarity events took place between 7 October 2023 and 5 September 2025. In contrast, just 3,120 pro-Israel demonstrations took place, more than two-thirds of them (2,159) held in Israel. 

What was striking about these actions was not simply their geographic breadth but their regularity. While the movement against the Iraq war in 2003 organised the largest single set of coordinated antiwar demonstrations in history, attracting an estimated 12 to 14 million people on 14 and 15 February, it did not sustain such mass mobilisations. The Palestine solidarity movement, by contrast, mobilised consistently over three years. London, for example, hosted the largest demonstrations in the UK, with 100,000 on 21 October, 70,000 on 28 October, 30,000 on 4 November, and 300,000 on 11 November 2003. Then, in 2024, 400,000 attended a demonstration on 9 March, followed by 200,000 again in March, April and October. 

Israel is a major participant in US-dominated imperial capitalist networks, and governments across the world (of all political colours) have been reluctant to break economically, politically or even symbolically from the Israeli-US coalition. Mass mobilisations, regardless of how mass and how determined they are, are unlikely on their own to force a government to break these relationships, especially in this new era of intensifying imperial competition. The stakes are simply too high. 

Nevertheless, the Palestine demonstrations were important for several reasons. They aimed not just to express moral outrage at Israel’s brutality but also to push their own governments for a change of policy. The demonstrations first demanded (with many local specificities) a ceasefire, and then, the longer the genocide continued, that their own governments break militarily, economically and diplomatically from Israel itself. 

Furthermore, the size and consistency of the demonstrations forced the issue of Gaza into the public debate. Governments responded differently to these protest movements, but most Western countries (with the notable exception of the USA) eventually backed the call for a ceasefire. (Of course, it was too late to stop the murder of tens of thousands of Gazans.). Some European governments, such as Spain and Ireland, moved more significantly in the direction of breaking ties with Israel, while others enacted more symbolic changes such as the recognition of Palestine and increased measures against Israeli settlements in the West Bank. None of these stances was anywhere near enough, but they likely would not have happened without the protest movement.

While protest movements’ impact on governments matters, the …
