author: Julius Gavroche
title: Lessons from high school students in rebellion
content:
from

lundimatin

 #536, 05/10/2026


A surprise lesson

. It was the surprise of the start of the school year, one that no one saw coming, let alone predicted. While everyone seemed resigned to waiting for the next presidential election to hope for change, high school students burst onto the scene and shook all political agendas. Starting in a few high schools in the Paris suburbs, the revolt quickly spread throughout France. Without any leading organisation, without a party or union pulling the strings; just groups of students self-organising, blocking the entrance to their schools, and spreading the word among themselves and on social media; a sign that embers were beginning to rekindle beneath the ashes, just waiting for a spark to ignite the blaze.


This has been a spontaneous, unpredictable, and sudden revolt, like all revolts. As with the emergence of the Yellow Vest movement in the fall of 2018, and so many other social uprisings before it, in the fall of 2026, all political attention seemed destined to focus, inevitably, on the upcoming presidential elections, once again reducing aspirations for change to the bleak choice of the ballot box, to delegating power over one’s own destiny to others.


Defying all predictions, and disregarding the electoral calendar with a carefree attitude, the high school students wanted to say, first and foremost, that they existed, that their present and future lives had value. Even though, as minors, they had no right to vote and no added value for political parties.


They had reasons to revolt. Those put forward, relayed by the student unions, denounced overcrowded classrooms, fragmented and restrictive schedules, unfilled teaching positions, and dilapidated and unsanitary school buildings. They also denounced the humiliation and incongruity of the cell phone ban in schools, given that their teachers, like the parliamentarians who voted for it, were constantly glued to their phones. They were treated like children who needed to be punished and disciplined, even though they were young adults who refused to resign themselves to a bleak and undesirable future.


Clearly, behind the structural reasons for the lack of resources and the state’s disinvestment in national education, lie deeper criticisms. At its core, it is a denunciation of the school system of a so-called Republic which, under the guise of formal equality, merely reproduces and perpetuates class and racial privilege and discrimination.


A lesson in sociology

. What is entirely new in the history of student revolts, from 1968 to the present day, is that the movement of autumn 2026 is not led by students from the city center, by offspring of the bourgeoisie who have (temporarily) deviated from their social class, but by high school students from working-class neighbourhoods. Moreover, those most mobilised in the struggle appear to be students from vocational high schools, already steered toward work and excluded from higher education. Furthermore, images of the blockades show that many of the rebellious high school students have Black or brown skin. These are young French people, of course, representing this new France which, while not recognised and appreciated by white supremacists (except, marginally, for the performances of PSG football players and the national football team), embodies its history and its future.


This is very likely why the State and its government decided, from the very first blockades, not to listen to the voices, the grievances, the demands of the striking high school students, but to repress them immediately and brutally. It’s unspoken, hidden, certainly not openly displayed, but how can one not suspect that behind the (completely unnecessary) decision to immediately resort to force in response to the students’ demands, there lies a deep-seated racism embodied by the Minister-Prefect of Police and so many officers under his command? That, like

Éric Zemmour

 and many other descendants of Oran settlers,

Laurent Nuñez

 is consumed by resentment and a visceral hatred towards Arabs and Muslims? That the police, accustomed to hunting down young Arabs and Black people in the housing projects under the pretext of fighting drugs, do not feel justified in beating high school students who fit the same physical profile?


A grammar lesson

. To unleash the full force of the repression, ministers, police officers, and complicit journalists set up the discrediting machine. While acknowledging …

author: groundxero
title: Jantar Mantar SIR Protests Day 2: Three Women Register Molestation Complaints Against Delhi Police Officers Including ACP, Journalists Protest Outside Police Station
content:
An independent journalist’s protest erupted outside the Parliament Street police station on 3 October 2026 after police refused to register an FIR in the case of an on duty female journalist’s complaint of molestation and assault against ACP Vivek Bhagat, only to find that several other FIRs had also not been registered. Repeated incidents of violence against women and journalists have surfaced during the protests against CEC Gyanesh Kumar. 


 


New Delhi, 3 October 2026


by

Mouli Sharma


 


After a long, spontaneous demonstration by over a hundred people, largely independent journalists, outside the Parliament Street police station between the hours of 6 PM and 11 PM, the Delhi police reluctantly accepted three complaints of molestation and assault against its officials, including ACP Vivek Bhagat.


 


The agitation began after Rosy, a journalist from News Diggy was allegedly assaulted by Bhagat while on duty covering the protests against Gyanesh Kumar in the now blockaded region of Central Delhi, following which she attempted to file an FIR against the powerful official, which the police refused to register.


 


“The Delhi Police Act entails the provision for preliminary investigation in the case of an allegation against a police officer,” said Inspector Ramesh Kumar Singh of the Parliamentary Street Police Station, who spoke to the protesting reporters after nearly five hours of continuous agitation. For these five hours, the police delayed providing even a receiving copy of the complaint or registering it in the police diary. Despite sexual assault being a cognizable offence (BNS 76), the universal provision for the immediate registry of an FIR in such a case apparently does not extend to police officers under the Delhi Police Act, 1978, said Kumar. He also mentioned that the, “Lalita Kumari judgment has been overturned, and we are no longer required to follow it,” referring to the landmark judgment which ruled out the conduct of ‘preliminary investigations’ of the kind that the police is now set to undertake in the case, which seeks to ascertain a complaint’s ‘veracity’ before the criminal investigative process (which begins with the FIR) has even begun.


 


Further, after the News Diggy team gave a call for a spontaneous protest by the city’s independent journalists in the early evening to ensure the receipt of the complaint and registry of an FIR (the former of which they succeeded in achieving after five gruelling hours outside the barricaded station), it was found that two other women had been attempting to register sexual assault complaints against police officers for their conduct during ostensible “security operations” in the region. A fourth complainant withdrew her submission upon facing familial and social pressure, while a fifth complainant, independent journalist Suhana Khan was categorically denied entry into the station.


 


“The worst part of the way these male officers conduct their so-called security operations,” Khan said, “which just means beating people, is they’ll often ask your name first. I was beaten on my privates during the July protests, I had to get stitches. My clothes were torn. And because they asked my name before doing so, I can say with certainty that they did this to me because my name is Suhana Khan.”


 


Journalists from Molitics, Khabar Lehriyan, Caravan, News Diggy, Newswine, Nation Asks, AT Live, Hind Samachaar, Online News India, and of course,

GroundXero

, were among many dozens of news platforms whose correspondents were at the scene, alongside several independent content creators, social media news-makers, and influencers like Harsh Yadav, Gajendra Singh (@desiptrakar), etc. A number of lawyers had also been called to scene after the police initially denied to accept her complaint, with Adv. Vertika Mani, Adv. Mujibur Rehman, Adv. Anupradha and Adv. Bharat Kaushik eventually made their way inside the station to represent all complainants upon pressure from protesting journalists.


 


“I was screaming myself hoarse for them to let me do my duty,” said Adv. Vertika Mani. She describes the situation as one that made her feel immensely helpless, with a group of women lawyers standing outside the jail-like barricades and a victim begging to be allowed to speak to lawyers engulfed within a sea of officers inside. She describes how the police were attempting to manipulate the victim, by asking her to point out her lawyer from among the group, knowing full …

author: S. Baum
title: TN Court Rules Killing of Woman May Have Been Justifiable Because She Was Trans
content:
The ruling, the first of its kind in Tennessee history, revives elements of the infamous “trans panic” defense.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

Paris Lee was shot six times and killed by Samuel Ward Jr.; this is an indisputable fact. Ward was convicted of voluntary manslaughter in May 2025. He claimed it was self-defense, but the jury didn’t buy it.

This week, however, the Tennessee Court of Criminal Appeals reversed his conviction. A three-judge panel declared that the jury was under the impression Lee was cisgender; that in not disclosing the victim’s status as a trans woman, the trial judge “misled” the jury; and that Ward was entitled to a new trial where he could use this fact to bolster his claim of self-defense.

This story was first reported by independent journalist Jamie Satterfield. Other outlets and LGBTQ organizations also reported on Lee’s death at the time, with some referring to her as Kitty Monroe, which was her name on social media.

“After a short deliberation, a Shelby County jury found Samuel Ward guilty of voluntary manslaughter in the shooting death of Paris Lee, concluding a case that revealed inconsistencies between the defendant’s claims and the physical evidence presented in court,” a May 2025 press release from the Shelby County District Attorney reads. “Ward claimed self-defense throughout the trial, but the jury rejected his narrative and found him guilty.”

The appellate judges did not contest any of the evidence. Rather, they took issue with one facet of the trial in particular: The original court had disallowed the defense from disclosing Lee’s sex assigned at birth to the jury, finding that it would cause an undue prejudice against the victim.

Ward’s defense appealed, and a panel of judges was tasked with answering several procedural questions: Did Ward have a right to use his victim’s sex assigned at birth as part of his defense? Moreover, did the trial judge dilute Ward’s right to defend himself by striking references to Lee’s assigned sex from the record?

“A deadly weapon is a deadly weapon is a deadly weapon,” the judge explained at trial. “Whether that person has a vagina or a penis has no bearing on the deadliness of a firearm.”

But the panel disagreed. They found that prohibiting the disclosure of Lee’s transgender status was prohibiting potentially exculpatory evidence for Ward.

“The State conceded that if the proof showed the victim’s assigned sex was the reason for the altercation between Defendant and the victim, it would be relevant to the adequate provocation element of voluntary manslaughter,” court documents read. “However, the State argued, the proof at trial would establish that the victim ‘was a large woman’ who was armed with a [firearm] and, therefore, the victim’s assigned sex was not relevant to the issue of self-defense.”

Conversely, Ward’s lawyers argued that Lee’s status as a trans woman impacted “how much fear” Ward felt, and therefore, how justifiable his actions were in the moment that he killed her.

What’s more: During trial, Ward waived his right to testify. He refused to take the stand unless he was allowed to call Lee’s gender into question, explicitly stating that he thought he would be judged more harshly by jurors for killing a presumed-cisgender woman than a transgender one.

The defense also argued that, while a jury may hold prejudice against Lee as a trans woman, Ward would face equal amounts of discrimination on the basis of his decision to sleep with transgender women.

According to the press release from the DA, the killing occurred after Ward went to Lee’s home, and a verbal altercation ensued. Lee asked Ward to leave, and he reportedly refused. Ward then claims that Lee pointed a gun at him.

In Ward’s telling, this caused him to fall backward down a staircase, with Lee still standing at the top. At the bottom of the stairs, he said he drew his gun and fired upward at Lee. Ward shot Lee six times. Police found only one bullet casing from Lee’s gun; if she fired her weapon at all, she only did so once. Ward was wholly uninjured.

author: Karen Gullo
title: Turkish Crackdown On LGBTQ+ Organizations Threatens Freedom of Expression and Association
content:
EFF strongly condemns Turkey’s state-led discriminatory, oppressive attacks on feminist and LGBTQ+ organisations, media platforms, student groups, and rights defenders and activists within the country.

Since mid-September, access to the websites and social media accounts of a dozen organizations have been blocked by court order, while over 60 members and activists have been detained, their offices and homes raided, mobile phones, laptops and other digital devices seized, and judicial proceedings launched against them.

These actions threaten the very existence of the LGBTQ+ organizations targeted, limiting their ability to carry out legitimate human rights work, deterring participation and support, and chilling the free speech rights of not just these groups, but any organization that even reports on LGBTQ+ oppression.

A little over a week ago, an Istanbul court shut down the website and social media accounts of T24, Turkey’s longest running independent digital news organization—which has covered government-backed campaigns against and earlier crackdowns on gay rights groups—alleging it had aired “LGBT propaganda” over the past year.

It’s all part of Turkey’s efforts to portray LGBTQ+ groups and support networks for those living with HIV as criminal organizations that must be suppressed, purportedly to protect family values. Homosexuality is not illegal in Turkey (unlike Uganda, Nigeria, and Egypt, where it is criminalized), but LGBTQ+ organizations and activists have in recent years faced increased government oppression, including criminal proceedings on allegations related to obscenity and violations of Turkey’s Law on Associations, which regulates the activities of nonprofits.

In its new crackdown, the government is targeting LGBTQ+ groups’ websites and social media channels for alleged obscene posts accessible to children. Kaos GL, Turkey’s oldest gay rights organization, said investigations are being led by the Cyber Crimes Bureau of the Ankara Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office, which took members of its Board of Directors into custody, raided their homes, and searched the organization’s offices, where electronic devices were seized.

According to Human Rights Watch, prosecutors in Istanbul said those targeted were suspected of “founding, leading, or being a member of a criminal organization,” as well as sex work and drug-related offenses. Publicly available law enforcement and judicial documents about the investigation reportedly don’t say which publications or posts are alleged to be obscene.

The prosecutor’s office launched an investigation of the organization and others under Article 226 of the Turkish Penal Code, which regulates the offense of “obscenity” (without clearly defining it), while the overall operation, dubbed “My Family is Safe” and launched as part of President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s “Decade of the Family” program, is being brought under Article 220 of the code. Justifying the crackdown by invoking family values and child safety suggests that the government is trying to enforce a moral code on society based on intolerance of and discrimination against LGBTQ+ people.

Framing the activities of LGBTQ+ rights organizations as violations of organized crime provisions is a new low for Turkey, where free speech and press freedoms have long been under attack. The implication from these raids and investigations is that the organizations’ legitimate civil society work advocating for the rights of queer people—monitoring human rights violations, offering legal aid, running news portals, sponsoring cultural events such as symposiums and film screenings, publishing an online magazine and supporting LGBTQ+ refugees—is suspected of being criminal threatens the basic human rights of the LGBTQ+ community in Turkey.

These actions send a dangerous message to people and organizations exercising freedom of speech and association in support of queer people. Under the penal code, directing a criminal organization is punishable by five to ten years in prison, while merely being a member carries a sentence of two to five years.

EFF joins hundreds of human, civil, LGBTQ+, and digital rights organizations around the world in calling for the immediate release of all those detained for exercising their rights to freedom of expression, association and legitimate human rights work, and the unblocking of all websites and social media accounts of affected organizations.

title: Bloquons l'offensive transphobe : rassemblement contre le colloque de l'Observatoire de la petite sirène au Sénat
content:
Nous appelons à un rassemblement contre la tenue du colloque annuel de l'Observatoire de la petite sirène au Sénat. Ce moteur de la transphobie en France s'en prend tout particulièrement aux mineur·es trans.


Ce vendredi 16 octobre, jour de l'existransinter, une opération de lobbying transphobe a lieu au parlement. Elle se tient avec le soutien de la sénatrice Jacqueline Eustache-Brinio qui était déjà à l'origine d'une proposition de loi visant à restreindre l'accès des mineur·es aux soins de transition, contre laquelle nous nous étions mobilisé·es en 2024. Empêchons-les d'avancer leur agenda transphobe, rendez-vous à midi devant le Sénat.


Qui est l'Observatoire de la petite sirène (

OPS

)

 

?


Cet autodéclaré observatoire est un collectif regroupant notamment des psychiatres et des psychanalystes, organisant la transphobie en France sous couvert de protection de l'enfance. Parmi leurs actions : lobbying pour retarder voire interdire la transition chez les jeunes, promotion des thérapies de conversion, pression sur des médecins pour interdire des transitions.


La «

 

protection de l'enfance

 

»


Cette prétendue «

 

protection de l'enfance

 

» a des conséquences désastreuses. Les thérapies de conversion, c'est 2 fois plus de tentatives de suicide, 4 fois plus en dessous de 10 ans. Les mineur·es trans empêché·es de transitionner sont davantage exposé·es au suicide. Iels sont littéralement privés de soins. Alors que les détransitions qui les obsèdent tant ne représentent que 0,5% des adolescents ayant commencé une hormonothérapie (Boskey, 2025).


Leur panique morale, des vies broyées


Les dangers dont ils parlent sont fantasmés : la seule inquiétude à laquelle ils répondent c'est à celle de voir des jeunes ne pas rentrer dans le moule cisgenre. Ils ont avant tout honte de ces enfants : ils ne les protègent pas mais les poussent à l'exclusion, à la dépression, au suicide. Leur programme ne met pas qu'en danger des enfants. Retarder les transitions, c'est aussi participer à la précarisation des adultes trans. Et avoir vécu une puberté dans le mauvais genre a des conséquences sur nos vies entières car malgré l'argent et les efforts investis, on ne rattrape pas les années perdues et on vit avec la crainte de ne jamais réussir à être perçu·es comme on le souhaite.


Arrêtons maintenant l'offensive transphobe


Si l'

OPS

 s'attaque aujourd'hui aux mineur·es, ce n'est qu'un premier pas dans le but de s'attaquer plus largement à toutes les personnes trans. C'est cette même obsession pour le contrôle de nos corps et le maintien des normes de genre que l'on voit avec le cas des athlètes par exemple. Ne les laissons pas gâcher la vie des enfants et des futurs adultes trans au nom de leur idéologie. Pour mettre un coup d'arrêt à leur agenda transphobe et pour l'autodétermination de tous·tes, retrouvons-nous au Sénat le 16 octobre à midi (métro Odéon,

RER

title: MKG: Di Îlonê de 2 rojnamegerên jin hatin girtin û 3 jî hatin desteserkirin
content:
Komeleya Rojnamegerên Jin a Mezopotamyayê (MKG) rapora xwe ya binpêkirina mafên jinên rojnameger a meha Îlona 2026an aşkere kir.


MKGê, di raporê de bal kişand ser astengiyên li qadê, şert û mercên xebatê yên ji bo rojnamegerên jin û sansura li ser çapemeniyê.


MKGê diyar kir ku di meha Îlonê de zext bi awayên cûr bi cûr li ser rojnamegerên jin berdewam kirin û wiha got: 


“Lêpirsîn û dozên li dijî çalakiyên rojnamegeriyê, astengiyên li pêşiya nûçeyan, binçavkirin û girtin, gef û êrîş û sansura dîjîtal qada xebatê ji bo rojnamegeran teng kir. Geşedanên di tevahiya mehê de nîşan dan, raporên nûçeyan û çalakiyên rojnamegeriyê wekî bingehek ji bo tawanbarkirinê têne bikaranîn. Darizandinên bi salane berdewam dikin, dozên nû tên vekirin û berdewama biryarên girtinê nîşan dide ku zexta darazê ya li ser rojnamegeran domdar bûye. Astengiyên li qadê şert û mercên xebatê ji bo rojnamegeran jî dijwar kirin. Destwerdana li ser nûçeyan, dûrxistina rojnamegeran a ji qadê, gef û êrîşan nîşan dan ku gihiştina nûçeyan her diçe bi sînordar dibe. Di meha Îlonê de, qada dîjîtal jî yek ji wan deveran bû ku zext lê zêde bûn. Xwegihandina platformên medya dîjîtal ên gelek koman, rojnameger, sazî û dezgehên medyayê, rêxistinên jinan û parêzvanên mafên mirovan, hate astengkirin. Bi vê yekê di heman demê de xwegihandina raya giştî ya dezgehên agahdariyê jî hatin sînordarkirin.”


“Divê astengiyên li pêşiya rojnamegeran werin rakirin”


MKGê di berdewamiya raporê de bi lêv kir ku zextên li ser rojnamegeran li cihên kar jî berdewam kir. MKGê da zanîn ku ji kar derxistin, mobîng û şert û mercên bêewle zêde bûne û hebûna jinan a di qada çapemeniyê de zehmet bûye û wiha hate gotin: 


“Bûyerên meha Îlonê nîşan didin ku dema rojnameger nûçeyan çêdikin, li qadê dixebitin, di pêvajoyên darazê de û li qada dîjîtal di bin zextê de ne. Binpêkirinên mafên mirovan ên li dijî rojnamegeran nikarin ji azadiya çapemeniyê û mafê raya giştî yê agahdarkirinê cûdatir bên nirxandin. Divê darizandin û çavtirsandina rojnamegeran a ji ber çalakiyên wan ên pîşeyî, astengkirina weşana nûçeyên wan û girtina platformên wan ên dîjîtal bi dawî bibe. Divê rojnamegerên girtî werin berdan û hemû astengiyên li pêşiya xebatên rojnamegeran werin rakirin.”

author: TGEU
title: Türkiye’s crackdown on LGBTI rights – the impact on trans people in prison
content:
Since 12 September 2026, Turkish authorities have intensified a nationwide crackdown on LGBTI people, organisations and human rights defenders. At least 117 people have reportedly been detained, with at least 83 held in pre-trial detention. 


The operation, branded “My Family is Safe” has involved arrests, raids on homes and organisations, digital restrictions, and the use of ‘public-morality’ and ‘obscenity’ provisions under Turkish criminal law. 


The impact on trans people


Criminalisation, discriminatory policing and restrictive prison practices in Türkiye come together to heighten risks for trans people in detention. At least 27 of those placed in pre-trial detention are trans women, many of whom have been charged with ‘prostitution’ and/or ‘obscenity’ offences. 


Trans detainees report strip searches and humiliating treatment and placement in detention arrangements that do not match their gender identity. Prison reports describe prolonged isolation, barriers to hormone treatment and HIV medication, limits on clothing and belongings, access to drinking water, overcrowding, and difficulty reaching legal and medical support.


The wider context in Türkiye


These developments should be understood against a broader deterioration in the legal and political environment for LGBTI people in Türkiye. Since 2025, restrictions on trans-specific healthcare, public expression and LGBTI civil society have grown. Proposed legislation would further limit legal gender recognition, trans healthcare and gender expression. Some restrictions not yet in law are reportedly already applied in practice.


Our calls to action


To the Turkish government:


Unconditionally release all persons detained for their human rights work and for exercising their rights to freedom of expression, association or peaceful organising.


End the use of vague provisions on ‘obscenity’ and ‘indecent acts’ to criminalise LGBTI people, particularly trans people, and the organisations defending their rights, including through investigations and prosecutions targeting lawful expression, advocacy and community organising.


End torture and ill-treatment in police custody and prisons toward trans and LGBTI+ people in prison, including humiliating and abusive strip searches. 


Ensure that trans people in prison are placed in detention facilities and accommodation arrangements that respect their gender identity. 


Guarantee continuous access to hormone treatment, HIV medication and other essential healthcare, including during transfer between detention facilities.


To the EU, Council of Europe, United Nations, Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE)/ Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR), diplomatic missions, human rights organisations, donors and partners:


Condemn the raids and detentions directly to the Turkish authorities.


Press for safeguards against further reprisals.


Defend human rights defenders and freedom of association, publicly and in political dialogue


To the EU and European governments:


Raise the detained people’s cases, especially trans prison conditions, with Turkish authorities.


Monitor detention and court proceedings, including through diplomatic presence at hearings.


Activate legal, protection and emergency support for those affected.


To European institutional funders:


Stand by civil society partners and maintain funding.


Reject attempts to criminalise international support for human rights work.


Your support makes change possible


We work across Europe and Central Asia to advance trans rights, build strong communities, and drive change through research, advocacy, and community-building.


Your donation helps us continue this vital work — defending trans lives, amplifying trans voices, and advocating for justice every day.

author: Girard Mariano Lopez
title: Taipei Gay Bar Raid Sparks Protest, Scrutiny Of City’s Commitments to LGBTQ+ Rights
content:
A POLICE RAID on a longstanding gay bar in Taipei sparked a lightning protest and demands for independent oversight after patrons alleged humiliation and discrimination, prompting disciplinary action against officers and an apology from the mayor weeks before the city’s annual Pride celebrations.

About 100 to 200 people gathered at 1 p.m. Oct. 4 outside a police substation near Red House, a landmark in Taipei’s LGBTQ+ district. After speeches, demonstrators marched through the busy neighborhood to the Ximending Police Station which reportedly dispatched the order to raid the gay bar, demanding an explanation and apology for the previous afternoon’s operation at Commander D.

The dispute has drawn scrutiny of police treatment of sexual minorities and intensified questions about whether Taipei’s promotion of LGBTQ+ inclusion abroad is reflected in its policing at home.

Officers entered the BDSM-themed bar Oct. 3 with what police described as a court-issued search warrant obtained under prosecutors’ supervision following complaints about suspected sexual offenses. Police said the establishment had received 13 complaints this year.

Authorities said 51 people were referred for suspected violations of the Social Order Maintenance Act and the operator for a suspected criminal offense. That account differed from protest speakers’ figure of 59 people taken for questioning.

Protest organizers said the operation lasted nearly five hours. They alleged officers refused to show customers the warrant, ordered people to squat and restricted conversation and cellphone use. Patrons also reported being prevented from putting on clothing before being taken to the police station.

Organizers said officers directed derogatory comments about sex toward a wheelchair user and handcuffed the manager, who they alleged was ordered to kneel after protesting police conduct.

Police initially denied insulting disabled patrons and maintained that officers followed lawful procedures. By Oct. 5, however, authorities acknowledged inappropriate remarks by four officers after reviewing recordings. Each received two reprimands, the supervising investigation chief received a demerit, and the Wanhua precinct chief requested two reprimands for inadequate supervision.

Police maintained that the warrant had been displayed, leaving conflicting accounts about whether customers were adequately informed of the search’s basis.

The operation followed a September council exchange in which Democratic Progressive Party Councilor Hung Chien-yi raised allegations that minors were entering the establishment and being treated as sexual playthings. Mayor Chiang Wan-an subsequently ordered police to investigate.

Commander D denied the allegations, saying it checked identification and ages at entry. The bar, which said it had operated for 14 years, distinguished private interactions between adult customers from activities arranged or directed by its management and said it would cooperate with lawful investigations.

Although speculation linked the raid to drugs, police publicly described its basis as suspected sexual offenses. At Sunday’s protest, Green Party city council candidate Wang Chen-ting rejected suggestions that the operation uncovered illegal drugs.

Wang said medications examined by officers included HIV prevention drugs and produced no positive drug findings. Wang also alleged that records showed eight police inspections of the venue within 15 days the previous month.

People taken for questioning were denied food and water for hours and faced leading questions about sexual activity, Wang said.

Protest organizers also reported police visits to Hunt and Locker Room, two other gay venues, that night. They demanded an explanation of the legal justification for the operations and questioned whether queer gathering places were being subjected to discriminatory scrutiny.

Outside Ximending Police Station, demonstrators called for the police chief to come down, explain the operation and apologize. Instead, Wanhua internal affairs officer Lin Sheng-wei addressed the crowd, promising an investigation and disciplinary action where warranted, without offering an apology.

“If our colleagues are at fault, they should be disciplined,” Lin said.

Organizer Yang Kang concluded by handing Lin a copy of Taiwan’s Code of Criminal Procedure, underscoring protesters’ demand that officers follow legal safeguards when exercising police powers.

Chiang, of the Kuomintang …

author: Amy Goodman
title: Nobel Peace Prize Awarded to Jurist Who Led UN Inquiry Into Genocide in Gaza
content:
South African human rights lawyer Navanethem “Navi” Pillay began her career defending anti-apartheid activists.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

The 2026 Nobel Peace Prize has been awarded to Navanethem “Navi” Pillay, the South African jurist who led the United Nations commission of inquiry that concluded that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. Pillay’s long career in international human rights law includes work as a defense attorney for anti-apartheid activists, president of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, a former judge at the International Criminal Court and the U.N.’s high commissioner for human rights from 2008 to 2014.

“Everybody in the human rights movement reveres Navi Pillay,” says war crimes prosecutor Reed Brody, who calls the award “a stinging rebuke to Donald Trump.” Brody, a member of the United Nations Group of Human Rights Experts on Nicaragua, also comments on the Trump administration’s decision to deport a Nicaraguan opposition activist, Jeffrey Jarquín, from the United States, where he was in the process of seeking asylum. Upon his return to Nicaragua, Jarquín was immediately imprisoned at the same facility in which he was once tortured.

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report. I’m Amy Goodman, with Juan González.

The Norwegian Nobel Committee has announced the winner of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. This is the chair of the Nobel Committee speaking in Oslo this morning.

JØRGEN WATNE FRYDNES: The Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 goes to a person who, with exceptional courage and integrity, has led the way towards a more comprehensive global legal order. This year’s laureate has been instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted. The Norwegian Nobel Committee has decided to award the Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 to Navanethem “Navi” Pillay for her efforts to promote peace and international law.

AMY GOODMAN: The South African human rights lawyer and international jurist Navi Pillay has been the United Nations high commissioner for human rights and a judge at both the International Criminal Court and at an international tribunal investigating the 1994 genocide in Rwanda. Most recently, she led the U.N. Independent International Commission of Inquiry that concluded that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.

Navi Pillay is now 85 years old. She was born into an Indian Tamil family in apartheid South Africa. The first woman to start a law practice in Natal, South Africa, in 1967, she began her legal career defending anti-apartheid activists, including Nelson Mandela, exposing torture and helping establish key rights for prisoners on Robben Island. The Nobel Committee also praised her work in South Africa.

JØRGEN WATNE FRYDNES: A common thread runs from her early work, defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against apartheid, to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time.

author: Marcelo Oliveira
title: Mulheres são maioria das vítimas de violência política, mesmo sendo minoria das candidatas
content:
O primeiro turno da campanha eleitoral de 2026 durou 50 dias e registrou 134 episódios de violência política contra candidatos e candidatas, além de agentes políticos.

Um aumento de 11% em relação aos 121 casos registrados no mesmo período da eleição municipal de 2022.


Os 134 episódios representam um caso de violência política a cada nove horas de campanha.

 E apesar das mulheres serem apenas 35% do total de candidatos, elas foram a maioria (52%) das vítimas do primeiro turno, segundo o levantamento.


Os dados integram a 4ª edição da pesquisa Violência Política e Eleitoral no Brasil, realizada pelas organizações de direitos humanos Terra de Direitos e Justiça Global, que pesquisa o tema desde 2016. O levantamento foi divulgado nesta quarta, dia 7 de outubro.


A porcentagem de

vítimas mulheres aumenta

 mais ainda quando a pesquisa separa apenas os casos envolvendo candidatas e candidatos. Dos 134 episódios de violência política durante o primeiro turno, 102 foram dirigidos a pessoas que disputavam o pleito. Desse total, 60 eram mulheres, quase 59% do total.


Para a coordenadora do Setor de Incidência da Terra de Direitos, Gisele Barbieri, “os dados trazem importantes achados para identificar os ambientes em que agentes políticos estão mais vulneráveis e pensar medidas de proteção. Quando eleitas, essas pessoas passam a ser vítimas de violências nos seus locais de atuação, seja no Parlamento ou no Executivo”, afirma.


Machismo e misoginia se misturam nos casos de violência política


A pesquisa mostra que a violência política é marcada pela discriminação de gênero e raça.

Quando se considera o universo completo de 70 casos de violência política contra mulheres, 45 casos envolveram machismo ou misoginia, nove envolveram racismo e cinco envolveram transfobia. Mulheres pretas foram vítimas de 25% dos casos de violência política medidos nesse primeiro turno.


A ameaça foi o tipo de violência política mais recorrente no período, com 64 casos registrados. Na sequência, aparecem 33 episódios de ofensa e 19 de agressão física. Também foram registrados 11 atentados, cinco casos de criminalização e dois assassinatos.


Mais da metade dos casos (71 ocorrências) aconteceu nas ruas, durante atividades públicas de campanha. O ambiente virtual concentrou 31,3% dos episódios.


Além disso, apenas candidatas sofreram ameaças de violência sexual. Em todos os sete casos, as vítimas eram mulheres.


“Enquanto os homens são atacados por sua atuação política, mulheres, pessoas negras e pessoas trans enfrentam também o racismo, o machismo e a transfobia que estruturam a sociedade brasileira”, afirmou em nota Glaucia Marinho, diretora-executiva da Justiça Global.


Policiais e outros agentes públicos foram a maioria dos autores


Em quase 20% dos casos o autor identificado da violência política era um agente público, incluindo parlamentares e forças de segurança.

Até o encerramento da coleta de dados pelas organizações autoras da pesquisa, nenhum dos 134 episódios havia resultado em alguma punição efetiva, limitando-se a medidas cautelares de urgência determinadas pela Justiça Eleitoral.


A região Nordeste liderou o número de casos (48), seguido pelo Sudeste (38). Entre os estados, São Paulo lidera com 16 casos, seguido por Rio Grande do Norte (13), Minas Gerais (12) e Rio Grande do Sul (10).


A presença de policiais entre os autores de violência política já havia sido detectada também em

levantamento

 realizado pela

Agência Pública

 durante o primeiro turno.

title: Los sepultureros de Gaza de Norman Finkelstein es una obra maestra
content:
Hay hechos sin consecuencias, libros sin seguimiento. ¿Qué haremos de esta monumental investigación y razonamiento que apela a nuestra conciencia y debería impulsarnos a la acción? Lo que está en juego es la esencia misma de la existencia civilizada, los valores de la Declaración Universal de los Derechos Humanos, los propósitos y principios de las Naciones Unidas. El genocidio en Gaza no es solo otro Holocausto monstruoso, es un espectáculo público.

[1]

 El fracaso de las Naciones Unidas para detenerlo y la inacción de la mayoría de los estadounidenses y europeos nos hacen a todos cómplices del crimen, porque

qui tacet consentire videtur

. Si solo somos

voyeurs

de esta masacre en curso, tenemos, como mínimo, responsabilidad moral. Por Alfred de Zayas 


En los últimos 30 años, Norman Finkelstein nos ha brindado muchos libros brillantes, entre ellos

Método y locura, Acuso, Saber demasiado,

Gaza

,

Más allá de la desfachatez

y

La industria del Holocausto.


Este libro de más de 400 páginas documenta el colapso civilizatorio de las clases dominantes en Occidente, la traición a todos los valores humanistas, el rechazo demasiado público por parte de Israel del derecho internacional y la moral, con la complicidad,

entre otros

, de Estados Unidos, Reino Unido, Francia, Alemania y la Unión Europea.


Todo esto se ve acompañado por la cacofonía de los medios de comunicación convencionales orwellianos, que difunden noticias falsas, historia falsa y leyes falsas, especialmente con respecto a los palestinos como pueblo, a quienes se les representa erróneamente como “terroristas”, cuando poseen el derecho, reconocido en el derecho internacional, a resistir la colonización y la ocupación.

[2]


Nelson Mandela también fue tildado de «terrorista», pero fue fundamental en la lucha por la liberación de su pueblo. Hoy todos reconocen que el fin del apartheid en Sudáfrica era algo que debió haberse hecho hace mucho tiempo. ¿Cuándo veremos el fin del apartheid en Israel y los Territorios Ocupados? Esto es lo que Jimmy Carter exigió en su libro

Palestina: Paz, no apartheid

.

[3]


Los políticos occidentales y los principales medios de comunicación han invertido los papeles y han culpado a la víctima de su desgracia. Israel es el terrorista que practica el terrorismo de Estado y coloca trampas explosivas en los buscapersonas, como demostró de forma obscena el primer ministro israelí Benjamin Netanyahu durante su diatriba en la Asamblea General de la ONU el 24 de septiembre de 2026.

[4]


Israel nació del terrorismo

[5]

 contra británicos y palestinos, ha sido un Estado agresor desde su creación, en un sentido muy real un

Estado fallido

, porque no ha aprendido a vivir en paz con sus vecinos.


Israel ha atacado Líbano, Siria, Irak, Irán, Egipto, etc. En una infame operación de falsa bandera, incluso atacó el buque de inteligencia de la Armada de los Estados Unidos USS

Liberty

[6]

 en junio de 1967, matando a 34 marineros estadounidenses, en un intento fallido de involucrar a los Estados Unidos en la guerra de agresión de Israel.


Israel ha sido un estado paria desde su creación en 1948, e incluso antes.


El genocidio de Gaza no es más que una continuación de la intención criminal de establecer un «Gran Israel» anacrónico e imperialista en medio del mundo árabe y musulmán.


[Fuente:

cartooningforpeace.org

]


Sin duda, los gobiernos de Israel, Estados Unidos y la UE están moralmente en bancarrota.

[7]


Lamentablemente, la

percepción

de la realidad es más determinante que la realidad misma. Dado que nuestras acciones están condicionadas por la información de la que disponemos, nuestro juicio se ve influenciado —e incluso subvertido— por las narrativas odiosas que recibimos de los principales medios de comunicación, y nuestras opiniones se distorsionan por el incesante discurso de odio y la propaganda contra los palestinos. Esto constituye una incitación al odio y a la violencia, en contravención del artículo 20 del Pacto Internacional de Derechos Civiles y Políticos.

[8]


Los principales medios de comunicación difunden la versión israelí y suprimen las opiniones disidentes. No solo nos mienten, sino que nos privan de información crucial que cambia radicalmente la situación.


El público es manipulado, pero muchos se dejan manipular. Como escribió Julio César en

De Bello Civili (II, 27, 2): «quae volumus, ea credimus libenter»

(Creemos lo que queremos creer). O peor aún, como decían los romanos …

Part One: The Bolshevik Counterrevolution

Lenin: Butcher of the Working Class

Timeline: A Revolution Derailed

The USSR: Force for Global Counterrevolution, Accomplice of Fascism

The Relevance of the Communist Counterrevolution

Part Two: Restless Specters of the Anarchist Dead

Golos Truda, The Voice of Labor

Since the mid-19th century, anarchists have maintained that the key to liberation is not to seize the state but to abolish it. From Paris to St. Petersburg, from Barcelona to Beijing, one generation of revolutionaries after another has had to learn this lesson the hard way. Shuffling politicians in and out of power changes nothing. What matters are the instruments of rule — the police, the military, the courts, the prison system, the bureaucracy. Whether it is a king, a dictator, or a Congress that directs these instruments, the experience on the receiving end remains roughly the same.

This explains why the outcome of the Egyptian revolution of 2011–2013 was not all that different from the outcome of the Russian Revolution of 1917–1921 or the French Revolution of 1848–1851. In each case, as soon as the people who made the revolution stopped attempting to carry out social change directly and shifted to investing their hopes in political representatives, power consolidated in the hands of a new autocracy. Whether the new tyrants hailed from the military, the aristocracy, or the underclass, whether they promised to restore order or to incarnate the power of the proletariat, the end result was roughly the same.

Government itself is a class relation. You can’t abolish class society without abolishing the asymmetry between ruler and ruled . The first condition for any government is that it must achieve a monopoly on coercive force. In struggling to achieve this monopoly, fascist despotisms, communist dictatorships, and liberal democracies come to resemble each other. And in order to achieve it, even the most ostensibly radical party must ultimately collude with other power players. This explains why the Bolsheviks employed tsarist officers and counterinsurgency methods, why they repeatedly took the side of the petite bourgeoisie against anarchists, first in Russia and later in Spain and elsewhere. History gives the lie to the old alibi that Bolshevik repression was necessary to abolish capitalism. The problem with Bolshevism was not that it used brutal force to push through a revolutionary agenda, but that it used brutal force to crush it.

It’s not particularly popular to acknowledge any of this today, when the flag of the Soviet Union has become a dim, receding screen onto which people can project whatever they wish. A generation that grew up after the fall of the Soviet Union has renewed the pipe dream that the state could solve all our problems if the right people were in charge. title: TEV-DEM condemns racist provocation in Hesekê
content:
Following a demonstration featuring anti-Kurdish demands in Hesekê, the Democratic Society Movement (TEV-DEM) warned against attempts to fuel ethnic tensions in the multi-ethnic city. At Friday’s rally in the predominantly Arab neighborhood of Xiwêran (Ghweiran), around 200 people called, among other things, for Kurds to be removed from institutions in Hesekê province.


During the demonstration, in which a particularly large number of children and young people participated, slogans were also chanted against Kurdish national symbols and flags. Kurdish flags were also reportedly burned following Friday prayers. In a statement on Sunday, TEV-DEM described the action as a racist provocation by a limited group and explicitly rejected attempts to portray it as reflecting the views or demands of the Arab population.


“Limited to a particular group”


According to TEV-DEM, the slogans voiced during the demonstration were aimed at inciting racism against the Kurdish population and other sections of society. The position expressed there was limited to a particular group, TEV-DEM stated. “Some of the rhetoric directly targeted the legitimate national and political rights of the Kurds. At the same time, rhetoric was used that fueled social discord and thereby served the enemies of Syria.”


TEV-DEM emphasized that the anti-Kurdish demands must not be attributed to the Arab population of Hesekê. The movement also rejected attempts to portray the provocation as an ethnic conflict between Kurds and Arabs.


Call for an investigation into the incidents


TEV-DEM called on the relevant authorities to launch a transparent and responsible investigation into the incidents, demanding that those who spread hatred and racist incitement be held accountable. At the same time, the movement warned against allowing Hesekê province to become a scene of ethnic conflict.


TEV-DEM said that Kurds, Arabs, Syriacs and other communities should not allow hate speech to turn them against one another but should instead remain committed to dialogue and peaceful coexistence.

author: Sonali Kolhatkar
title: An Abolitionist Vision for the World We Want
content:
A recent New York Times editorial by Tim Wu, a former antitrust adviser for the Biden administration, caught my eye for the criticism it leveled at Democrats for making affordability a central issue ahead of the midterm elections. Wu contends that the party needs to go further and focus not merely on the high price tags of necessities, but on the unfairness of the entire economic system.

While this is a refreshing shift in the right direction, it doesn’t go nearly far enough. It’s true that a majority of Americans across the political spectrum believe our economy is rigged in favor of the rich. But merely pointing out the obvious is unlikely to attract a huge shift in voting toward the Democratic Party.

Moreover, Wu says nothing about the racist rage that has defined President Donald Trump and the Republican Party’s decimation of our democracy, about the devastation to communities of color, immigrants, women, LGBTQ+ people, and other marginalized members of our society. Nor does he acknowledge the corporate harms that Democrats failed to tackle when they were in power and are now being accelerated under Republicans: fossil fuel emissions, tech domination, and AI, harms that disproportionately impactpoor people and people of color.

To Wu and most Democratic Party consultants, these issues are distinct and, depending on the cultural tides, are either worth tackling or anathema.

In fact, they are intimately linked. White supremacy feeds capitalism by distracting poor whites from billionaire-fueled inequality and climate devastation using immigrants and people of color as scapegoats. To take on an unfair economy without addressing the systematically racist impacts of policing, immigration, corporate oligarchy, and the climate crisis does us all a disservice. Moreover, there is an absence of a radical vision for tackling economic and racial justice risks to prevent repeating the same crises in the future.

Democratic Party leaders are falling deeply short by offering little more than undoing Trump’s worst excesses. It is a conservative position to seek a return to the “good old days,” when a predatory capitalist system was overseen by articulate, sensible-sounding statesmen who didn’t embarrass the nation on the global stage, who championed police and prisons as tools of safety, who echoed Trump’s rhetoric on “border security,” who preserved corporate profiteering in healthcare, who embraced endless war as long as it was their party’s doing, and so on.

The Democratic Party is essentially a modern-day conservative party, while Republicans are the extremist, fascist party.

No wonder Americans in general dislike both major parties at roughly the same rate. And while the Democrats’ chances of taking control of Congress appear to be surging ahead of the midterm elections, it is likely because the pendulum is swinging away from Republicans, rather than towardDemocrats and their milquetoast agenda.

So, what can Democrats do to ensure victory?

Frankly, it is not our job as voters—or for that matter, the job of newspaper editorialists—to offer advice to political parties.

Our job as voters, especially in this moment, is to seize power in a system that has rendered us powerless and articulate our demands loudly and clearly. Politicians win our votes by acceding to our agenda. Not the other way around.

Therefore, the far more important question is, what do we, the voters, want?

If we agree that the economic system is rigged against the majority of Americans, then how do we unrig it? Is it as basic as “a promise to level out a lopsided economy,” as Wu advises, while ignoring other issues? Is it as simple as a rallying cry to “tax the rich,” as some Democratic-leaning states are doing?

If we want to end the wild pendulum swings of American politics, which are veering us further into the abyss of authoritarianism with each election, we need a complete reset on all fronts, not merely a return to a more balanced economy.

We require, I would argue, an “abolitionist mindset.”

Black abolitionists, who are better versed than the rest of us on what it’s like to be on the receiving end of systemic harms, have long articulated a vision for a better world where we all can thrive: a world where we reverse the equations of how our collective wealth is spent and where we refuse to let our needs be continually defunded.

Black abolitionists like Angela Davis, Ruth Wilson Gilmore, Mariame Kaba, and Andrea J. Ritchie have already shown …

title: FIERTÉS VÉNÈRES — Pride radicale du Sud
content:
Texte d'appel et programme de la Pride Radicale du Sud de la France


Transpédégouines et antifas uni•exs contre le fascisme !


Dans un climat d'extrême droitisation et de fascisation, la seule réponse est lutter et s'organiser collectivement !


Pas de Pride dépolitisée.


Nous refusons l'homonationalisme et l'instrumentalisation nationaliste et raciste de nos vies.


Stonewall était une émeute.


Nous inscrivons cette Pride contre les violences policières et le racisme d'État, et en solidarité avec la Palestine.


S'organiser au-delà des urnes.


Nous appelons à investir les mouvements sociaux et à construire une coalition antifasciste et queer dans le Sud de la France.


FIERTÉS VÉNÈRES — Pride radicale du Sud


📍 Nîmes · 10 octobre


Dans un climax d'extrême droitisation et de fascisation, où ces idéologies et ces pratiques titillent beaucoup d'LGBT (et comme par hasard, beaucoup d'hommes gays),

nous, sujectivités islamogauchistes, wokistantifa, euphoriques des genres autres, réceptacles de plaisirs pervers, nous appelons à créer une Marche Vénère à Nîmes afin de montrer que nous ne laisserons pas passer cette gangrène dans nos territoires du Sud de la France.


Beaucoup de Prides sont vidées de leur sens : festives et sans revendications. Menacées dans les villes de droite/extrême droite, elles sont récupérées à des fins de marketing dans les villes de « gauche », pour masquer des politiques par ailleurs droitardes et racistes. D'un drapeau à la mairie et des paillettes sur un char commerçant, on s'en nettoie le cul.

Nous voulons des Fiertés qui déchiquettent, des Fiertés shlags, irrécupérables et sales.


 Homonationalisme, non merci


Une partie de nos communautés et des associations LGBTQIA+ a fait le choix du silence et de la complicité pour obtenir une « inclusivité » qui n'essaie même plus de ravager les normes sociales, à tel point que le RN lui-même compte désormais plus de candidats homos que tous les autres partis. C'est ça,

l'homonationalisme : nos vies utilisées comme argument pour légitimer des politiques nationalistes, racistes et impérialistes, chez nous comme ailleurs.

 C'est ce même mécanisme qu'on a vu à l'œuvre après les attentats à la Pride de Berlin cet été, récupéré en un instant par les droites de toute sorte, ainsi que par les gauches libérales, pour alimenter l'islamophobie ambiante et le racisme. Nos existences ne serviront de caution à personne : ni à la droite, ni à l'extrême droite, ni à une gauche molle. Et c'est là, sur la question de la Palestine, que nous revenons à charge, plus hystériques que jamais :

non, un génocide d'un peuple n'est pas acceptable au prétexte qu'on présume ce peuple lgbtphobe. Nous nous battons pour la fin de l'occupation coloniale sioniste, de la rivière à la mer. Localement, cela passe par la rupture des jumelages avec des villes israéliennes

, pour que cesse toute complicité dans ce génocide mené par l'État fasciste israélien. De la droite à la « gauche » de nos mairies, la réponse est la même...


 Stonewall était une émeute


Les Prides ne descendent pas d'une marche festive et pacifique mais d'une émeute.

Des personnes trans, noires, latinas, travailleuses du sexe se sont soulevées contre une descente de police. Effacer cette origine, c'est désarmer le sens même de nos cortèges

 : nous devons continuer un mouvement né dans l'affrontement avec la police et l'état. Nous devons nous opposer à toute forme de violence étatique et policière, qu'elle touche des personnes LGBT, des travailleur·euses du sexe, des personnes arabes ou noires. Nous continuons à crier les noms de Nahel, d'Adama, tués par le bras armé de l'État, la police.

Nous nous opposons à la loi RIPOST et à la loi « présomption de légitime défense », adoptée le 21 juillet 2026 : un tir de policier ou de gendarme sera désormais présumé légal d'office, sans qu'il y ait besoin d'enquêter pour vérifier s'il y avait vraiment un motif de tirer.

 Cette loi prolonge une doctrine du maintien de l'ordre qui traque et

tue déjà, massivement, les personnes racisées, précaires et marginalisées

, en écartant par avance presque toute possibilité de justice.

author: Aaron Hemens, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: In Tk̓emlúps, community gathers to ‘reclaim our space’ and denounce white nationalism
content:
At the same site where a white nationalist demonstration occurred in Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc on Sunday, more than 100 Secwépemc people and their allies returned to the area two days later to reclaim the space. They drummed, sang and prayed to cleanse the spot, which is located a few hundred metres away from the former Kamloops Indian Residential School.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


Content warning: This article contains details about residential “schools.” Please read with care for your spirit.


On the eve of Orange Shirt Day, more than 100 people gathered in Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc to cleanse and reclaim a site where a white nationalist demonstration occurred earlier this week.


For nearly three hours on Tuesday night, Secwépemc people and their allies drummed, sang and prayed — for the land and the people, and for all the families impacted by residential “schools.”


Secwépemc people and their allies drum, sing and pray on Tuesday, near the site where a white nationalist demonstration took place in Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc two days prior.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


Ashley Michel from Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc organized Tuesday’s gathering with four other Secwépemc (Shuswap) mothers.


After seeing images of a group of masked white nationalists circulating on social media early this week, she told IndigiNews that they felt they had to come together to create a safer place for their children, and to help ground the community ahead of the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation — also known as Orange Shirt Day — on Sept. 30.


“We’re all mothers. We don’t want our children growing up in a world like this. We brainstormed, and we just wanted to come together and cleanse the area,” said Michel, who is the owner of Four Generations Creations.


The organizers of Tuesday’s gathering in Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc. From left to right: Ashley Michel, Cam Gottfriedson, Morning-Star Peters, Stephanie Lindley and Willow Peters.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


“We wanted to start things off in a good way and reclaim our space – take back our area and make it safe again. Especially for our children and our survivors.”


The group of about two dozen white nationalists were seen at Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc reserve lands early Sunday morning. They hid their faces behind white masks and held a flag with the message “got bones?” — with images that quickly gathered outrage online.


The space where the group had gathered is a few hundred metres away from the former Kamloops Indian Residential School (KIRS) site and is located on the institution’s former grounds, which originally spanned 360 acres. 


At the same site where a white nationalist demonstration occurred in Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc on Sunday, more than 100 Secwépemc people and their allies returned to the area two days later to reclaim the space.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


In 2021

, leadership at Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc revealed that they had identified evidence of 215 unmarked graves on the site, which unleashed a national reckoning about children’s deaths at the institutions.


“Sunday was just an example of what we at Tk’emlúps te Secwépemc are facing on a daily basis; on a weekly basis; on a monthly basis,” said Jeanette Jules, a Secwépemc knowledge keeper who helps manage the First Nation’s Le Estcwicwéy̓ (the missing children from KIRS) case. 


“Since 2021, we’ve kept emails, texts, phone messages. Some of them are really disturbing and disgusting.”


Secwépemc people and their allies drum, sing and pray on Tuesday, near the site where a white nationalist demonstration took place in Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc two days prior.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc Kúkwpi7 (Chief) Rosanne Casimir

said on Sunday

 that the group have ties to a group called Second Sons Canada, who are “linked to white supremacist and white nationalist ideology.”


“That blackness that they brought — that heaviness that they brought — is being lifted,” said Jules.


On Monday

, Tk̓emlúps RCMP said in a press release that they are investigating the incident. They described the masked men and their activities as “a cowardly attempt to avoid accountability for their actions and messages that are clearly intended to intimidate, provoke fear and division.”

Photo by Aaron Hemens

author: Progressive International
title: From Law to Justice
content:
As Trump attacked the ICC and Netanyahu faced a walkout at the UN, forty states gathered to put an arms embargo, protections for the Court and a new UN mechanism modelled on the Special Committee against Apartheid.

Last week, the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) counted what remained of Gaza’s economy after almost three years of genocide and almost two decades of siege. Ninety-two per cent of its economic establishments have been damaged or destroyed. Unemployment has reached 78 per cent. GDP per person fell to $212 last year — barely 17 per cent of its pre-genocide level — while less than 1.5 per cent of Gaza’s cropland remains accessible and undamaged. Recovery and reconstruction will cost at least $71.5 billion. Pedro Manuel Moreno, acting head of UNCTAD, called it “the world’s most severe economic crisis on record”.

These were the conditions in which the governments of the world assembled in New York for the 81st United Nations General Assembly. On Monday 21 September, a thousand gathered at Riverside Church to celebrate the Charter on which the institution was founded, hosted by South Africa. Martin Luther King Jr stood in the same church in 1967 to deliver Beyond Vietnam. Nelson Mandela came there four months after his release from prison and thanked the movements that had sustained sanctions against apartheid — before urging them to keep up the pressure until victory was secured. “We acted because we know what global solidarity can do,” South African Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola told the gathering. The Hague Group, he said, embodies a “shared conviction that concrete action is needed.”

A day later, Donald Trump used the General Assembly podium to attack the International Criminal Court. He called it an “evil” and “rogue institution” and urged its 125 member states to withdraw. His administration has already imposed financial sanctions and visa restrictions on ICC officials and threatened further measures that could stifle the Court’s ability to operate. Trump has said the campaign is aimed at protecting Benjamin Netanyahu, for whom the Court issued an arrest warrant in 2024 over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.

On Thursday, Netanyahu himself took the same podium. Dozens of delegates walked out as he began speaking. He held aloft a pager, invoking Israel’s 2024 terror attack in Lebanon: “Remember the beepers? Hezbollah certainly remembers them.”

Netanyahu denied that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza, denounced his critics as “moral cowards” and praised Trump as Israel’s greatest partner. Outside the UN, protesters blocked streets demanding an end to US arms supplies to Israel; at least 30 were arrested.

By Friday morning, another gathering was underway inside UN headquarters. In the Trusteeship Council Chamber, once at the centre of the UN’s work of decolonisation, forty states — represented by foreign ministers and senior diplomats — joined The Hague Group’s largest meeting yet, co-sponsored by South Africa and Malaysia in defence of international law.

Minister Lamola opened by recalling the machinery built against apartheid: the UN Special Committee established in 1962 to monitor and organise international action, followed by the campaign that turned a voluntary arms embargo into a mandatory Security Council measure in 1977. The Hague Group itself had begun with nine states in January 2025. “Our task today,” Lamola told the room, “is to turn concern into compliance, and law into protection.”

The states gathered in New York discussed a series of concrete proposals. One would create a new UN mechanism drawing on the Special Committee against Apartheid to monitor compliance with international law and coordinate action between states. Another would continue efforts for a Security Council arms embargo on Israel. For the ICC, states discussed blocking statutes against sanctions on the Court, measures to keep it operating under pressure, and coordinated action to protect judges and prosecutors from retaliation. Norway pledged to work on the Court’s “business continuity”, while other interventions stressed cooperation to ensure that its decisions can still be carried out. South Africa and Malaysia committed to continue consultations with participating governments on how to put the proposals into practice.

“The law is clear,” Indonesia’s representative told the room. “Our challenge now is to give it practical consequence.” That same week, UNCTAD had …

author: Shireen Akram-Boshar
title: Martin Soto, Organizer of Delaney Hall Hunger Strike, Released After 8 Months
content:
Soto was abducted by ICE in February while buying diapers for his son.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Martin Soto, who helped lead a hunger strike at Delaney Hall immigration jail in Newark, New Jersey, earlier this year, was released from detention with an ankle monitor on Tuesday evening.

Martin was released after U.S. District Court Judge Jamel Semper ruled that his detention was illegal, citing the conditions of his confinement, his deteriorating mental health, and lack of sufficient reason to continue his detention.

Martin was abducted by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) while buying diapers for his 11-month-old son in February, and was central to organizing the hunger strike at Delaney Hall that began in May. The strike lasted for a month and put a national spotlight on the inhumane conditions at the for-profit immigration jail — including medical neglect, deprivation of legal counsel, and coerced deportation of people being detained.

Martin faced retaliation at the ICE detention center almost immediately.

From the first day of the hunger strike, Martin’s wife, Gabriela Soto, protested outside of Delaney Hall with other family members of hunger striking detainees, translating calls from Martin and others inside who described the conditions they were facing. Guards at Delaney retaliated by cutting phone access for those detained.

ICE agents and staff at Delaney Hall reportedly singled out Martin as the leader of the strike on the first day, asking him, “If we release you right now, will you tell your wife to stop the protest outside?”

ICE agents then transferred Martin from Delaney to New Jersey’s Elizabeth Detention Center in an attempt to crush the hunger strike. But instead of stopping the hunger strike, his transfer led to sustained mass protests outside of Delaney Hall. Activists attempted to block his transfer by forming a blockade, which led to daily protests as well as clashes with ICE followed by the state police.

During the protests, Gabriela regularly spoke about the squalid conditions at Delaney Hall, where three immigrants have died since it was reopened as a detention center run by GEO Group in May 2025. More than 50 people have died in ICE custody across the U.S. throughout President Donald Trump’s second term.

In an article for Truthout, Gabriela wrote that she “learned about the abuses firsthand. Martin told me that in May, all detainees in Unit 2 were fed food infested with worms, and when they refused to eat the worm-ridden food, the guards told them either eat or you will starve until the next day.”

“Meanwhile, when Martin got sick, he would go three or four weeks without getting seen, much less treated.”

After his transfer to Elizabeth Detention Center, Martin was held in solitary confinement for four months, from mid-May to mid-September. During this time, Gabriela experienced a miscarriage, which she says was due to the stress of her husband being detained.

In late June, ICE transferred the hunger strikers out of Delaney Hall en masse — forcibly moving some 200 of the 300 hunger strikers and effectively ending the strike.

But the hunger strike and solidarity protests, as well as Gabriela’s continued agitation, eventually led to Martin’s release — though he remains in an ankle monitor pending the outcome of his immigration case.

“I am so thankful for everybody that has helped me,” Gabriela said in a comment after Martin’s release. “These months have been very, very difficult. Not only did I lose our home, not only did I lose our child, but it made me — this experience made me stronger to keep fighting to have the reunitement of our family.”

As Trump cracks down on political speech, independent media is increasingly necessary.

Truthout produces reporting you won’t see in the mainstream: journalism from the frontlines of global conflict, interviews with grassroots movement leaders, high-quality legal analysis and more.

author: Publicación Abierta
title: Solo el martirio de millones de migrantes puede garantizar la victoria del imperio capitalista.
content:
Producto de La globalización neoliberal la crisis de los refugiados es una de las tragedias más masacrantes de la historia contemporánea. Son millones de fugitivos que luchan por hacer realidad esa consigna de

“vencer o morir”

.  Pasa el tiempo y torturados por la angustia existencial  para  los “nuevos bárbaros” no existen barreras infranqueables, ni murallas, ni fosos, ni campos electrificados o minados, ni alambre de púas, ni accidentes geográficos, desiertos, montañas, ríos, mares u océanos; ni tampoco ejércitos o armadas que los detengan. Europa es el cielo si lo comparamos con el infierno del que escaparon donde reina la miseria, la inseguridad, la violencia, las enfermedades o el hambre.


Los conflictos bélicos -ya sean de alta o baja intensidad- se extienden a lo largo y ancho del planeta: en Afganistán, Kurdistán, India, Pakistán, Irán, en Palestina, Líbano, Afganistán, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Somalia, Eritrea, Etiopía, Sudán, Camerún, Nigeria, Mali, República Centroafricana, Burkina Faso, R.D Congo, Yemen, etc. 

Esto significa más refugiados, más desplazados susceptibles de engrosar el éxodo bíblico.  Todos al asalto Primer Mundo opulento y desarrollado

 por la frontera turca, los Balcanes o las islas griegas en el Mediterráneo,  la costa Libia, argelina o tunecina hasta alcanzar la isla de Lampedusa en Italia, o por Ceuta y Melilla cruzando el estrecho de Gibraltar para desembarcar en las playas de Andalucía; o desde Senegal o Gambia o Mauritania con rumbo a las Islas Canarias y en América  al asalto del imperio americano por el río Bravo o el Mar Caribe; en Asia por el mar de la China, el Mar de Timor y el Océano Índico hasta las costas de Australia.


Se ha bombardeado y demolido sistemáticamente pueblos y ciudades, quieren aplastar a

 la población civil, enterrarlos vivos como se ha comprobado en Siria, el Líbano, Palestina, el Yemen y la única posibilidad de supervivencia es cruzar la frontera de la UE.


El número de refugiados que tiene a su cargo

ACNUR

(Agencia de la ONU para protección y asistencia de los refugiados) es de unos 30 millones, mientras la cifra global de refugiados es de 42 millones. Las personas víctimas del desplazamiento forzado en el mundo sube hasta los 118 millones.


 


Cualquier país de la Unión Europea está obligado por ley internacional a recibir y estudiar solicitudes de asilo político o de carácter humanitario sin depender estrictamente de una nacionalidad especifica sino de los motivos individuales de persecución

. Aunque se aplican normativas de retorno estrictas para casos rechazados si se les califica como migrantes por causas económicas. El estatuto de refugiado o el de asilo político de la UE les asegura recibir todos los meses una paga y beneficiarse de las ayudas estatales, alojamiento, educación o sanidad.


 


África actualmente tiene una población aproximada de 1.500 millones de habitantes de los cuales más de 50% son pobres de solemnidad y que si tuvieran posibilidad de elegir emigrarían sin ninguna duda a Europa

. Y no lo hacen a EE.UU porque geográficamente los separa el océano Atlántico. Con solo un 2 o 3% (8 millones) que lograran entrar en Europa crearían una crisis social insostenible y el sistema colapsaría.


Hoy en día ya no se capturan esclavos en África para venderlos en los mercados negreros porque son los propios nativos quienes pagan a las mafias, a los contrabandistas, a los coyotes para que los conduzcan hasta la tierra de promisión. Media humanidad se niega a aceptar esa sentencia que reza:

“Nacer pobres para morir pobres”

. Qué más da morir de inanición en el desierto o ahogados en el mar Mediterráneo o en el océano Atlántico porque de hecho ya están muertos.


 


Los sin tierra, los sin techo, los analfabetas, los huérfanos, los hambrientos y sedientos también quieren participar en el gran banquete capitalista

, esos seres invisibles pertenecientes al mundo de ultratumba huyen despavoridos en busca de ese espejismo que se trasmite en vivo y en directo que transmiten las cadenas de televisión a través de las antenas parabólicas, el Internet o los teléfonos celulares. 

El bombardeo publicitario es más poderoso que una lluvia de obuses o misiles

. Seducidos por la propaganda del lujo y la opulencia de ese mundo delirante de la “gran Babylon” de rascacielos dorados donde el genio de la lámpara maravillosa es capaz de cumplir todos nuestros deseos.

author: Kodao Productions
title: Love, death, struggle: Palestinian refugee couple hopes to return to Gaza
content:
Filipina Fatima Cargolio met her Palestinian husband Naji Al-Abdala while both were working at Al-Ain three decades ago. They had a daughter and a son in the UAE before eventually moving to Gaza, Naji’s homeland.


“Life was good for us in Gaza. We were operating a store near Al-Quds University selling spices, chocolates and biscuits,” Fatima recalled. She said they had their own house, a farm and their children were enrolled in the university.


Everything drastically changed when October 7, 2023 came, Fatima said. She counted 30 drone attacks in their neighborhood, targeting the police headquarters nearby, from seven o’clock in the morning. Naji and Fatima hunkered down beside their house’s interior walls, trying not to get hit.


When the initial aerial attacks abated, her daughter came with her four-year old son Amir. She told them she could not find her husband. Later reports by friends confirmed they have lost him to the Israeli attacks.


Refugees in the Philippines


Fatima and Naji did not want to leave Gaza at first. But as soon as stores could no longer open, electricity and water were cut off, they agreed to be repatriated to the Philippines via Egypt.


“We were among the third batch of Gazan refugees that flew to the Philippines a month and a half since the Israeli siege. We left on November 9 and arrived in Manila on November 14 of that year,” Fatima said.


Safe in the Philippines, Naji and Fatima thought their son-in-law’s death would be the last in their family. A month later, however, on December 15, their own son died of a heart attack, leaving a widow behind.


“The doctors told me the stress of the war in Gaza, his uprooting from the only life he’d known, and our forced evacuation contributed to our son’s death,” Fatima said.


To struggle is to live


Fatima serving a UP student who bought chicken biryani. (R. Villanueva)


The couple fought through their grief and started to look for ways to earn a living. With support from Arab friends in the Philippines as well as Filipino organizations, they started selling Palestinian food wherever allowed.


On Tuesdays to Thursdays, they sell to University of the Philippine students, faculty and staff within campus. They are also invited to sell during activities, such as in food bazaars in government offices and events.


“Our beef and grilled chicken biryani are our bestsellers,” Naji said. The couple also sells chicken and beef shawarma, somosa, cheese and nuts baklava, zainab fingers, layali lobnan sweets, roz bel laban, qataye sweets, Palestinian kunafa, beef rendang, maqlouba rice, kabsa rice, and uzi rice.


“We also accept bulk orders through my

Facebook account

,” Fatima said.


Naji and Fatima patiently explain to curious passersby how carefully their food is prepared. Naji tells them he only uses authentic Middle East spices when cooking. They have also made friends with repeat customers.


ALSO READ: 

Gazan refugees struggle to feel ‘real Ramadan’ in the Philippines


Life goes on


The only topic that could make the couple stop talking about their food is their grandson Amir, now seven years old. “He already speaks fluent Filipino!” Fatima exclaimed. Naji, proud grandfather, also intimated his grandson already has a crush among the family’s Filipino friends.


The couple said they do not know when the Israeli war would end. “If there would be real ceasefire, I would want to go back to Gaza, sell anything that I could from what remains of our properties there, and use that as capital for a food business here in the Philippines,” Naji said.


It is the Philippine-born Fatima, however, who said she still wishes to go back to Gaza permanently. “We are Gazans. We want to go back to Gaza,” she said.


Philippine-Palestine Friendship Association members in a rally near the US embassy on Wednesday, third anniversary of the Al-Aqsa Flood. (Photo by Nuel M. Bacarra/Kodao)


Solidarity and support


On the third anniversary of the Al-Aqsa Flood on Wednesday, Fatima said she watched reports of how Filipino activist groups, led by the

Philippine-Palestine Friendship Association

, marched to the United States Embassy in Manila to denounce the North American country’s support of the Israeli genocide of Palestinians.


“I cried while watching the reports. Aside from helping us with our livelihood here in the Philippines, they risk being arrested for standing up for us refugees, us Palestinians,” Fatima said.


“I love them very much,” she added. # …
