author: Sophie Lemcke
title: So ist es, als Huhn in der Fleischindustrie leben zu müssen
content:
Die Hühnermast ist ein grausames System, das auf maximale Schnelligkeit, Wachstum und Profit ausgelegt ist und mit einem gewaltvollen Tod für die Tiere endet.


Wie fühlt es sich an, als „Masthuhn“ geboren zu werden

, ohne die Möglichkeit, der leidvollen Industrie zu entkommen

?


Der einzige Grund, weshalb die Industrie dich „produziert“ hat: Du sollst so schnell wie möglich so schwer wie möglich werden – und wirst dann getötet.


Du kommst in einem Hühnerschlupfbetrieb mit tausenden anderen Küken zur Welt. Um dich herum piepsen sie verzweifelt. Und auch du suchst nach Nähe und Wärme. Aber da ist keine Mutter, in deren Gefieder du dich kuscheln kannst – und du wirst sie auch niemals kennenlernen.

Noch am ersten Tag deines Lebens wirst du über Förderbänder geschleudert und in eine Kiste gepackt. Dann beginnt die oftmals stundenlange Fahrt zum Mastbetrieb – eingepfercht mit Dutzenden anderen Küken, ohne Wasser, ohne Nahrung.


Foto: Andrew Skowron


Du kommst in einer riesigen Halle an. Hier wirst du die nächsten rund 5 Wochen verbringen – die einzigen Wochen deines Lebens.


Um dich herum Tausende andere Küken. Du teilst dir einen Quadratmeter mit bis zu 23 anderen Tieren. Jetzt seid ihr noch klein, doch das wird sich schnell ändern.


Du wächst. Unnatürlich schnell. Das Futter steht dir Tag und Nacht zur Verfügung – hochkalorisch, proteinreich, entwickelt für maximales Wachstum in kürzester Zeit.


Du hast keinen Platz, um dich natürlich zu bewegen, es gibt nichts zum Erkunden. Keinerlei Möglichkeiten, deine natürlichen Verhaltensweisen auszuleben. Es ist trist und laut. Da ist nur diese Enge.


Die Luft ist stickig. Der Ammoniakgeruch von den Ausscheidungen Tausender Tiere brennt in deinen Augen, in deinen Lungen. Du bekommst Atemwegserkrankungen. Jeder Atemzug tut weh.


Dein Körper wurde durch jahrzehntelange Züchtung so manipuliert, dass du in wenigen Wochen das Gewicht erreichst, für das ein Huhn unter natürlichen Bedingungen Monate bräuchte.


Foto: Andrew Skowron


Deine Brustmuskeln wachsen so schnell und werden so schwer, dass deine Knochen dein Gewicht nicht mehr tragen können. Deine Beine verformen sich. Dein Herz ist zu klein für deinen massiven Körper, es hat Probleme, deine Organe mit ausreichend Blut zu versorgen. Du hast Schmerzen beim Gehen und deine Gelenke sind entzündet.


Um dich herum sind Hühner, die gar nicht mehr aufstehen können. Sie liegen in ihrem eigenen Kot und leiden unter extremen Schmerzen. Sie verdursten und verhungern.


Andere Hühner werden aufgrund der Enge von ihren Artgenossen versehentlich totgetrampelt und erdrückt – ihre Körper verwesen zwischen dir und den tausenden anderen Tieren. Auch du hast keine Chance, den anderen Hühnern auszuweichen.


Dann ist es soweit. Menschen kommen und packen dich. An deinen Beinen, kopfüber, werden du und deine Artgenossen gegriffen und in enge Transportkisten geworfen. Deine ohnehin schon schmerzenden Beine brechen unter der groben Behandlung. Du hast Schmerzen und Todesangst.


Zusammengepfercht, ohne Wasser, ohne Futter, geht es zum Schlachthof. Die Fahrt kann Stunden dauern. Manche Hühner sterben bereits im Transporter – vor Stress, vor Erschöpfung, erdrückt von anderen Tieren.


Foto: Andrew Skowron


Im Schlachthof riechst du Blut. Du hörst die Schreie anderer Hühner. Dann bist du selbst an der Reihe. Unter grausamen Bedingungen wirst du betäubt und getötet. Du bist gerade einmal 35 bis 42 Tage alt geworden.


Es ist unvorstellbar, was Hühner in der Fleischindustrie erleiden müssen.


Die Wahrheit hinter „Hähnchenfleisch“


Wie grausam das kurze Leben von sogenannten Masthühnern ist, haben wir schon mehrfach bei Undercover-Recherchen aufgedeckt, beispielsweise in einem (jetzt ehemaligen) Zuliefererbetrieb der großen Marke Wiesenhof. Hier erfährst du mehr über unsere Aufdeckungen und kannst unsere Petition für strengere Tierschutzvorgaben, -kontrollen und -strafen unterzeichnen:


Jetzt für Hühner unterschreiben 


In Deutschland wird mehr Fleisch von Hühnern konsumiert als produziert – und die Nachfrage ist in den vergangenen Jahren stetig gestiegen. Unterstütze dieses grausame System nicht: Entscheide dich konsequent für pflanzliche Lebensmittel.


In den meisten Supermärkten findest du mittlerweile eine Vielfalt tierfreundlicher Alternativen, die hervorragende Proteinquellen sind – probiere sie aus. Oder koche unsere zahlreichen pflanzlichen Rezepte von Love Veg nach, wie unsere

knusprigen Tofu-Nuggets

.

author: L214
title: Marche pour la fermeture des abattoirs
content:
Chaque année, des milliards d’animaux sont tués pour l’alimentation : environ 69 milliards d’animaux terrestres et plus de 1 000 milliards de poissons dans le monde. Derrière ces chiffres se trouvent des individus sensibles, capables de ressentir la douleur, la peur et la détresse.

La Marche pour la fermeture des abattoirs est un appel à mettre fin à cette hécatombe. L’élevage, la pêche et l’abattage condamnent des êtres sensibles à une vie d’exploitation, puis à une mort violente et prématurée, alors même que nous n’avons pas besoin de produits d’origine animale pour vivre en bonne santé.

C’est dans ce contexte qu’aura lieu la nouvelle édition de la Marche pour la fermeture des abattoirs à Paris le 3 octobre 2026. Une Vegan Place (village associatif et commerçant) sera organisée le même jour pour apporter une touche gourmande et festive à l’événement.

title: The Rural Connections Behind Illegal Hunting
content:
Thanks to Wiltshire Hunt Sabs for this guest post, who, alongside Cirencester Illegal Hunt Watch, Bristol Hunt Sabs and Bath Hunt Sabs, have been keeping the pressure on the Beaufort Hunt.


The Duke of Beaufort’s Hunt is one of Britain’s most prominent fox hunts and has been terrorising wildlife across the countryside surrounding the Badminton Estate in Gloucestershire for hundreds of years. But the Beaufort Hunt does not exist in isolation. Behind it lies a wider rural network of landowners, estate managers and property professionals.


One of the most striking examples is Rupert Sturgis, Partner and Head of Knight Frank’s Cirencester office.


Rupert Sturgis, Partner and Head of Knight Frank, Cirencester. Image: Wiltshire Hunt Sabs


Knight Frank’s website describes Sturgis as specialising in the sale of town and country property across Gloucestershire and North Wiltshire.


Screenshot:

Knight Frank


He is also a Field Master of the Beaufort Hunt.


On Saturday we filmed Rupert directing the field riders to surround a covert. This is so foxes become trapped inside, whilst hounds are sent in to kill them. It’s a classic cubbing technique that teaches the new hounds to kill.


Rupert Sturgis directing the field to surround the covert in a classic cubbing formation. Image: Wiltshire Hunt Sabs


Watch the video below


Rupert’s role with the hunt is not recent. In 2015, Horse & Hound described him as an estate agent who was then in his 12th season as a Beaufort Field Master.


Image: Wiltshire Hunt Sabs


The Field describes him as a Beaufort Field Master, quoting him discussing the hunting country where they were openly hunting foxes just last Saturday, and where our drone was shot down in December 2025:

“Field Master Rupert Sturgis recommends the Widleys hedges as part of a run west from Common Wood Farm”

.


Beanie Sturgis laying a trail of cigarette ash. Image: Wiltshire Hunt Sabs


His wife, Beanie Sturgis, is also a Beaufort Field Master. Badminton Horse Trials states that she married Rupert in 2007 and describes her as a Beaufort Field Master, as well as an event organiser, show judge and course designer. Beanie accepted a community resolution in respect of a hate crime committed against a hunt sab in October 2024.


Knight Frank and the Badminton Estate


The connection between Knight Frank and the Badminton Estate goes well beyond Rupert Sturgis. In fact, Knight Frank has been involved with the estate for decades, with senior figures from the firm becoming closely involved in the management structure surrounding Badminton.


In its 2015 Rural Report, Knight Frank stated that it had been involved with the Badminton Estate for 15 years. The report featured Simon Dring, then Badminton’s senior resident agent, who said he had worked at the estate for more than 30 years, including 15 years as senior resident agent. He described working closely with the Duke and his family, as well as coordinating the various specialists and advisers involved with the estate.


Dring retired from the Knight Frank LLP partnership on 31 December 2016, but his relationship with Badminton continued for almost another decade. He remained the estate’s senior resident agent until his retirement from Badminton in late 2025.


Dring once hilariously told us, via deluded hunt supporters, that we couldn’t fly our drone in the ‘Duke’s air space’.


Companies House records show that he was secretary of Swangrove Estates Ltd from 31 March 2000 until 9 March 2026. The company is registered at the Estate Office, Badminton, and its stated business is mixed farming. He was also secretary of Swangrove Holdings Ltd from 31 March 2000 until 9 March 2026, another company registered at the Badminton Estate Office.


Both companies show current officers including members of the Somerset family alongside other directors. The records show the overlap between the people managing the estate and the companies through which its interests are held.


And Dring is not the only former Knight Frank figure with a connection to the Badminton Estate.


Christopher Smith, who was a Knight Frank partner heading its rural consultancy, renewables and energy consultancy, is now listed as a person with significant control of Badminton Hospitality Ltd, with ownership and voting rights of 75% or more. His correspondence address is the Badminton Estate Office.


Alexander (Sandy) Douglas provides another link. He has been a director of Swangrove Estates Ltd since 2000 …

title: Jeff Shantz - From Climate Crisis to Climate Culling
content:
Author

: Jeff Shantz

Title

: From Climate Crisis to Climate Culling

Subtitle

: Dis-Ecologies of Snuff Capital

Date

: 1996, Summer

Source

: Scanned from Anarcho-Syndicalist Review #94, Summer, 2026


 We have entered a period which I have taken to calling snuff capitalism—accumulation by elimination. Capital has moved past the mere accumulation by dispossession that David Harvey has written about extensively. Beyond dispossession, which Harvey argues clears routes for capital circulation, capital has moved to eliminate anything and everything that might pose a drain on accumulation (anything that might “waste” a penny for capital). This includes even minimal social spending that might support poor and unemployed working-class people, such as social housing, unemployment benefits, welfare, health care, etc. Increasingly it involves eliminating the poor and unemployed themselves—those deemed by capital to be useless to production or consumption —as through assisted suicide and elimination of supports for drug users (safe supply, harm reduction) or unhoused people such that the expected outcome is most likely death. It can include removal of health and safety protections for workers (in industries where capital believes those workers can be readily replaced). War, of course, remains a key means for capital to kill people.


 Capitalist eliminationism also includes active pursuit of ecocide. This is occurring through the elimination of regulations on industry, opening previously protected natural spaces for extraction, conversion of land into pesticide wastelands for industrial farming, mining of the seas and oceans, etc. We see numerous examples, such as the Trump regime’s plans to open pristine areas for oil drilling, as in the Arctic. Perversely, the United States government has formed a committee that has the power to decide when extinction is acceptable. The Endangered Species Committee—colloquially known as the God Squad—was created under the Endangered Species Act. It can exempt projects from law when protecting a species interferes with major economic interests. After three decades without meeting, the committee recently approved drilling in the Gulf of Mexico that could lead to extinction of the critically endangered Rice’s whale (only 51 of which are still alive).


 Ecocidal eliminationism also includes new wars and occupations. The recently launched Israel-US war on Iran is causing immense ecological crises in addition to the thousands of people murdered in the imperialist assault. I will address this in detail in an upcoming article.


 Climate crises provide opportunities for eliminationism on mass scales at accelerated pace. For capital, it is a low-cost way for clearing away human and natural obstacles to accumulation. And it allows them to do so in a way that permits them to make claims of blamelessness (as opposed to wars for example).


 Most of the people and places most severely impacted by climate crises are poor— excluded from production and consumption for capital by regimes of enforced scarcity. While reasonable people would view this as an atrocity, and reason to more quickly address climate destruction, for capital it is a boon—and reason to allow, or even encourage, climate crises to occur, and occur more precipitously.


 Entire regions and areas are designated for culling. Mike Davis refers to national sacrifice zones, “using this term to think about the ecological disaster to which certain regions of the US have been relegated, since neither these spaces nor their inhabitants are considered to be productive elements of the capitalist system.” (Sayak Valencia, 2018,

Gore Capitalism

. South Pasadena: Semiotext(e), p. 182)


Accelerating Past the Point...


 There are more and more indications that some of the world’s tipping points, such as drastic changes to ocean currents, could be breached in a future that is no longer very distant. Today’s rate of global warming—more than 1.3 degrees C (2.3 degrees F) in only the last hundred years—is already completely unprecedented in human history.


 And it is only getting worse. Global warming is accelerating, going from 1.4 to 1.6 degrees C in 2023 to two degrees C and rising by the 2030s. It could blow past two degrees before the end of the century. New research published in March 2026 in Geophysical Research Letters, finds that the rate of global warming has accelerated since 2015, even after accounting for other phenomena such as …

author: Austin Corona
title: The bipartisan energy bill tearing the climate movement apart
content:
In order to solve climate change, you have to do two things — stop burning fossil fuels, and build clean energy to replace them. The last few decades in the United States have witnessed a long back-and-forth over which of the two goals is more important, and over how to achieve either of them. Is it more important to pass a carbon tax, or subsidize electric vehicles? To block a new oil pipeline, or build a lot of solar and wind? 


On this question, the coalition known as the climate movement has fractured into two broad groups. On one side, there are activists, lawyers, and environmentalists, who tend to focus on blocking and reducing fossil fuel use. On the other, there are renewable energy companies and policy wonks, who tend to focus on building more clean energy.


These factions have clashed in the past, but over the past week a kind of civil war has erupted between the different elements of the climate movement. The inciting incident was the release of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, a long-awaited Senate bill that is designed to enable the construction of more power plants, transmission lines, and gas pipelines. The bill does this by weakening some of the nation’s bedrock environmental laws, speeding up the timeline for government agencies to issue permits, and making it harder to cancel projects that have already gotten federal approval. 


For climate-conscious supporters of the bill, it’s better for the planet to build a lot of clean energy even if it means some fossil fuels get built as well, and even if they cause some damage to the environment on the way. Supporters of the effort argue that if the U.S. builds out new clean capacity, it will be easier to wean off fossil fuels, which are the primary cause of global warming and all its myriad consequences. Opponents say that’s a Faustian bargain, one that will jeopardize tribal nations, other marginalized communities, and endangered species.


“It is definitely exposing a potential fault line between the environmental community and clean energy interests,” said Representative Jared Huffman, a Democrat who represents Northern California, in an interview with Grist. 


Representative Jared Huffman, a Democrat from California, is skeptical of the Senate permitting reform bill.


Photo by Andrew Harnik / Getty Images


BAAJA is the product of months of bipartisan negotiation between four members of the Senate committees focused on energy and the environment. The two Democrats in the talks were Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, who are both climate hawks and clean energy advocates. The Republicans were Mike Lee of Utah and Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia, who are advocates of fossil fuels and critics of environmental regulation. Despite their ideological differences, the four senators managed to reach a compromise on a

sprawling 400-page bill

 with hundreds of individual provisions. 


The so-called “four corners” reached a deal just before Congress left for its fall recess, and the Senate will not return to take up the bill until after the midterm elections. The bill has not even made it through committee yet, and it also faces an uncertain fate in the House of Representatives. The next few weeks will see a scramble of lobbying as supporters and opponents of the bill try to sway senators and representatives for or away from the bill.


So far, at least, the builders seem to have more influence than the blockers, at least within the climate movement. President Donald Trump has spent the last two years

repealing


most


federal


climate policy

 and blocking the development of new clean energy, and many climate advocates seem willing to accept an imperfect deal rather than hold out hope of fixing Trump’s damage after he leaves office.


“It’s a lot easier to prevent things from being built than to build things, and that applies both to fossil fuels and to renewables,” said Zeke Hausfather, a climate expert at the science nonprofit Berkeley Earth, who also directs climate research for the tech company Stripe. “I don’t want us to run roughshod over any community, but we also can’t give everyone a veto for an issue as important as climate change. So ultimately, we need to strike a balance there.”


The case in favor: Build more


A big challenge with building clean energy is that it takes up a lot of space. Solar farms and wind farms can cover thousands of acres of land, and the …

author: Grist staff
title: Trump’s Gutting of the Endangered Species Act Will Imperil Hundreds of Species
content:
Razing the habitat of an endangered or threatened species will no longer come with federal penalties.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

The Supreme Court once billed the Endangered Species Act as “the most comprehensive legislation for the preservation of endangered species ever enacted by any nation.” Federal protections have been key to saving nearly 300 U.S. species — including the bald eagle, American alligator, and grizzly bear — from permanent extinction.

Each year, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, which is primarily responsible for implementing the law, evaluates species and lists them as “endangered” or “threatened.” When federal activity or private development has the potential to harm a listed species or its habitat, project developers are required to consult with the Service or obtain a permit prior to construction.

For the last several decades, the interpretation of two words in particular — “take” and “harm” — have formed the backbone of the Nixon-era law. Its prohibition of “taking” an animal criminalized any attempts to “harass, harm, pursue, hunt, shoot, wound, kill, trap, capture, or collect” at-risk species. And the provision on “harm” ensured that degrading a listed species’ habitat could be penalized. These definitions have been key to the success of the law.

But that all changed last month when the Trump administration determined that razing the habitat where endangered or threatened species breed, feed, and shelter would no longer face federal penalties. In a separate internal memo, the administration also reinterpreted the definition of “take,” limiting it to instances of intentional killing of an endangered species. (Nearly two dozen attorneys general have sued over some of these changes.)

“These rule changes, when you zoom out, are an assault on threatened and endangered species unlike we’ve ever seen before,” said Elizabeth Forsyth, a senior attorney in the biodiversity defense program with Earthjustice, a nonprofit environmental law organization. “It’s an effort to eliminate habitat protections, eliminate automatic protections for threatened species, and give industry power.”

Climate change is making matters worse, as species struggle to adapt to warming temperatures and changing ecosystems. Below, Grist reporters look at how 10 species — from lovable sea otters to a misunderstood snake — might fare as the regulatory framework that has kept them afloat is weakened.

North Atlantic right whales got their name perversely. Because they stick close to shore and to the surface, and float when killed, they were the “right whale” to hunt. So right that humans hunted them nearly to extinction before the practice was banned in the 1930s.

That’s not why right whales are dying today.

“Nobody goes out and says, ‘I’m gonna hit a right whale with my ship,’” said Delcianna Winders, director of the Animal Law and Policy Institute at Vermont Law and Graduate School. But it happens anyway.

Though it’s not always possible to determine the cause of death for a whale, research shows that the leading cause is human activity: Ships strike the whales and fishing gear ensnares them, leading to injury and death. It happens often enough that North Atlantic right whales have been experiencing an unusual mortality event since 2017, in which 43 have died and 133 have been spotted injured or in poor health. About 380 whales remain, only 70 of whom are breeding females.

Well before the latest changes to the Endangered Species Act, the Trump administration had already begun rolling back protections for right whales. In March, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration announced plans to rescind ocean speed restrictions designed to reduce the risk of vessel strikes. The agency later declined to expand the whales’ designated critical habitat to include their migratory route.

The administration will likely use its new definition of “take” to bolster those actions, Winders said. “Now they can point to this and say, ‘Look, we can’t have speed limits under the law because it only applies to intentional direct activities.’”

author: Unknown
title: Satellite images document ecological destruction in Southern Kurdistan
content:
Satellite images from twenty areas in the Duhok province in Southern Kurdistan (Northern Iraq)  document the extent of ecological destruction linked to the Turkish occupation. Comparisons of the images show how formerly forested mountain slopes were extensively cleared within just a few years and opened up by new roads. The regions of Zaxo and Amêdî, where the Turkish army has been expanding its military infrastructure for years, have been particularly affected, according to a report by the Mezopotamya News Agency (MA).


Particularly since the intensification of Turkish incursions into Zap, Avaşîn and Metîna in 2017, numerous roads and military bases have been constructed in the mountainous regions. Forest areas are cleared for their construction, fragmenting previously contiguous landscapes. At the same time, large quantities of timber have been transported from the affected areas to Turkey for years.


Deforestation in the mountainous regions of Behdînan


The Behdînan region, particularly the areas of Zaxo, Duhok, Berwarî Bala and Amêdî, has been especially severely affected. Deforestation there has once again intensified recently. According to research conducted on the ground, the companies involved are stepping up their operations ahead of winter. The felled trees are loaded onto trucks under military supervision and transported across the border into Turkey.


According to the research, Turkish companies are involved in logging operations. Hundreds of thousands of trees are reported to have been felled in the affected areas in recent years. Among the locations where logging is currently particularly intensive are the villages of Mîska, Qumri, Hirûrê, Kêste, Tirwaniş and Nizdûrê in Berwarî Bala.


Çiyayê Basêr / Barzan / Amêdî, 2017-2022


​​​​


The continued destruction of the forests has met with resistance from the local population. Residents of the affected areas are calling on both the Iraqi federal government and the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) to take action against the deforestation.


Ali Teter, governor of the KDP-run Duhok province, rejected reports of the logging. He claimed that the published images had been taken in Turkey and did not show deforestation within the Kurdistan Region of Iraq. Journalists on the ground disputed this account and confirmed that the trees are being felled in Southern Kurdistan and subsequently transported to Turkey.


Twenty sites examined over several years


The scale of the environmental damage is evident from comparisons of satellite images from twenty areas in Duhok province. The images cover different periods between 2013 and 2023 and show both the loss of extensive tree cover and the construction of new roads and access routes.


The changes are particularly striking north of the village of Dêreşîş in the Zaxo region. While an image from 2018 still shows largely contiguous forest cover on Mount Celde, by 2023 the area had been extensively deforested. Numerous roads and tracks cut across the slopes, with only scattered patches of the former tree cover remaining.


Dêreşîş, 2018-2023


The landscape northeast of the village of Êkmale in the Zaxo-Batîfa region also changed considerably within a short period. Between 2017 and 2019, a large proportion of the vegetation disappeared from one of the areas examined. The previously predominantly forested slope was replaced by extensive barren areas and a branching network of roads and tracks.


Êkmale, 2017-2019


Another example can be found in the Amêdî region, around two kilometers northeast of the Gilalte stream near the former settlement of Horkî. A comparison of images from 2015 and 2021 shows a significant decline in vegetation. The more recent image reveals largely barren mountain slopes crisscrossed by numerous roads and tracks.


Horkî, 2015-2021


Other areas examined are located west and east of the town of Gelûk, around Senat, and on the slopes of the Gurvil and Girê Heşkî mountains. These also include areas near Kûxkê and Barzan in Amêdî. The comparisons demonstrate that the environmental damage is not confined to individual military sites but extends across large parts of the mountainous Behdînan region.


Çiyayê Qîra / Gelûk, 2018-2020


The scale of the destruction extends beyond satellite imagery


The satellite images analyzed extend through 2023. The deforestation and expansion of military infrastructure in the years that followed are therefore not yet reflected in these image comparisons. In …

author: Önder Algedik
title: COP31: A fair, not a climate summit
content:
The Pacific finally got its pre-COP meeting this week and only around 30 leaders gathered in Fiji and Tuvalu, with only five countries from outside the Pacific.

Vanuatu’s climate minister said he was hoping for more, adding that it “reflects the lack of attention and priority given to what Pacific nations consider the greatest threat to their future”.

The co-host, who did turn up, made the contradiction clear.

Australia’s energy minister Chris Bowen said in Nadi, Fiji, that “as a fossil fuel exporting nation, we can bring something different to the table”. He certainly can. Labor has approved 37 new or expanded fossil fuel projects since 2022.

The other COP31 host is preparing for Antalya in its own way. In September alone, Türkiye blocked at least 1270 X accounts, journalists and Amnesty Türkiye among them, more than in the whole of last year. Green Left itself is blocked in Türkiye: I can only read it through a virtual private network.

The COP31 host agreement, made public only last month, tells accredited participants they have a “duty” not to interfere in Türkiye’s “internal affairs”, a clause Brazil dropped for COP30.

Put the two together and the division of labour is clear. One host keeps approving the fuel. The other prepares to silence those who might object to it. This is climate politics as it actually works.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s first report in 1990 called for emissions to be cut “immediately” by more than 60%. By 2019, its sixth report found, they were 54% higher.

Last year global energy demand grew 2.7%, with oil, gas and coal all growing.

The problem, then, is not “climate change”, a phrase that turns policy into weather. The problem is a climate-changing policy — the deliberate fueling of climate change, through more and expanded coal mines, liquified natural gas terminals and 20-year gas contracts.

The system behind the deals and who pays the bill has a name — the fossil order.

COP31 is no longer a climate summit. It is a climate-changing summit and, increasingly, a climate fair. Its Action Agenda lists 10 themes, from zero waste to electrification. None names coal, oil or gas.

Its “global business partner”, Koç Holding, owns Türkiye’s oil refineries. Its “electrification partner”, Sabancı, co-owns a lignite power plant. Its “global banking partner” will run a 400-square-metre pavilion. In Antalya, the stands will be busy and the products on display will be green. An end to fossil fuels will not be up for discussion.

Asking for a “better COP” means asking for a “better fair”.

Stopping new fossil fuel projects is no longer enough; we need to start shutting down the coal, oil and gas which is being mined now.

Free public transport, the public ownership of energy and climate-friendly cities are revolutionary demands today. They do not just make new oil wells unnecessary, they empty the ones already pumping and let us begin to close mines, wells and gas lines.

The freedom to say all this out loud, in Antalya, is a challenge to the status quo.

Movements can win these demands. Australia’s High Court ruled on October 7 that the states planning bodies must consider how the burning of fossil fuels, exported from Australia, contribute to climate damage.

“We cannot dig up coal, ship it overseas, watch it drive climate change, and pretend the consequences have nothing to do with us,” said Wendy Wales, one of the retired teachers behind the campaign to get Australia to minimise all greenhouse gas emissions, including emissions produced from burning the exported coal emissions.

Wales said the court decision “has finally made a change in direction in our laws. The [planning rules] will now have to reflect the need to consider climate impacts of our scope three emissions from the coal that we export.”

The real climate summit has to be taken to the streets and wherever people dare to name the fossil order creating the climate emergency, which is devastating communities, who have had the least to do with creating problem.

[Önder Algedik is a climate researcher and activist with 350Ankara. His new book, Ya Fosil Düzen Ya Devrim (Fossil Order or Revolution), is published by İletişim this month.]

title: Contre Janco et son monde !
content:
Cette brochure s'appuie sur la BD Le monde sans fin de Jancovici (les numéros des pages desquelles sont tirées les citations sont entre parenthèses) pour illustrer l'incompatibilité profonde entre l'analyse des écologistes et les fantasmes des technologistes. Cette critique n'a pas la prétention d'être exhaustive. De plus, les nombreuses références qui ponctuent le texte, comme autant d'invitations à aller plus loin, témoignent du temps qu'il m'a manqué pour développer plus en profondeur la pensée naturienne, anti-industrielle, qui me nourrit. J'ai préféré me concentrer sur un ensemble de pistes à explorer ainsi qu'à démontrer en quoi cette critique me semble constructive et stratégiquement bénéfique à la lutte pour la nature et la liberté.


Introduction


Certes, il y a plein de choses intéressantes dans cette BD et dans le discours de Jancovici de façon générale. Il comprend très bien certaines limites physiques du système actuel et sait parfaitement vulgariser des notions parfois complexes avancées par les chercheurs du GIEC notamment. D'un point de vue scientifique son discours parait clair, limpide, d'une grande rigueur et en de nombreux points implacable. Il paraît seulement., En effet, ses omissions et sa grille de lecture techno-centrée évacuent de nombreuses réalités pourtant largement avérées. D'un point de vue politique, nous sommes bien loin du discours des écologistes qui défendent la nature et la liberté comme conditions essentielles d'une vie bonne, juste, égalitaire et soutenable.


Je crois qu'il est important, dans le contexte des luttes actuelles, de critiquer et dénoncer ces discours qui, définitivement, ne vont pas « dans le bon sens ». Malgré toutes les bonnes intentions qu'on peut lui prêter et malgré la rigueur apparente de ses analyses, l'horizon politique qu'il dessine n'est pas enviable et doit être combattu.


« Notre tâche consiste à proposer une critique impitoyable, et de nos prétendus amis bien plus que de nos ennemis manifestes. Nous renonçons avec plaisir, en adoptant cette attitude, à une popularité démagogique. »


 Karl Marx & Friedrich Engels, « Gottfried Kinkel »


 « Pour progresser sur une route qui sera brumeuse et ardue, le mouvement écologique devra s'exercer à la critique de soi et de ses pseudo-alliés ; et pour ce travail de dépollution intellectuelle et morale, les matériaux ne manqueront pas. »


 Bernard Charbonneau


Technologistes vs Écologistes


Aujourd'hui, quand on parle d'écologie, plusieurs courants coexistent et s'affrontent. On peut, notamment, différencier schématiquement les écologistes des technologistes :


https://www.partage-le.com/2022/01/29/leur-ecologie-et-la-notre-technologistes-contre-naturiens-par-nicolas-casaux/

.


Évidemment, seuls les technologistes ont la faveur des grands médias. C'est pour cela que, dans cette opposition asymétrique, les écologistes ont peu de chance d'exister auprès du grand public. Jancovici est un technologiste comme beaucoup de figures écolos mainstreams. A l'inverse, les écologistes portent les idées des courants anti-industriels, luddites, anarchistes naturiens, anarcho-primitivistes…


Une grande différence entre ces deux visions de l'écologie réside dans l'analyse du monde actuel et passé et dans les objectifs politiques qui en découlent.


Les écologistes, philosophiquement écocentristes, qui placent la vie au centre, ont pour objectif de préserver et régénérer la diversité biotique sur Terre. (L'écocentrisme reconnaît que des formes de vie existent par et pour elles-mêmes dans la nature, et qu'elles sont dignes de considération morale indépendamment des services qu'elles pourraient rendre à l'espèce humaine). Pour eux le problème est la civilisation, en tant qu'organisation sociale intrinsèquement expansionniste, hiérarchisée, extractiviste, patriarcale, inégalitaire, militarisée (la civilisation industrielle, ou contemporaine, étant sûrement la pire), qui détruit la nature et aliène les individus. Ils souhaitent donc que l'effondrement de la civilisation advienne le plus rapidement possible, avant l'effondrement des communautés biotiques, avant l'effondrement de la vie sur Terre. Il ne peut pas, par définition, exister de civilisation soutenable.


(pour en savoir plus sur le concept de civilisation, ses implications sociales et les destructions écologiques inhérentes à son maintien, il existe Endgame, un très bon livre de Derrick Jensen en 2 tomes et traduit en français aux Éditions LIBRE. J'invite aussi à la …

title: What will Nunavut look like by the end of the century?
content:
By the end of this century, there’s an even chance that winter temperatures will exceed 10 C across much of


Heavy rains wash out a bridge in Pond Inlet on Sept. 5. (Photo courtesy of Andrew Tagak)


Nunavut, and that glaciers in western Canada could lose more than 75 per cent of their ice, say scientists behind a new climate change forecast,

Canada’s Changing Climate.


That report, released in September by climate scientists with Environment and Climate Change Canada and other academics, predicts what Canada’s Arctic might look like if average global temperatures exceed pre-industrial levels by 1.5 C.


That’s the threshold most nations committed, under the 2015 Paris Agreement, to avoid crossing in order to prevent the most severe and irreversible impacts of climate change.


It also considers what could happen if average temperatures rise to 4 C above pre-industrial levels.


The planet is expected to exceed the 1.5 C threshold in the next few years, according to a United Nations Environment Programme

report

 on climate change also released in September. The Arctic has already warmed three times faster than the global average since 1970, according to the federal Environment Department.


Many climate scientists agree some impacts, like sea-level changes, glacier melt, and permafrost thaw, will be irreversible. The oceans are projected to lose sea ice as well, but this loss may be temporary if temperatures stabilize. These changes will alter ecosystems and habitats in significant ways.


Sea ice reflects far more heat than the ocean does, for instance.


A road once used by ATVs in Pond Inlet on Sept. 5, 2026, is damaged following coastal erosion. (Photo courtesy of Andrew Tagak)


“You see ice- and snow-covered surfaces replaced by dark water that’s now absorbing more heat,” said Gregory W. Thiemann, associate dean of the Faculty of Environmental and Urban Change at York University.


Permafrost also operates as a carbon sink. When it thaws, it releases greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide and methane into the atmosphere, contributing to an increase in global greenhouse gas emissions. The northern permafrost region, which covers Canada, Alaska, Siberia, and Greenland, contains up to three times the amount of carbon currently in the atmosphere, which is why even small releases drastically influence global emissions, a 2025

study

 in the journal Science highlights.


Permafrost thaw also causes the ground itself to sink. This causes landslides and coastal erosion, threatening homes, roads and other critical infrastructure.


The damage could be “catastrophic,” said Daniel Fortier, a University of Montreal geography professor who studies permafrost, climate change and adaptation in the North.


“The High Arctic is reacting very strongly,” he said, adding permafrost thaw will persist at a rapid pace for some time before the ground begins to stabilize once again.


“Images we see of landslides and gullies forming and things like that, it’s true, it’s happening, but it’s not going to stay like that for 30 years,” he added. “It’s a short-term response.”


Cameron DeLong, director of the Government of Nunavut’s Climate Change Secretariat, described permafrost thaw as the most pressing issue communities are facing.


“We’re seeing the impact of that on a variety of fronts,” he said, adding his office works with builders to ensure they can access the right information about how to plan projects with climate resilience in mind.


Thermosyphon systems, which measure underground temperatures, have been integrated into many buildings in Nunavut, including the new airport terminal in Rankin Inlet, according to Nunavut’s Transportation and Infrastructure Department. These systems, like the one at the Iqaluit Airport, can also be used to remove heat from below to stop thawing.


DeLong said the GN’s adaptation and mitigation priorities include expanding maps of permafrost and climate hazards, which is currently happening in Iqaluit; staying up to date on coastal erosion; emergency planning to assess how well communities are prepared for major weather events like flooding; and updating infrastructure like culverts to reduce the chances of heavy rain causing flooding.


Heavy rain in Pond Inlet last month caused damage to roads and culverts throughout the hamlet.


Resident Andrew Tagak said the flooding was unlike anything he had seen before.

author: Josiah David Quising
title: Family, advocates remember 1987 killing of peasant leader, son
content:
Almost four decades later, they still remember. Friends and family held a memorial and candle lighting activity on October 3 to remember Valeriano Caro and his son who were killed 39 years ago by members of the Composite Reaction Force, a unit of the Regional Special Action Force, under the Cory Aquino administration.

Caro was a peasant leader from Kilusang Magbubukid ng Pilipinas (KMP) and chairperson of the Kahublagan sang Mangunguma sa Isla sang Panay (KAMIPA).

He and his son Rolito were killed in Barangay Galang, Oton, Iloilo on October 3, 1987. The memorial and candle-lighting were held on the roadside near the site where they were killed.

According to his wife in a report published by Amnesty International in 1988, Valeriano and her son were taken by the military at around 9:25 a.m. and were shot by a military officer just 70 meters from their own home.

On his 39th death anniversary, Valeriano’s family recalled his dedication to the plight of farmers in Panay.

“His legacy lives on in the continuing struggle to free farmers from landlessness, from bondage to the land, and from abuses at the hands of the regime,” Panay Alliance Karapatan said in a statement. (DAA)

author: Esperanza
title: Comunidad Temulemu vuelve a la Corte Interamericana de Derechos Humanos por el caso de su werken Rafael Pichun Collonao
content:
La comunidad Temulemu interpondrá una demanda ante la Comisión Interamericana de Derechos Humanos, por el caso de su werken Rafael Pichun Collonao, privado de libertad en la cárcel de Angol desde abril del 2024, condenado a 7 y 8 años de cárcel por su supuesta “participación organizativa” en el llamado caso Quilleco.


Según el Lonco Juan Pichun, el estado de Chile vulnera su propia legislación y lo que hoy vive su hermano Rafael repite lo que vivió su padre en la CIDH por el caso lonkos, en el año 2013:


“Hoy en día no sólo se vulneran los derechos Mapuches, el mismo estado a través de los poderes judiciales, a través de los persecutores, están vulnerando los mismos derechos que el estado ha impulsado y legislado, y en ese marco creemos que es importante llevar el caso de Rafael como un caso donde se vulneran varios derechos, como por ejemplo los derechos a la defensa, con el uso de testigos secretos, sin rostro.


Es una discriminación por parte del estado, dentro de sus mismos contextos jurídicos, ellos mismos han vulnerado su propia legislación.


Esta es la segunda vez que llevaremos un caso de la familia a un contexto internacional. Ya el estado de Chile fue condenado, y Rafael es parte de ese fallo de la CIDH, en el llamado caso lonkos, donde mi padre pudo lograr su inocencia a través de este tribunal internacional y eso mismo queremos acreditar, que en la acusación que le hacen a Rafael se vulneran también los derechos a una defensa”.


El werken rafael Pichun fue condenado en el denominado caso Quilleco, proceso judicial donde se presentó como única prueba un mensaje de whatsapp que el Werkén recibe, lo que la comunidad y los abogados defensores consideran insuficiente para mantenerlo hoy en la cárcel.


“Si hoy día ponemos a un Mapuche y a un no Mapuche en las mismas condiciones, en un mismo juicio, el que no es mapuche va a salir libre y nuestra gente va a ser condenada a una alta condena”.

Radio Kurruf

author: Karin Jervert
title: Mad in the World at the Mad in Norway International Film Festival
content:
A

s a ‘voices and visions gal’, as I call myself, who recently reclaimed her life from psychiatric abuse and over-medication, every little life thing I do is so big and impactful that one of my friends at home has a running joke about me. She texts me after every event, trip, workshop, or talk and asks, “Are you changed?” and my answer is always “Yes!” because returning to life after losing so much to psychiatry has a mind-blowing impact even in the minutia others gloss over. Everyday things that “normal” people ignore, or feel are just living—to me are a miracle of sorts.


This is what I expressed at the restaurant when I toasted a room full of friends and colleagues in the Mad in the World Network who had come to Norway for a Mad in the World meeting and the Mad in Norway International Film Festival. Earlier in the day, a lot of jet-lagged folks sat around a room excitedly talking together about what would be possible in the future. At the restaurant, I spoke of the miracle of the moment we were living in just then, the fact that all of us arrived in person in Lillehammer to meet and to enjoy these films on rethinking mental health.


I looked around that room and saw my heroes. All fighting in their own way for the thriving, health, and sovereignty of people in mental distress around the world. To me, it was an epic gathering, the impact of which we will continue to see ripples of in the coming months.


A few years ago, many of us met in Copenhagen, and the effect was a bit of the same. Our in-person smiles, hugs, laughter, and learning gave us heart in the fight for informed consent and human rights in psychiatry. We inspired each other with our individual and collective efforts. I am always aware of the resistance we face—the derision from psychiatry, the trolls, the personal attacks, and the fear. Every time I am in a room with these people, I see not only our strength and our hearts, but what we are up against. And I know we will keep fighting together on this path. And I am grateful we have each other.


Mad in the World at Mad in Norway International Film Festival, Lillehammer, Norway


And as always, when I arrived home again to the USA, I really was changed. So, I can report back to my friend, that yes, life—and this work—is still a beautiful miracle to me.


The schedule was well-organized, each film well-selected, and the panels after the films were informative. It was a wonderful privilege to encounter in person the directors, thinkers, artists, musicians, members of clinical teams, and parents involved. There was not a moment that one of the 208 attendees was left without something to enjoy, grow in, or experience something new and exciting—let alone the beauty of the town itself.


Even the late-night showings were well-attended. Late one evening, when the credits rolled on The Dance Club, the entire audience got up and danced. Some of my favorite people I spotted smiling and dancing in the aisles, a beautiful sight to see! This film was so beautiful I recommend that you check it out. Grete Johnsen—who, by the way, was a huge part of our everyday, who was always waiting at the welcome desk with a smile (and a few Post-It notes for me to attend to)—has put up links directing to where most of these films can be screened. You can find those here. So, those of you who could not attend can at least enjoy some of the films on various streaming platforms.


There were so many wonderful films it is impossible to mention them all here in this brief review.


As an organizer I am most proud of creating the art show, which you can view here. It was an honor to see the work of many survivors on the big screen. Another wonderful privilege was hosting, with Alan Robinson from Locura en Argentina, the music and poetry show. The musicians and poets showcased at this event brought the night to another magical place filled with powerful expressions of self-empowerment after psychiatric harm. They reminded us of the collective joy art can bring. The highlight was a circle dance, hands clasped, around the entire theater while the Mad in Brasil team—with the musicians from the Creative Humanities Score (another great movie!)—led us in music and singing and dancing together. I saw enormous smiles and childlike joy on so many of my beloved colleagues and friends’ faces. A moment I won’t soon forget.


So as to not go on forever about this amazing event, I’ll now summarize in brief. This festival was a hard-won success …

title: Tlaib, Democrats Call for Israel to Release Palestinian Doctors From Detention
content:
Israel has killed over 1,700 Palestinian health care workers in three years of genocide in Gaza.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

A group of House Democrats has called for Israel to release hundreds of health care workers, including physicians like Hussam Abu Safiya, from detention as Israel’s genocide in Gaza reaches into its fourth year.

Six Democrats, led by Rep. Jesús “Chuy” García (Illinois), released a joint statement on Tuesday condemning Israel for its “systematic persecution” of Palestinian health care workers and demanding their release from arbitrary detention.

“Over the last three years, the Israeli government has systematically destroyed the health system in Palestine, murdering at least 1,700 Palestinian doctors, nurses, paramedics, and other healthcare workers and destroying dozens of hospitals. It has arrested and arbitrarily detained hundreds of Palestinian healthcare workers, including at least 16 physicians who continue to be held in inhumane conditions,” the lawmakers wrote.

The Democrats specifically call for the release of Abu Safiya, who Israel has held in its torture camps for nearly two years, where they have starved and tortured him, his lawyer says. Abu Safiya is a pediatrician who served as the director of Kamal Adwan Hospital in northern Gaza when Israel besieged the area.

The world watched in December 2024 as Israel’s ground raid closed in on Kamal Adwan, with Israeli forces eventually ordering the entire facility to be evacuated, setting it ablaze and arresting Abu Safiya. The hospital was left in ruins after Israeli soldiers were done with it.

“Among [those detained] is Dr. Hussam Abu Safiya, whom the Israeli government has arbitrarily detained since 2024 and tortured to the point of near-death after previously murdering his son and brutally attacking his hospital,” the lawmakers went on.

The statement was signed by Representatives Pramila Jayapal (Washington), Summer Lee (Pennsylvania), Ilhan Omar (Minnesota), Delia C. Ramirez (Illinois), and Rashida Tlaib (D-Michigan).

Israel's systematic destruction of the Palestinian healthcare system and targeting of healthcare workers is at the heart of its genocide. We must stand up for those targeted for saving lives. Free Dr. Hussam Abu Safiya. Free Dr. Mazen Rantisi. Free Dr. Dima Amin.…

The Democrats also called for an end to arms transfers to Israel and urged Congress to block the Trump administration’s planned $2.8 billion package of 2,000-pound bombs to Israel — which is slated to be paid for by U.S. taxpayers. Other Democrats have also vowed to work against that transfer.

In three years of genocide in Gaza, Israel has killed more than 1,700 health care workers and has left zero hospitals fully functioning in the enclave. Israeli forces have also detained more than 400 health care workers from Gaza without charges or a trial in their torture camps.

Israel has killed nearly 600 aid workers since October 7, 2023, according to UN counts.

“Over the past three years, people’s ability to access health care in Gaza has deteriorated dramatically, with medical facilities lying in ruins, hospitals increasingly running out of basic supplies, and patients unable to access essential medicines and treatments. Restrictions on essential supplies such as engine oil and spare parts are also crippling the infrastructure needed to keep hospitals, ambulances, and water systems running, with generators breaking down and water-trucking operations reduced,” said Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) in a statement on Monday.

“It will take generations to recover from the harm that has already been done over the past three years, and in the preceding decades, while the excruciating consequences of Israel’s ongoing genocide are still being felt every day,” said Amande Bazerolle, the head of MSF’s emergency response in Gaza.

title: Görme Engelli Kadın Milli Futbol Takımı namağlup Avrupa Şampiyonu oldu
content:
Türkiye Görme Engelliler Spor Federasyonunun ev sahipliğinde, Türkiye Futbol Federasyonu Hasan Doğan Milli Takımlar Kamp ve Eğitim Tesisleri'nde düzenlenen turnuvanın finalinde ay-yıldızlı takım, Polonya ile karşı karşıya geldi.

Kaptan Gülşah Aktürk ve Kevser Ökmen'in golleriyle rakibini 2-0 mağlup eden Türkiye, böylece tarihinde ilk kez katıldığı Avrupa Şampiyonası'nda namağlup altın madalyanın sahibi oldu.

Organizasyon boyunca 4 galibiyet ve 1 beraberlik yaşayan milliler, 7 kez ağları havalandırırken kalesinde gol görmedi.

Şampiyonanın tamamlanmasının ardından düzenlenen ödül töreninde Avrupa şampiyonu milli takım, elde ettiği tarihi başarının sevincini yaşadı.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Béla
title: Join our next PeerNetz session: building peer-led trans healthcare
content:
As part of our Peer Networking Zone (PeerNetz), TGEU is hosting a meeting to explore healthcare designed by and for trans people, rooted in community knowledge and care. We’ll be joined by Trans Healthcare Action, the organisation behind Kindred, Ireland’s first peer-led trans health clinic.


The session will be interactive, with practical exercises and space to explore how Kindred’s experience and lessons could translate to different contexts across Europe and Central Asia.


About the session


Date & time:


15 October, 16:00 – 17:30 CEST

Location:

 Online via Zoom

Cost:

 Free

Target audience:

 Trans communities and activists 


Register here


What the session will cover 


Trans Healthcare Actions will share how Kindred was created through co-creation between the local trans community and allied healthcare professionals, and walk us through the clinic’s foundation, model, structure, services and vision.


The session will also explore how the Irish social, legal and medical landscape shaped their approach, and invite participants to think about their own contexts: What gaps exist in trans healthcare? What community networks and resources are already available? What might help or hinder efforts to build similar community-led care?


Register here


Your support makes change possible


We work across Europe and Central Asia to advance trans rights, build strong communities, and drive change through research, advocacy, and community-building.


Your donation helps us continue this vital work — defending trans lives, amplifying trans voices, and advocating for justice every day.

title: Le temps des promesses
content:
Alors que la jeunesse française embrase le pays, nous avons interviewé Christian Ingrao pour son nouveau livre

Le Temps des promesses

. La situation présente est le produit d'une lente glaciation de l'espérance qui avait été annoncée non par des prophètes, mais par des historiens, des économistes, des ingénieurs agronomes, et toutes ces littératures grises qui enregistrent, en même temps qu'elles font, l'espérance et ses vacillements. Nous vivons les derniers moments d'une série de promesses nées aux lendemains de la mutation anthropologique des guerres mondiales, et dont la force d'élan et d'entraînement s'est tarie au tournant des années 1980. En réactivant une méthode matérialiste inspirée de Engels et Marx, Ingrao parvient à reconstruire la « sociogenèse de l'espérance », depuis une multitude d'observatoires, dont le temps présent nous dit la fin.

author: Ndivhuwo Mukwevho
title: Limpopo district hospital ‘filthy’, ‘broken’ and leaderless
content:
Filthy conditions, a shortage of warm water, a broken emergency communications system, and unresolved complaints from nurses are some of the adversities being faced by both patients and healthcare workers at Nkhensani hospital in Giyani, Limpopo.


The root cause


According to healthcare workers stationed at the hospital, the woes at the public facility are fuelled by a lack of leadership. For the past eight years, the hospital has not had a permanent CEO. Five individuals have, in ten years, acted as CEOs on a temporary basis but were never permanently appointed.


The Limpopo department of health has blamed a lack of suitable candidates as the main reason for not appointing a permanent CEO. The CEO position has been vacant since 2016 following the removal of Themba Mhlanga.


“We are leaderless at this hospital and everyone does what they want; hence everything is a mess at Nkhensani. I can confidently tell that at night, patients at this hospital bath using cold water as warm water gets finished in the early hours of the morning; and the kitchen does not operate during the night and those who want tea or coffee are always left wanting,” said a staff nurse stationed at Nkhensani hospital.


Lives of patients at risk


The nurse further said that the hospital is filthy and rarely cleaned: “This hospital is never cleaned, we often go for days without it being cleaned and no one cares and cleaners are also never reprimanded as there is no one to reprimand them and they do as they like. This puts the lives of patients and healthcare workers at risk.”


The emergency communications system has not been working for months at the hospital and nurses are forced to use their personal cell phones during emergencies. “Alerting doctors of emergencies at this hospital has become extra difficult as we have to use our own personal cell phones because the hospital does not have a working emergency dial; it has not been working for months. What if I do not have airtime and a patient is in need of a doctor urgently? It might lead to an avoidable death of a patient,” she said.


The nurse also told

Elitsha

 that she has personally raised most of these issues with previous acting CEOs but nothing has ever been done to address her concerns. “Even if you complain to those superior to you, nothing is ever done to address your concerns. No one is prepared to take responsibility and all this has got to do with the lack of leadership at Nkhensani hospital,” she said.


Derrick Mashaba, a local community member in Giyani residing about 2 kilometres away from Nkhensani, told

Elitsha

 that he has witnessed the tumble of the hospital over the past decade. “We have witnessed the fall of our precious hospital over the past ten years. We have seen overcrowding, dilapidating buildings, shortage of water and lack of leadership, and all this has contributed to the fall of the mighty hospital,” said Mashaba.


It hurts him to see the fall of the hospital which is so close to his home. “This is a district hospital and it is supposed to be the best in our region but it is not being prioritised. A hospital as big as this one cannot operate without a permanent CEO; it is wrong and it is something which is supposed to be addressed immediately,” he said.


Limpopo health spokesperson, Neil Shikwambana said that the department is working towards appointing a permanent CEO. “The recruitment process is underway and an acting CEO has been appointed to ensure continuity during this process,” he said.

author: Slingshot robot #1
title: Mental Health Reminders
content:
These are dark times. It is, in fact, the world that is crazy – despair and anxiety are natural responses to watching society destroy itself for the wealthy and powerful. But by reaching out to each other, we can find the courage to stay engaged with the world, to survive, and to fight back. Mental health and mental health crises vary a lot between people, and are often intertwined with class, race, gender, and activism. These suggestions are generic, but may be useful for yourself or others. If you find yourself or someone you love having delusional thinking or consider self-harm or other violence, these suggestions probably aren’t enough. Remember that it is okay to reach out for professional help!

• Our brains are connected to our bodies, so physical health can help with mental distress. Eating healthy food on a regular schedule and getting enough sleep are necessary for mental stability and sustained activism. Exercise, dance, and physical movement help, too. So can fresh air and having a stable, calming place to stay. Try to recognize if you’re missing one of these, and if that’s causing distress.

• An important component of mental health is the ability to know ourselves, understand our needs, and be able to talk about them to the other people in our lives. This can be really challenging and can often take guidance from others who have learned how to do it with one another.

• It can help to have language for mental crisis that feels comfortable and makes more sense than the dominant medical language. Transmission of language often happens in groups. Talk to friends about the different ways you can feel “off” and develop your own shorthand to describe them.

• Joining a mutual support group of peers listening to and helping peers as equals can be validating, while not necessarily endorsing your feelings. You can form one yourself or join an ongoing group.

• If possible, find a therapist or counselor who supports your self-determination. Ask about confidentiality if someone else — such as your parents, boss, or governmental program — is paying.

• Drugs and alcohol usually make mental health problems worse.

• Psychiatric drugs such as those for depression or bipolar disorder can help some people reduce distress and maintain stability, while other people with similar symptoms may experience distress or harm from the same drugs. Figuring out what works for you can be a process because people differ.

• Nature and wilderness can be our greatest healers. Spend some time outside the city to get centered. Get away from pollution, which is in itself mind-altering. Look up “Ecopsychology” to learn more.

• Allow social, political, and environmental crises unfolding around you to radicalize you, rather than driving you to despair. Actually articulate the world you would want to be living in; work towards it. Remember change happens collectively – look for ways to plug in. Small acts like talking to neighbors or submitting art to Slingshot can help you feel political agency between larger or more radical actions.

• Many communities have 24 hour a day crisis hotlines or crisis centers. Call 800-SUICIDE if you’re thinking about killing yourself or 800 646-HOPE to reach a rape crisis line for survivors of sexual violence. Warning: if you call and say you want to kill yourself police may arrive at your door.

• Things that can help your mental health day-to-day might not be as effective when you’re in crisis. Review the above reminders, and try to eat, exercise, journal, etc., but it’s okay if that isn’t helping.

• Distracting yourself from depressed or anxious thoughts can help: listening to music, making art, washing dishes, doing a project alone or with others. Embrace sensation: use your hands or massage your fingers. Hold onto an ice cube, or take a hot or cold shower. Give yourself time to gather resources.

• Some current emotional crises may be caused by traumas from the past, which may need to be emotionally and consciously processed in order not to keep recurring; that processing might take time.

• When in crisis, it may help to realize that the feeling will eventually pass and your life will begin to feel manageable and meaningful again later. Depression may feel like lack of feelings and a lack of connection to feeling. Anxiety may feel like rapidly cycling concern for what might happen. Both inhibit your ability to perceive and understand the world correctly. Your perceptions of hopelessness are NOT …

content:
