title: La transphobie de l'empire Křetínský avec l'association « Toutes des Femmes » dans Médias et antifascisme
content:
Texte d'annonce de l'épisode du vendredi 9 octobre 2026 de l'émission «

 

Médias et antifascisme

 

» diffusé tous les deuxièmes vendredis du mois sur la station Radio Libertaire (89.4

FM

 en Île-de-France et anarchiste.info/radio/libertaire).


Nous recevons vendredi 9 octobre prochain à 11h30 l'association «

 

Toutes des Femmes

 

» (

https://toutesdesfemmes.fr/

) pour évoquer notamment le colloque de «

 

l'Observatoire de la Petite Sirène

 

» le 16 octobre au Palais du Luxembourg à Paris :

https://www.observatoirepetitesirene.org/colloque-2026

. Il devait se tenir initialement le 22 juin dernier au Collège de France mais a été annulé par la direction de cet établissement.


La «

 

Haute-Commissaire à l'Enfance de la République

 

» Sarah El-Haïry devait d'ailleurs y participer. Cet événement est finalement rendu possible par la sénatrice Jacqueline Eustache-Brinio du parti «

 

Les Républicains

 

» qui chapeaute son déroulement.


Eustache-Brinio est de plus l'auteure de la proposition de loi sur la «

 

prise en charge des mineurs en questionnement de genre

 

». Cette loi est actuellement bloquée en commission des affaires sociales à l'Assemblée Nationale en attendant les recommandations à son sujet de la Haute Autorité de Santé (

HAS

) dont nous parlions dans notre épisode du 12 décembre dernier :

https://www.anarchiste.info/radio/libertaire/emission/medias-et-antifascisme/2025/12/12/

.


Ce climat nous préoccupe du fait par exemple de son instrumentalisation par le magazine hebdomadaire Marianne acheté en 2018 par le milliardaire tchèque Daniel Křetínský. L'empire Křetínský s'évertue en effet à s'acharner sur des associations comme le Planning Familial ou OUTrans.


Accusations d'islamisme, d'entrisme, de transgenrisme, de sécessionnisme, de séparatisme ou de radicalisme, tout est bon pour les dénoncer. L'une des toiles de fond de ces attaques est l'obligation pour Marianne de surmonter un redressement judiciaire comme nous l'abordons dans notre texte sorti dans le numéro 1885 du journal mensuel de la Fédération Anarchiste «

 

Le Monde Libertaire

 

» :

https://paris-luttes.info/l-institut-iliade-bollore-sterin-21023

.


Křetínský constitue d'autant plus un danger qu'il possède la Fnac et le groupe Editis qui comprend en tout 55 maisons d'édition. Il dirige aussi les «

 

médias

 

» Franc-Tireur et T18 dont nous pouvons dire qu'ils brillent autant par leur médiocrité que par leur vacuité.


Vous pouvez nous suggérer des thèmes à traiter, passer à l'antenne voire coanimer en nous écrivant via nos comptes Facebook et Bluesky «

title: AKP, Fatma Betül Sayan Kaya’ya kapıyı gösterdi
content:
AKP, fon soruşturmasında adı gündeme geldikten sonra Genel Başkan Yardımcılığı görevinden ayrılan eski Aile ve Sosyal Politikalar Bakanı Fatma Betül Sayan Kaya’yı partiden uzaklaştırdığını açıkladı. 


AKP Genel Sekreteri Eyyüp Kadir İnan, Kaya’nın artık parti üyesi ve mensubu olmadığını açıkladı. İnan, kararın parti yönetiminin iradesiyle alındığını da açıkça ortaya koydu:


“AK Parti olarak Cumhurbaşkanımızın talimatları doğrultusunda, yetkili kurullarımızın tespiti doğrultusunda zaten gereken işlemleri yaptık. Bugün Fatma Betül Hanım partimizin üyesi değildir, partimizin mensubu da değildir.”


İnan’ın açıklaması, Kaya’nın eşi İlyas Kaya ile birlikte aynı gün İstanbul Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığı’nda “şüpheli” sıfatıyla ifade vermesinden birkaç saat sonra geldi.


İhraç mı, zorunlu istifa mı?


AKP yönetimi, Kaya’nın parti üyeliğinin hangi usulle sona erdiğini açıklamadı.


İnan’ın “Cumhurbaşkanımızın talimatları” ve “gereken işlemleri yaptık” sözleri, ayrılığın Kaya’nın kendi tercihiyle gerçekleşmediğini gösteriyor. Ancak Kaya hakkında disiplin kurulu tarafından kesin çıkarma kararı verilip verilmediği ya da kendisinden üyelikten istifa etmesinin istenip istenmediği de kamuoyuna açıklanmadı. 


AKP’ye yakın Star gazetesi dahil çok sayıda yayın, gelişmeyi “Kaya AKP’den ihraç edildi” diye duyurdu. Star da haberini İnan’ın aynı açıklamasına dayandırdı; ayrıca bir disiplin kurulu kararına göndermede bulunmadı. 


Kaya’nın AKP üyeliğinin parti yönetiminin müdahalesinden sonra sona erdiği yönetim açısından netleşmiş görünse de, bunun AKP tüzüğünün ve disiplin yönetmeliğinin hangi hükmünün ihlali nedeniyle gerçekleştirildiği açık değil. 


11 gün önce yalnızca görevlerinden ayrılmıştı


Kaya 26 Eylül’de AKP’de yürüttüğü görevlerden “affını” istemişti.


Kaya açıklamasında, hakkındaki iddiaların araştırılması sırasında bulunduğu makamın tartışmaya konu edilmemesi gerektiğini söylemiş ve “yürütmekte olduğum tüm görevlerimden affımı Sayın Genel Başkanımızdan istedim” demişti. AA ve TRT de gelişmeyi “partideki tüm görevlerinden affını istedi” şeklinde duyurmuştu.


Böylece Kaya, 26 Eylül’de AKP yönetimindeki görevlerini bırakmasına rağmen parti üyesi olarak kalmıştı.


AKP Genel Sekreteri’nin 7 Ekim’deki açıklaması bu statünün de sona erdiği anlamına geliyor.


Önce TMSF’ye ödeme, ardından savcılık


Partinin Kaya’ya kapıyı göstermesine giden süreç son üç günde hızlandı.


Fatma Betül Sayan Kaya ile eşi İlyas Kaya’nın dondurulan hesaplarındaki yatırımlarının anapara dışındaki bölümünü, 5 Ekim’de Tasarruf Mevduatı Sigorta Fonu’nun (TMSF) “isteğe bağlı iade hesabına” gönderdikleri açıklandı.


İstanbul Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığı, SPK’nın “gönüllü ödeme” yöntemi kapsamında Kaya çiftinin yaptığı başvuru üzerine transferin gerçekleştirilmesine izin verdi. Kamuoyuna açıklanan bilgilerde ne kadar para iade edildiği belirtilmedi.


İki gün sonra Kaya ve eşi İstanbul Adliyesi’ne çağrıldı.


İstanbul Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığı Terörizmin Finansmanı ve Aklama Suçları Soruşturma Bürosu tarafından yürütülen sermaye piyasası soruşturması kapsamında Betül Kayan Saya ve eşi savcıya “şüpheli” sıfatıyla ifade verdi. Yaklaşık bir saat süren işlemlerin ardından Kaya çifti adliyeden ayrıldı.


Reuters da Adalet Bakanlığı kaynaklarına dayanarak Kaya ile eşinin soruşturmada şüpheli olarak yer aldığını ve Sermaye Piyasası Kurulu’nun (SPK) haklarında Sermaye Piyasası Kanunu kapsamında suç duyurusunda bulunmasının beklendiğini bildirdi.


AKP’nin siyasi mesafesi büyüdü


AKP Genel Sekreteri, Kaya’nın artık parti mensubu olmadığını duyurduktan sonra soruşturmayla ilgili siyasi değerlendirme yapmaktan da kaçındı:


“Geri kalan konu hukuki bir konudur, ona da yargı karar verir.”


(AEK)

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Trump Has Granted $6B in Contracts to Arms Makers His Sons Have Invested In
content:
Trump has previously said that his children have “inside information” about government actions.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Military contractors with investments from President Donald Trump’s sons have raked in billions of dollars in government deals and contracts since June 2025, when their venture capital company first obtained a major stake in military technology company Anduril, new reporting finds.

Last year, 1789 Capital, of which Donald Trump Jr. is a partner, invested $2.5 billion into Anduril. According to an analysis of the government’s public contracts by ABC, since then, Anduril has been awarded 135 contracts from the U.S. government, with $1.8 billion of it having been paid out thus far.

In all, military contractors with backing from Donald Trump Jr. or Eric Trump have gotten $6 billion in “active or promised government contracts,” the analysis found.

The Pentagon and a spokesperson for the two brothers denied any impropriety. “No company receives preferential treatment. The War Department always looks for solutions to benefit the warfighter, not any pre-selected entity. Outside affiliations, investors, or political connections play absolutely no role in the Department’s funding decisions,” a Pentagon official said.

However, ABC uncovered several instances in which companies were granted Pentagon contracts for the first time after Donald Trump Jr. or Eric Trump joined their teams.

A drone manufacturer named Unusual Machines was granted a contract for 3,500 motors, and potentially 20,000 more, in 2025, months after Donald Trump Jr. was named an adviser for the company. And another drone company, Powerus, got its first Pentagon contract just one month after the two brothers were listed as “notable investors” for the company in March 2026.

A Pentagon spokesperson defended the contracts, saying that “defense procurement is merit-based” and that “neither Donald Trump Jr. nor Eric Trump is an advisor to Powerus, and neither is involved in the company’s day-to-day business.”

“Their interest is indirect, held through American Ventures, an investor in the company,” the spokesperson told the outlet.

Previous reports have found instances of companies being granted large investments after receiving backing from 1789 Capital.

At an event in Maryland on Tuesday, Trump announced a new partnership with Anduril, billionaire Palmer Luckey’s autonomous military technology company, in its project to build a new shipyard called “Arsenal- 2.” The company will be providing a $3.7 billion investment into building the factory in Maryland, while the Navy will contribute $2.9 billion, he announced.

Bizarrely, Trump said that the public will be receiving “a 40 percent stake” in the shipyard, which he called “proof to our commitment to ensuring the shipyard’s enduring success.” It’s unclear what he meant by this, as the shipyard is being paid for by public money — and the $2.9 billion contributed by the Navy is actually more than 40 percent of the project’s $6.6 billion price tag.

At the event, Trump praised Luckey as a friend and a “brilliant guy.” Last week, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced that Luckey will help lead a new military task force called “Project Meridian,” which is tasked with shaping the future of warfare.

Democrats have previously launched efforts to probe potentially corrupt deals involving 1789 Capital’s investments. In August, Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Maryland), ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, opened an investigation into the firm, pointing out that it grew from managing $150 million in investment capital to over $3 billion since Donald Trump Jr. was named a partner just days after his dad was elected president.

“Whether government decisions and contracts are being manipulated to ensure that your firm and the President’s family get a cut of the action or your firm and the President’s family are being given advance insider information about those forthcoming decisions and contracts (or more likely both), these practices constitute clear violations of laws banning governmental conflicts of interest, political insider trading, exploitation of public office for financial gain and fraud,” Raskin said.

In July, Trump openly bragged that his status as the president gives his children access to “inside information.”

“Almost anything they do, if they want to buy a truck, if they want to buy, you …

author: Lilli Akpaleeapik
title: Boil water advisory issued for Taloyoak
content:
Nunavut’s Health Department issued a boil water advisory for Taloyoak due to the mechanical failure of a pump at the water treatment plant.


Any water used for consumption must be brought to a rolling boil for a minimum of one minute, either on the stove or with a kettle that does not have an automatic shut off, according to the advisory.


The advisory applies to water for drinking, preparing infant formulas, making juice or ice cubes, washing produce, cooking and brushing teeth.


Residents are also reminded that a camp stove should be used outdoors to avoid the risk of carbon monoxide poisoning.


The Health Department will notify community members when the boil advisory has been lifted.

title: Palestinian Arts Workers Call for Solidarity
content:
Palestinian cultural workers living through apartheid, occupation, and genocide are

calling for solidarity

 from their counterparts abroad.


Not every artist has as large a platform as rapper Macklemore, children’s TV star Miss Rachel, or country singer Zach Bryan—who wore a “Free Palestine” shirt last weekend while playing a packed show at the same stadium where billionaire Robert Kraft had barred Macklemore for saying those words—but there’s plenty that artists and art workers can do to end complicity in Israel’s ongoing atrocities.


We as Palestinians have long decried Israel’s war crimes and crimes against humanity. Now the

Palestinian Performing Arts Network

 (PPAN), representing hundreds of Palestinian dancers, actors, musicians, playwrights, and circus performers, has

outlined

 four ways that U.S. arts unions can lend solidarity:


1. Reject the blacklisting and censorship of members who speak out on behalf of Palestinian rights.


For example, British Actors’ Equity

passed a motion in the UK’s Trade Union Congress

, representing 5 million workers, affirming the right of artists to “critique institutions and bring attention to issues through overtly political art without fear of censorship or losing their public funding.”


In the U.S., over 700 entertainment industry union members signed a 2024

open letter calling on SAG-AFTRA

 to back a ceasefire, protect members from blacklisting, and condemn the targeting of journalists.


2. Refuse to work with institutions and corporations—such as venues, festivals, publishers, broadcasters, and foundations—that are verifiably complicit in Israel’s crimes against Palestinians, and divest union funds from such corporations.


In fall 2025, over 5,500 film industry workers

signed such a pledge

. Earlier that year, Norway’s actors union Norsk Skuespillerforbund (NSF)

recommended that its members

 “reject work and collaboration with Israeli cultural institutions that operate in violation of the Palestinian cultural boycott.”


3. Exclude Israel from international labor federations

title: Escuela Popular Campesina José Bengoa Cabello: Diez años sembrando educación popular desde Curaco de Vélez
content:
La Escuela Popular Campesina José Bengoa Cabello de Curaco de Vélez, Chiloé, celebró sus diez años de vida con dos jornadas que reunieron a estudiantes, profesoras y profesores, organizaciones sociales, artistas, artesanas y artesanos, voluntariado y comunidad, marcando además la inauguración oficial de esta nueva etapa que lleva el nombre de José Bengoa Cabello, manteniendo viva una memoria que no queremos solamente recordar, sino proyectar desde nuestros territorios.


El encuentro comenzó reuniendo a estudiantes y profesorado de la Escuela Popular Campesina José Bengoa Cabello de Curaco de Vélez (Chiloé) y de la Escuela Ismenia Ortiz Lizama de Palquibudis (Curicó), compartiendo una asamblea entre ambas experiencias campesinas, para continuar con Saberes del Mar, junto al profesor Constantino Contreras, y el conversatorio de Género y Ruralidad con Ximena Valdés, «porque hablar del mundo rural es también reconocer a las mujeres, sus trabajos, aquello que históricamente ha permanecido invisibilizado y las transformaciones que aún necesitamos impulsar», destacaron en la presentación.


Seguidamente, el 29 de agosto, el Gimnasio Bordemar de la Población Vista Hermosa de Curaco de Vélez acogió una extensa jornada. Desde la organización, se señaló: «Quisimos expresar aquello que somos y en lo que creemos, uniendo cultura, formación, organización y autogestión, con puestos de artesanía de nuestras ferias, organizaciones sociales, estudiantes, voluntariado y productos de ambas escuelas, haciendo posible que una parte importante de la actividad se financiara desde nuestro propio trabajo colectivo».


La organización del festival de la Escuela, también resaltó:

«Para nosotros la autonomía y la autogestión no son solamente principios escritos, son prácticas que se aprenden haciendo, compartiendo responsabilidades y poniendo cada cual algo de sí para sostener lo que hemos decidido construir en común».


Como señala Janett Cárdenas, esta trayectoria también nos invita a preguntarnos para qué educamos y desde dónde lo hacemos:


«Seguimos apostando a que la educación es una acción transformadora y una herramienta política que ponemos a disposición de quienes queremos transformar este modelo de injusticia, porque educarnos es también organizarnos, recuperar nuestra memoria y reconocernos en nuestros propios saberes, comprendiendo que desde el campo, el mar, las semillas, la artesanía, la cultura y la experiencia de quienes nos antecedieron se construye conocimiento para transformar nuestra realidad.»


La jornada permitió también reconocer a personas que han acompañado ese andar: Ximena Valdés, en memoria de José Bengoa; Sergio Faumangaun, director de la Escuela Campesina Águila Sur; la familia Gamin, en memoria de don Enrique Gamin; Mirian Alarcón, voluntaria y profesora de Agricultura Campesina desde el comienzo de este camino en 2016; y Patricio Larco, profesor de Acuicultura.


La cultura, inseparable de la manera de comprender la formación y la vida comunitaria, estuvo presente con Patricio Guerrero, Raíces Curacanas, Amaranto, Maribel Manquecoy, Javier Chandía, el bloque infantil integrado por Luis Soussi y Natali, Daniela Reyes, Aliwen, Nancy San Martín y su banda, Los Pirulonkos, Almas Chilotas y Rancheritos Vientos del Sur, quienes generosamente acompañaron esta celebración con música, voces y expresiones nacidas también desde nuestros territorios.


«Mirar estos diez años es reconocer que la Escuela ha podido sostenerse gracias a estudiantes, profesoras y profesores voluntarios, campesinas y campesinos, artistas, organizaciones y familias que han compartido conocimientos, trabajo, semillas, alimentos, música, tiempo y afectos, haciendo posible una experiencia que no pretende enseñar desde arriba, sino construir conocimiento desde aquello que cada una y cada uno sabe y aporta»

, señaló la declaración de la Escuela.


Agregan en su declaratoria:

«Cumplir una década no significa cerrar una historia, sino mirar lo caminado para continuar, ahora llevando el nombre de José Bengoa Cabello y recogiendo esa invitación a SER, HACER y PENSAR, desde Chiloé, desde nuestras insularidades y desde el mundo campesino, convencidos de que mientras existan saberes que compartir y comunidades dispuestas a organizarse, existirán también posibilidades de transformación»

.

author: Tareq S. Hajjaj
title: Children Born in Gaza Over Last 3 Years Have No Memory of World Before Genocide
content:
Israel’s genocide has narrowed Palestinian children’s expectations of life’s possibilities.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

When I left Gaza in 2024, after six months of living through genocide, I wanted one thing above all else: to spare my only child a life spent permanently at war. I did not want him to grow up believing that the whole world looked like Gaza.

But I left more than fifteen nieces and nephews behind. Many were still too young to understand the world they had been born into. They were learning what a home was, what a school was, what it meant to be alive, at the very moment those things were being destroyed around them.

I spent the next year and a half in Cairo. It took me a long time to learn how to inhabit ordinary life again. Whenever I saw a garden, a playground, a school, or children playing freely and safely in the street, I could not simply enjoy the sight. Gaza was always there, beneath it.

A garden brought back the rubble. A school brought back the children who no longer had one. Even safety became a reminder of those still denied it.

There was a comparison I could not stop making: why could children elsewhere grow up among their families and the people who loved them, while Gaza’s children remained trapped in this unending cycle of occupation, bombardment, destruction, genocide, and hunger? How could a child starve to death in a world with so much food?

I kept thinking about the children whose first understanding of life was taking shape inside the genocide. My niece, Elaf, was a year and a half old when I left. She was still at the beginning of everything.

Then her life changed entirely. A tent became her home. Missiles and bombs became the sounds she fell asleep to. Rubble shaped the landscape through which she was learning to see the world, and daily death shaped her first knowledge of life.

What could she know of the world beyond Gaza’s walls? What reason did she have to imagine that elsewhere, children slept without bombardment, lived in homes that stood, and went to schools built to shelter them?

I feared she would grow up believing that life in Gaza was simply life.

At first, I thought this was a danger facing mainly the youngest children: those born during the genocide, or too young to remember anything before it. But children who were two or three when it began, and are now five or six, are also learning to see the world as rubble upon rubble.

During a video call with my brother Osama, who has eight children, his six-year-old son, Muhammad, saw me sitting on a sofa in a brightly lit room.

“Uncle, how did your tent fit that sofa?” He asked. I did not know how to answer.

His question took me far from the room where I was sitting. Muhammad had lived in a beautiful home before the genocide. But now, when he looked at his uncle’s home, he was left wondering how such lavish furniture could fit into the only kind of home he had come to expect.

He had more questions. “Is your tent made of fabric pieces, or is it ready-made? Do you have a community kitchen that gives you food?”

These were simply the only frames of reference he had to try to understand my life, asking whether the arrangements that governed his own survival also governed mine. Shelter meant a tent. Food meant waiting for a meal to be distributed.

There was nothing strange about his questions. What was unbearable was how much sense they made within the life imposed on him.

The change reaches older children, too. My nieces, Amira and Heba, respectively 12 and 10, remember life before. Yet I can hear their expectations for ordinary life shrinking.

They no longer ask for much from a school. They hope it might be something more than tents pressed against one another: perhaps a wooden structure with a roof of corrugated steel sheets.

During one call with my brother, Amira sat beside him as we discussed my son starting school.

“Are your schools tents, or are they wooden?” she asked. Those were the possibilities she offered me. I asked what she liked about her own school.

“We leave our cramped tent and go to a bigger one,” she said. “We can play more freely. There is a little space where we can play.”

Her answer stayed with me. Even that small difference — being able to move from one cramped space to another slightly less cramped one — mattered.

author: infolibre
title: Υποχρεωτική η καθαρογραφή αθωωτικών αποφάσεων από το Εφετείο Αθηνών
content:
Όπως αναφέρει στο Δελτίο Τύπου που ακολουθεί ο Κώστας Παπαδάκης, μέλος του Δ.Σ. του Δ.Σ.Α. και εισηγητής του σχετικού αιτήματος, στην υποστήριξή του ενώπιον της Ολομέλειας του Εφετείου Αθηνών: “

Το επόμενο βήμα είναι να μην περιοριστεί μόνο στο Εφετείο Αθηνών αλλά να επεκταθεί σε όλα τα δικαστήρια και εν τέλει να νομοθετηθεί με ανάλογη τροποποίηση του άρθρου 142 παρ. 4 Κ.Ποιν.Δ, ώστε να είναι υποχρεωτική παντού η καθαρογραφή όλων των αθωωτικών αποφάσεων χωρίς καμμία προϋπόθεση..”

ου Υπουργού Δικαιοσύνης (επισυνάπτεται) έγινε δεκτή η γνώμη που περιλαμβάνεται στην υπ αριθμ. 1/2026 απόφαση της Ολομέλειας του Εφετείου Αθηνών σχετικά με την καθαρογραφή των αθωωτικών αποφάσεων.


Με την υπ. αριθμ. 61301οικ/30.9.2026 Απόφαση του Υπουργού Δικαιοσύνης (επισυνάπτεται) έγινε δεκτή η γνώμη που περιλαμβάνεται στην υπ αριθμ. 1/2026 απόφαση της Ολομέλειας του Εφετείου Αθηνών σχετικά με την καθαρογραφή των αθωωτικών αποφάσεων.


Η απόφαση είχε ληφθεί από την Ολομέλεια του Εφετείου Αθηνών στις 19.2.2026, όπου είχε κληθεί και παρέστη η αντιπροσωπεία του Δ.Σ. του Δ.Σ.Α. αποτελούμενη από τον πρόεδρό του κ. Ανδρέα Κουτσόλαμπρο και μέλη του Δ.Σ,. του, μεταξύ των οποίων και ο υπογράφων ως εισηγητής που ανέπτυξε τα σχετικά αιτήματα. Ενώ είχε προηγηθεί η διοργάνωση εκδήλωσης στις 11.2.2026 στα γραφεία του Δ.Σ.Α. στις για την προβολή του αιτήματος.


Το αίτημα είχε στηριχθεί πάνδημα από όλους τους δικηγορικούς φορείς και από τις Ενώσεις Ποινικολόγων και πολλά νομικά περιοδικά. Όχι ωστόσο από τις δικαστικές και εισαγγελικές ενώσεις.


Σύμφωνα με την παραπάνω Υ.Α. η καθαρογραφή των αθωωτικών αποφάσεων του Εφετείου Αθηνών καθίσταται η υποχρεωτική εφόσον το ζητήσει ο κατηγορούμενος εντός 6 μηνών από την έκδοση τους χωρίς να απαιτείται η επίκληση εννόμου συμφέροντος.


Ανεξάρτητα από την καθυστέρηση έκδοσής της Υ.Α. πρόκειται για μία μεγάλη νίκη που πιστώνεται σε όσους συνέβαλαν με κάθε τρόπο διότι άρχισε να αποκαθίσταται μια μεγάλη αδικία, της οποίας οι πτυχές έχουν αναλυθεί λεπτομερώς, αλλά και ένα έλλειμα δικαίου που είχε οδηγήσει στην εξαφάνιση της επιτυχούς υπερασπιστικής νομολογίας.


Το επόμενο βήμα είναι να μην περιοριστεί μόνο στο Εφετείο Αθηνών αλλά να επεκταθεί σε όλα τα δικαστήρια και εν τέλει να νομοθετηθεί με ανάλογη τροποποίηση του άρθρου 142 παρ. 4 Κ.Ποιν.Δ, ώστε να είναι υποχρεωτική παντού η καθαρογραφή όλων των αθωωτικών αποφάσεων χωρίς καμμία προϋπόθεση.


Με θερμές ευχαριστίες προς όσους/ες συνέβαλαν.


Αθήνα, 7.10.2026


Κώστας Παπαδάκης


Δικηγόρος, Μέλος του Δ.Σ. του Δ.Σ.Α.

author: Emran Feroz
title: The War on Afghanistan Was Launched 25 Years Ago. It Still Hasn’t Ended.
content:
The war inaugurated a terrible new global order in which armed drones kill civilians who are neither named nor counted.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

“There were nights full of terror. Our village was bombed constantly,” says Zalmay Khan. Afterward, he goes to pray. Because of his wounds, he cannot kneel, so he prays sitting down.

Khan is in his early twenties and now works as a Taliban intelligence officer. As a boy, he says, he learned to read the sky before he learned to read words. His village in Wardak province, near Kabul, was bombed, then bombed again. First came American planes, then NATO’s, then those of the Afghan army the West had built. By night it got worse, when jets and armed foreign contractors hit villages and killed civilians seemingly at random.

“I became a Mujahed [a Taliban fighter] naturally,” Khan tells me.

He is not an outlier. In village after village on my most recent trip to Afghanistan a few weeks ago, I met men who grew up as the so-called war on terror’s raw material. Some wear the Taliban’s turbans, and some do not. Almost all of them say the same thing, with remarkable calm: The American narrative of this war belongs to the past. After two decades of war and destruction, it is their turn to control narratives and to rule the country.

October 7, 2026, marks exactly 25 years since the United States began bombing Afghanistan. The anniversary will pass in Washington with little reflection. In Afghanistan, the reality of it is lived daily.

The war on terror made history in a way few people remember. In its opening weeks, the United States used an armed drone against a target in Afghanistan, one of the first such attacks ever, in an attempt to kill the Taliban’s founder, Mullah Mohammad Omar, in Kandahar. Omar was not hit on October 7, 2001. He survived and reportedly died of natural causes a decade later, which the Taliban kept secret for years.

Who died instead? The record offers almost nothing: no definitive or officially confirmed names, ages, villages. One news report cites unnamed Kandahar residents suggesting the raid killed Omar’s 10-year-old son and the child’s stepfather, but the Taliban’s ambassador to Pakistan declined to confirm or deny this report.

In other words, the first known attempt to kill a man with an armed drone killed people no one has ever definitively identified, and it set the template for the type of warfare that would dominate over the next decades. No one can say who the victims were. But if the pattern of the following years is any guide, many were likely civilians, like the thousands of victims who came after them. During the Obama years, Afghanistan officially became the world’s most drone-bombed country.

That template repeated itself so often that Afghans developed names for the many men who were declared dead after supposed “surgical strikes,” but who then reappeared alive: mord-e zinda (the living dead) in Farsi and khyali marr (the not truly dead) in Pashto. I call them “Taliban ghosts.”

It continued across successive U.S. administrations, even across the bureaucratic, supposedly methodical “kill lists” infamously used by the Obama administration used to mark people for death from the skies.

The first known attempt to kill a man with an armed drone killed people no one has ever definitively identified, and it set the template for the type of warfare that would dominate over the next decades.

The obvious question was almost never asked: If Omar was not the victim, who was killed instead? In the logic of the drone war, a body is a statistic, and a body in a targeted area becomes a militant by default. The dead were not counted, and the stories of their families, who were left to count for themselves, largely continued to go unknown.

Strikes did not only create ghosts. They also created recruits. Researchers, journalists, and Afghan elders have long described the same pattern: A village is hit, a family is destroyed, and the Taliban offer the survivors the only form of justice made available to them. By the end of the war, entire districts had made that choice, not out of ideological conviction but out of grief.

author: Charlotte Rene Woods
title: VA Ballot Measure Would Restore Formerly Incarcerated People’s Voting Rights
content:
The state permanently disenfranchises people with felony convictions unless pardoned or successfully petition one.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

Quadaire Patterson will vote for the first time this fall, a fact that brought a smile to his face on a recent afternoon as his 1-year-old daughter Trinity frolicked around the living room of the Henrico County home he shares with his wife.

He said he has been thinking about how future elections can shape Trinity’s future. But presently, he is eager to vote for a proposed amendment that could cement voting rights for formerly incarcerated people, like himself, into Virginia’s constitution.

Patterson, who was incarcerated at 19 years old after committing an armed robbery, served 16 years of a 20 year sentence before being released early in 2024 through a good behavior program.

He and wife Santia Nance joined other formerly incarcerated people and their families to advocate for the law change that allowed his early release. He has frequented the state capitol in the years since to lend insight to criminal justice legislation, despite being unable to vote for lawmakers himself.

That changed this summer when Gov. Abigail Spanberger restored his voting rights along with more than 60,000 formerly incarcerated Virginians. But the restoration process remains subjective; the amendment aims to make it a certainty.

“Voting rights have been deduced down to a privilege that can be handed out and restricted,” Patterson said. “This amendment restores it back to the people.”

Virginia’s current constitution permanently disenfranchises people with all felony convictions unless they are pardoned by a governor or successfully petition one.

Restorations trended downwards under former Gov. Glenn Youngkin. For years, it had been unclear which formerly incarcerated people would get their voting rights back, and the criteria guiding that decision was murky.

After trying unsuccessfully to pass the restoration amendment, lawmakers saw a new opportunity when Democrats gained majorities in the legislature in 2023 and tried again.

The current amendment had to pass the General Assembly two years in a row and will appear on statewide ballots this fall, where voters will approve or reject it.

Most Republican state lawmakers have consistently blocked the restoration amendment. Del. Mike Cherry, R-Colonial Heights, is an exception.

Cherry sponsored an earlier version of the amendment in 2022, which failed. And when the latest attempt advanced earlier this year, he joined his Democratic colleagues in voting for it.

He first offered adjustments that would have limited the measure’s scope: one to exclude people with violent offenses, and another mandating formerly incarcerated people pay restitution in full before getting their voting rights back.

Those efforts were unsuccessful.

In an interview with The Mercury, Cherry described his tweaks as a way “to bring some of my other colleagues along with me.”

This was in reference to GOP lawmakers who staunchly opposed restoring rights to people convicted of murder or manslaughter.

“That’s where (some of my Republican colleagues) fall on it. They want the victims to be restored,” Cherry explained. “They don’t like the fact that someone can get their rights back if they’ve disenfranchised someone else permanently.”

He said he understood their perspective but still supported the amendment, even without his proposed changes.

“If a judge didn’t give you a life sentence, we shouldn’t give you a life sentence as a society,” he said. “Once you’ve been adjudicated for your crime and you’ve served your time, then your right should be restored.”

Similarly, Patterson likened the state’s disenfranchisement to “this extra sentence that carries on.”

Other formerly incarcerated people released as part of the good behavior law have gone onto serve local government commissions, become peer recovery specialists, launch nonprofit organizations, or join lobbying and advocacy groups.

Nance, Patterson’s wife, said it’s important for those experiences to gain visibility, especially for those behind bars.

“I’m big on having our story reflect what potential there is for incarcerated people currently,” she said.

Patterson said the time he spent separated from society made him eager to not just rejoin it, but help shape it.
